Rust — The Complete Learning Path

A structured, project-driven course in Rust: the language, the toolchain, the ecosystem, and the things people actually ship with it.

Everything here is written to be read in order once, then used as a reference forever. Every module has runnable code, the errors you will actually hit, and the reasoning behind the design of the language.

Who this is for

You are Start at Skip
New to systems programming Module 01 nothing
Coming from Python / JS / Go Module 01, skim 02.01–02.02 —
Coming from C / C++ Module 02.03 (Ownership) 02.01, 02.02
Here to build a web service 01 → 02.03 → 02.11 → 04.02 04.06, 04.07
Here to build a CLI tool 01 → 02.03 → 03.01 → 04.01 —

No prior Rust needed. Comfort with any programming language is assumed.

How to use this material

Read with a terminal open. Type the examples; do not copy them. Rust's compiler is the best teacher in the ecosystem and it only teaches you when it rejects your code.

Do the exercises. Each module ends with a short set. They are small on purpose — the point is to force a compiler error you then have to reason about.

Read the errors. Rust error messages are unusually good: they name the problem, point at both locations involved, and frequently print the exact fix. Learning to read error[E0382] fluently is a real skill and it is worth more than memorising syntax.

Do not fight the borrow checker with clone(). When you hit a borrow error, the question is always "who should own this?" — not "how do I silence this?". clone() and Rc<RefCell<T>> are legitimate tools; using them to avoid thinking is how people end up writing slow Rust that feels like Java.

What Rust is good at, honestly

Genuinely excellent: CLI tools, network services, parsers and compilers, embedded firmware, WebAssembly, anything where you need C-level performance with memory safety, and anything that must run for months without leaking.

Good, with more work: game development (Bevy is young but real), GUI desktop apps (the ecosystem is fragmented), machine learning (use Python to train, Rust to serve), rapid prototyping (compile times and strictness slow you down early).

Not the tool: throwaway scripts, heavy data exploration, anything where the library ecosystem you need exists only in Python.

Conventions used here

  • Code blocks are labelled with a language: rust, toml, bash, sql, tsx.
  • $ at the start of a shell line means "run this in your terminal".
  • Bold lead-ins in blockquotes mark a gotcha, a rule of thumb, or a common trap.
  • Version numbers are the ones stable at the time of writing. Crate APIs move; the compiler and cargo doc are the final authority.
  • The capstone's code lives in capstone/ alongside this file.

01 · Install and Toolchain

Rust ships as a set of tools, not a single compiler. Understanding what each piece does saves you hours later.

The pieces

Tool What it is You use it for
rustup Toolchain installer and version manager Installing Rust, switching versions, adding targets
rustc The compiler Almost never called directly
cargo Build system + package manager + test runner Everything
rustfmt Auto-formatter cargo fmt
clippy Linter with ~750 checks cargo clippy
rust-analyzer Language server Editor autocomplete, inline errors
rustdoc Documentation generator cargo doc --open

You install rustup. rustup installs the rest.

Install

Linux / macOS:

$ curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

Windows: download and run rustup-init.exe. You will be asked to install the Visual Studio C++ Build Tools — accept it. Rust uses the system linker, and on Windows that means MSVC. (The x86_64-pc-windows-gnu target avoids this but causes more problems than it solves.)

Then, in a fresh shell:

$ rustc --version
rustc 1.85.0 (4d91de4e4 2025-02-17)

$ cargo --version
cargo 1.85.0

Gotcha: if cargo: command not found, your shell has not re-read its profile. Run source "$HOME/.cargo/env" or open a new terminal. On Windows this is almost always a PATH issue fixed by restarting the terminal.

What rustup actually manages

rustup keeps toolchains side by side and switches between them per project.

$ rustup show                    # active toolchain, installed targets
$ rustup update                  # update everything to latest stable
$ rustup toolchain list          # stable, beta, nightly, plus pinned versions
$ rustup toolchain install 1.75.0
$ rustup default stable
$ rustup component add clippy rustfmt
$ rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown

Channels

Channel Meaning Use for
stable Released every 6 weeks, guaranteed backwards compatible Everything production
beta Next stable, for testing Catching breakage early
nightly Daily, enables unstable features via #![feature(...)] Experiments, some tooling

Rule: use stable. Nightly is a research tool, not a default. The one common exception is cargo +nightly fmt for unstable formatting options, and cargo miri for undefined-behaviour checking.

Pin the toolchain per project

Create rust-toolchain.toml in the repo root:

[toolchain]
channel = "1.85.0"
components = ["rustfmt", "clippy"]
targets = ["x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"]

Now anyone who runs cargo build in that directory gets exactly 1.85.0 — rustup downloads it automatically. This is the single highest-value file in a Rust repo for reproducibility, and it costs six lines.

Editions

Editions let the language change syntax without breaking old code. A crate declares its edition in Cargo.toml; editions interoperate freely.

Edition Landed Headline change
2015 1.0 Original
2018 1.31 use paths, dyn Trait, NLL borrow checker
2021 1.56 Disjoint closure captures, IntoIterator for arrays, panic macros
2024 1.85 gen keyword, unsafe extern, RPIT lifetime capture, if let temporary scope

New projects: use edition = "2024" if your toolchain is 1.85+, otherwise "2021". There is no performance difference.

Rule of thumb: an edition is a syntax boundary, not an API boundary. Crates on different editions link together with no friction. Do not delay an upgrade for "compatibility" reasons.

Editor setup

VS Code — install the rust-analyzer extension. Disable any other Rust extension you have; two language servers fight each other.

Settings worth adding (.vscode/settings.json):

{
  "rust-analyzer.check.command": "clippy",
  "rust-analyzer.cargo.features": "all",
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "[rust]": { "editor.defaultFormatter": "rust-lang.rust-analyzer" }
}

check.command: clippy makes inline diagnostics come from Clippy instead of plain cargo check — you see lint warnings as you type, which is a large quality-of-life win.

Neovim / Emacs / Zed / JetBrains all speak LSP; point them at rust-analyzer. JetBrains has a dedicated Rust plugin (RustRover) with a debugger.

Debugging: lldb or gdb work with Rust. For a nicer experience install rust-gdb / rust-lldb (ships with rustup) which loads Rust pretty-printers so you can inspect String, Vec, HashMap as values instead of raw pointers.

Cargo's global directories

~/.cargo/bin/          # cargo, rustc, rustup, cargo-clippy, installed binaries
~/.cargo/registry/     # downloaded crate sources and index cache
~/.cargo/git/          # git dependencies
~/.rustup/toolchains/  # the actual compilers
target/                # per-project build artifacts (safe to delete)

Gotcha: target/ grows fast — 2–10 GB for a large workspace is normal. cargo clean reclaims it, but you lose all incremental state and the next build is a full rebuild. For space pressure use cargo-sweep to delete only artifacts older than N days.

Working offline

Cargo caches everything it downloads. To build without network:

$ cargo fetch          # populate the cache for the current project
$ cargo build --offline

For fully air-gapped builds, cargo vendor copies all dependency sources into vendor/ and a .cargo/config.toml points at them:

$ cargo vendor vendor/

Verifying a healthy install

$ rustc --version && cargo --version
$ cargo new /tmp/smoke && cd /tmp/smoke
$ cargo run
Hello, world!
$ cargo clippy -- -D warnings
$ cargo fmt --check

If all five succeed, you have a working Rust development environment.

Exercises

  1. Install Rust, then install the 1.75.0 toolchain alongside stable. Print both versions with rustup run 1.75.0 rustc --version.
  2. Add the wasm32-unknown-unknown target. Confirm it appears in rustup show.
  3. Create rust-toolchain.toml in a test project pinning 1.85.0, then run cargo build and watch rustup download it.
  4. Run cargo new --help and read the full flag list. What does --vcs none do, and when would you want it?

02 · Hello, Cargo — Your First Project

cargo is the reason Rust projects are pleasant to work in. It is a build system, dependency manager, test runner, doc generator and release tool, and it is the only one you need.

Create a project

$ cargo new hello
     Created binary (application) `hello` package
$ cd hello
$ tree
.
├── Cargo.toml
└── src
    └── main.rs

# Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "hello"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]

// src/main.rs
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}

$ cargo run
   Compiling hello v0.1.0 (/home/you/hello)
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.42s
     Running `target/debug/hello`
Hello, world!

That compile time is the entire crate. Your first real project will take longer because it compiles dependencies — once. Incremental builds after that are fast.

The five commands you will type forever

Command What it does When
cargo check Type-checks without producing a binary While writing code — 2–5× faster than build
cargo build Compiles to target/debug/ Before running
cargo run build then execute Iterating
cargo test Builds and runs tests Constantly
cargo build --release Optimised build to target/release/ Shipping, benchmarking

Rule of thumb: bind cargo check to a keyboard shortcut in your editor. You will run it hundreds of times a day. It skips code generation and linking, which is most of the time on incremental builds.

Debug vs release

dev (default) release
Optimisation opt-level = 0 opt-level = 3
Debug symbols yes no
Integer overflow panics wraps silently
debug_assert! runs compiled out
Speed 10–100× slower baseline 
$ cargo run --release
$ ./target/release/hello

Gotcha: integer overflow panics in debug and wraps in release. A test that passes in cargo test can behave differently in production. Use checked_add, saturating_add or wrapping_add when the boundary matters.

A real first program

Enough ceremony. Here is something with actual logic: a word-frequency counter, which touches files, HashMap, iterators and error handling.

use std::collections::HashMap;
use std::env;
use std::fs;
use std::process::ExitCode;

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    let path = match env::args().nth(1) {
        Some(p) => p,
        None => {
            eprintln!("usage: wordcount <FILE>");
            return ExitCode::from(2);
        }
    };

    let text = match fs::read_to_string(&path) {
        Ok(t) => t,
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("could not read {path}: {e}");
            return ExitCode::FAILURE;
        }
    };

    let mut counts: HashMap<&str, usize> = HashMap::new();
    for word in text.split_whitespace() {
        let word = word.trim_matches(|c: char| !c.is_alphanumeric());
        if word.is_empty() {
            continue;
        }
        *counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }

    let mut ranked: Vec<(&str, usize)> = counts.into_iter().collect();
    ranked.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1).then(a.0.cmp(b.0)));

    for (word, n) in ranked.iter().take(10) {
        println!("{n:>5}  {word}");
    }

    ExitCode::SUCCESS
}

$ cargo run -- Cargo.toml
    3  name
    1  dependencies
    ...

Things worth noticing, because each becomes a whole module later:

  • env::args().nth(1) returns Option<String> — no null, no exception.
  • fs::read_to_string returns Result<String, io::Error> — failure is a value.
  • counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) — the entry API, which avoids a double lookup.
  • &str keys borrowed from text — the map borrows instead of copying (module 02.03).
  • ExitCode instead of std::process::exit — destructors still run.
  • println!("{n:>5} {word}") — inline format args, right-aligned width 5.

Cargo.toml explained

[package]
name = "hello"                  # crate name; also the binary name
version = "0.1.0"               # semver, published to crates.io
edition = "2021"                # syntax generation
rust-version = "1.75"           # MSRV — minimum supported Rust version
description = "Counts words"    # shown on crates.io
license = "MIT OR Apache-2.0"   # dual license is the Rust norm
authors = ["You <you@example.com>"]
repository = "https://github.com/you/hello"

[dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
anyhow = "1.0.86"

[dev-dependencies]              # tests, benches, examples only
criterion = "0.5"

[build-dependencies]            # build.rs only
cc = "1"

[[bin]]                         # multiple binaries
name = "hello"
path = "src/main.rs"

[profile.release]
lto = "thin"
codegen-units = 1
strip = true

Version requirements are not exact versions

serde = "1"          # ^1  → >=1.0.0, <2.0.0
serde = "1.0.200"    # ^1.0.200 → >=1.0.200, <2.0.0
serde = "=1.0.200"   # exactly 1.0.200
serde = "~1.0.200"   # >=1.0.200, <1.1.0

Cargo picks the newest version satisfying all constraints in the graph and records the result in Cargo.lock. Commit Cargo.lock for binaries (reproducible builds) — it is optional for libraries but increasingly committed anyway.

Adding dependencies

$ cargo add serde --features derive
$ cargo add anyhow
$ cargo add tokio --features full
$ cargo add --dev criterion
$ cargo remove anyhow

cargo add resolves the latest compatible version, checks features exist, and writes the correct line. It is strictly better than hand-editing Cargo.toml.

Inspect what you actually got:

$ cargo tree                 # dependency tree
$ cargo tree -i serde        # who depends on serde (reverse)
$ cargo tree -d              # only duplicated crates
$ cargo tree --depth 1       # direct deps only

Gotcha: cargo tree -d showing a crate twice at different major versions is normal (rand 0.8 + rand 0.9) and mostly harmless. It becomes a problem when the type appears in your public API, because then your users cannot pass their version to you.

Your first library crate

$ cargo new --lib greet

// src/lib.rs
/// Returns a greeting for `name`.
///
/// # Examples
///
/// ```
/// assert_eq!(greet::greeting("Ada"), "Hello, Ada!");
/// ```
pub fn greeting(name: &str) -> String {
    format!("Hello, {name}!")
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn greets_by_name() {
        assert_eq!(greeting("Ada"), "Hello, Ada!");
    }
}

$ cargo test
running 1 test
test tests::greets_by_name ... ok

   Doc-tests greet
running 1 test
test src/lib.rs - greeting (line 6) ... ok

Two tests ran from one file: the unit test, and the doc test compiled from the example in the doc comment. That is why Rust docs do not rot — the examples in them are executed by CI.

cargo doc --open now renders greeting with that example inlined and runnable.

Exercises

  1. Extend the word counter: accept multiple files, aggregate counts across all of them, and skip words shorter than 3 characters.
  2. Add --top N support using env::args(). What happens with a non-numeric argument? Decide: panic or error message? Justify your choice.
  3. Make greet a library with a binary that uses it. You will need both src/lib.rs and src/main.rs in one package. Does use greet::greeting; work from main.rs? (It should.)
  4. Run cargo tree on any project. Find one crate that appears at two different versions and explain why.

03 · Project Layout and Workspaces

A Rust project's shape tells you a lot about its maturity. This module covers the layout that scales, and the workspace tooling that makes a multi-crate repo buildable in one command.

The canonical layout

myapp/
├── Cargo.toml
├── Cargo.lock
├── rust-toolchain.toml
├── README.md
├── .gitignore
├── .github/workflows/ci.yml
├── src/
│   ├── main.rs            # thin: parse args, call into lib, map errors
│   ├── lib.rs             # the actual logic — testable
│   ├── config.rs
│   ├── error.rs
│   └── handlers/
│       ├── mod.rs         # or handlers.rs
│       └── users.rs
├── tests/                 # integration tests: separate crates, public API only
│   └── api.rs
├── benches/
│   └── throughput.rs
├── examples/
│   └── quickstart.rs
├── migrations/            # sqlx migrations
└── assets/

Why lib.rs + main.rs

Put logic in lib.rs, keep main.rs to ~20 lines. Three benefits:

  1. Integration tests in tests/ can only import the library. If everything lives in main.rs, you cannot test it from tests/.
  2. examples/ can reuse it. Examples are tiny binaries that depend on your library.
  3. You can split the binary later — a second [[bin]] or a separate server crate — without moving code.
// src/lib.rs
pub mod config;
pub mod error;
pub mod handlers;

pub use error::{AppError, AppResult};

pub fn run(cfg: config::Config) -> AppResult<()> {
    // real work
    Ok(())
}

// src/main.rs
use std::process::ExitCode;

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    let cfg = match myapp::config::Config::from_env() {
        Ok(c) => c,
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("config error: {e}");
            return ExitCode::FAILURE;
        }
    };
    match myapp::run(cfg) {
        Ok(()) => ExitCode::SUCCESS,
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("fatal: {e:#}");
            ExitCode::FAILURE
        }
    }
}

Module files: foo.rs or foo/mod.rs?

Both work. Modern convention is foo.rs + foo/ side by side:

src/
├── handlers.rs          # declares submodules
└── handlers/
    ├── users.rs
    └── billing.rs

// src/handlers.rs
pub mod billing;
pub mod users;

mod.rs style still works and some codebases prefer it. Pick one per repo and be consistent — mixing both in one tree confuses rust-analyzer's file navigation.

.gitignore

/target
**/*.rs.bk
*.pdb
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

Cargo.lock is not ignored for binaries — commit it. For libraries it is optional; committing it is now common practice because it makes CI reproducible.

Workspaces: many crates, one build

Once you have a server, a CLI, a shared domain crate and a migration crate, you want one cargo build at the root and one shared target/ directory.

myapp/
├── Cargo.toml           # the workspace root — virtual manifest
├── crates/
│   ├── core/            # domain types, no I/O
│   │   ├── Cargo.toml
│   │   └── src/lib.rs
│   ├── api/             # HTTP layer
│   │   ├── Cargo.toml
│   │   └── src/main.rs
│   └── worker/          # background jobs
│       ├── Cargo.toml
│       └── src/main.rs
└── target/              # shared by every member

# ./Cargo.toml  — virtual manifest: no [package], only [workspace]
[workspace]
resolver = "2"
members = ["crates/core", "crates/api", "crates/worker"]

# Dependencies declared once, inherited by members — one place to bump versions
[workspace.dependencies]
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
sqlx = { version = "0.8", features = ["runtime-tokio", "postgres", "macros"] }
tracing = "0.1"
thiserror = "2"

[workspace.package]
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"
license = "MIT OR Apache-2.0"

# crates/api/Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "api"
version.workspace = true
edition.workspace = true
license.workspace = true

[dependencies]
core = { path = "../core" }
serde.workspace = true
tokio.workspace = true
tracing.workspace = true

# crates/core/Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "core"
version.workspace = true
edition.workspace = true

[dependencies]
serde.workspace = true
thiserror.workspace = true

Gotcha: version.workspace = true requires [workspace.package] to define version. Forgetting it gives error: failed to load manifest ... missing field. Also note that a workspace member's crate name is what you use — here the crate is literally called core, which shadows the std core crate name and causes confusing import errors. Name it domain or app-core instead.

Workspace commands

$ cargo build                    # all members
$ cargo build -p api             # one member
$ cargo test --workspace
$ cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
$ cargo run -p worker
$ cargo metadata --no-deps --format-version 1 | jq '.packages[].name'

Shared dev settings

[workspace.lints.rust]
unsafe_code = "warn"
missing_debug_implementations = "warn"

[workspace.lints.clippy]
all = { level = "warn", priority = -1 }
unwrap_used = "warn"

# each member
[lints]
workspace = true

Lint configuration at the workspace level means a new crate cannot accidentally be less strict than the rest. priority = -1 is needed so the group all does not override the individual lint that follows.

Splitting into crates: when?

Symptom Do this
cargo build takes 3+ minutes Split rarely-changed code into a crate; it stops recompiling
Two binaries share code Shared library crate
You want to unit-test without a DB core crate with no I/O dependencies
Compile-time feature flags differ per binary Separate crates
Just "for tidiness" Don't. Modules are free; crates cost compile time

Rule of thumb: start with modules. Split into crates when compile time or feature-flag isolation forces you to, not before. Each crate boundary is a real API you now have to maintain.

Feature flags: conditional compilation

[features]
default = ["json"]
json = ["dep:serde_json"]
postgres = ["sqlx/postgres"]
metrics = ["dep:prometheus"]

#[cfg(feature = "metrics")]
pub mod metrics;

#[cfg(feature = "postgres")]
pub fn pg_pool() -> sqlx::PgPool { /* ... */ }

$ cargo build --no-default-features --features postgres
$ cargo tree -e features -i serde   # why is serde enabled?

Gotcha: features are additive and unified across the whole graph. If any crate in the graph enables tokio/full, you get full. You cannot use a feature to remove something. Design features as "add capability", never "turn off the other thing".

Practical exercise: build the skeleton

$ cargo new --lib crates/domain
$ cargo new crates/api
$ cargo new crates/worker

Then write the root Cargo.toml as a virtual manifest, add version.workspace = true to each member, and confirm:

$ cargo build --workspace
$ cargo run -p api

Exercises

  1. Convert a single-crate project into a workspace with domain, api and worker members. Share serde and tokio via [workspace.dependencies].
  2. Add a metrics feature to domain that compiles a module only when enabled. Verify with cargo build -p domain --features metrics and cargo doc -p domain --no-default-features.
  3. Add [workspace.lints] forbidding unwrap_used. Fix the resulting warnings in a real function — this is a good preview of module 02.07.
  4. Add tests/ integration tests that use only the public API of domain. Confirm they cannot see private items.

01 · Variables, Types, Mutability

Rust's type system is strict and its inference is good. You write types where they document intent, and let inference handle the obvious cases.

Bindings

fn main() {
    let x = 5;            // immutable binding, inferred i32
    let mut y = 5;        // mutable binding
    y += 1;               // fine

    let x = x + 1;        // shadowing: a NEW x, type may change
    let x = "now a str";  // legal — same name, different type

    const MAX: u32 = 100_000;   // compile-time constant, needs a type
    static GREETING: &str = "hi"; // 'static lifetime, one memory location

    println!("{x} {y} {MAX} {GREETING}");
}

Immutable by default

let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
v.push(4);

error[E0596]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable, as it is not declared as mutable
 --> src/main.rs:3:5
  |
2 |     let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
  |         - help: consider changing this to be mutable: `mut v`
3 |     v.push(4);
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^ cannot borrow as mutable

This is not ceremony. Immutability by default means: when reading unfamiliar code you can assume most things do not change, and the compiler enforces it.

Shadowing vs mut

let x = 1; let x = x + 1; let mut x = 1; x += 1;
Type can change yes no
New memory location yes same
Usable inside closures while old value borrowed yes no
Value moved from the old binding possible n/a

Shadowing is idiomatic for transforming a value — parse a string, then re-bind as a number:

let input = "42";
let input: u32 = input.parse().expect("not a number");

const vs static

const LIMIT: usize = 1024;             // inlined at every use site
static VERSION: &str = env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"); // one address, may be mutable with unsafe

Use const by default. Use static when you need a stable address or a non-Copy shared value (usually wrapped in OnceLock / LazyLock).

use std::sync::LazyLock;
static CONFIG: LazyLock<Config> = LazyLock::new(|| Config::from_env());

Primitive types

Category Types Notes
Signed ints i8 i16 i32 i64 i128 isize i32 is the default
Unsigned u8 u16 u32 u64 u128 usize u8 for bytes, usize for indices/lengths
Floats f32 f64 f64 default; no Eq, no Hash
Bool bool 1 byte
Char char 4 bytes, a Unicode scalar value — not a byte
String slice &str borrowed UTF-8, &'static str for literals
String String owned, growable UTF-8
Unit () the type of "no value"
Never ! type of panic!, return, loop {}

Numeric literals

let a = 98_222;          // underscores for readability
let b = 0xff;            // hex
let c = 0o77;            // octal
let d = 0b1010_1010;     // binary
let e = b'A';            // byte literal, u8
let f = 6.022e23;        // float
let g: u8 = 255;

Integer literals default to i32 unless context forces otherwise. This compiles because context supplies the type:

let v: Vec<u64> = vec![1, 2, 3];   // literals are u64

Conversions are explicit

Rust never implicitly converts between numeric types.

let a: i32 = 10;
let b: i64 = a;              // error[E0308]: mismatched types
let b: i64 = a as i64;       // ok — explicit cast

let x: u8 = 300;             // error: literal out of range for `u8`
let y = 300u16 as u8;        // ok, truncates to 44 — silent!

as truncates and wraps silently. When that matters, use the checked family:

let big: u16 = 300;
assert_eq!(big.checked_add(65_000), None);
assert_eq!(big.saturating_add(65_000), u16::MAX);
assert_eq!(big.wrapping_add(65_000), 44);          // wraps around
assert_eq!(u8::try_from(300).is_err(), true);      // fallible, no silent loss

Rule of thumb: use as only for widening (u32 as u64, f32 as f64) or when you have proven the range. Use try_from for narrowing.

Integer overflow

Build a + b overflowing
debug panics: "attempt to add with overflow"
release wraps silently 
let mut n: u8 = 255;
n += 1;                    // panics in debug, becomes 0 in release

This is the classic "works on my machine" bug. If overflow is possible, be explicit: checked_*, saturating_*, wrapping_*.

Strings: &str vs String

The distinction trips up everyone. It is worth getting right early.

let literal: &'static str = "hello";     // in the binary, immutable, borrowed
let owned: String = String::from("hello"); // on the heap, growable, owned

let s: &str = &owned;                    // String derefs to &str — free
let o: String = literal.to_string();     // copy into a String — allocates
&str String
Ownership borrows owns
Growable no yes
Cost to pass pointer + length (16 bytes) move or borrow
Where it lives anywhere (stack, static, inside a String) heap

Rule of thumb: take &str in function parameters, return String when you must allocate.

fn greet(name: &str) -> String {          // accepts &String too, via deref coercion
    format!("Hello, {name}!")
}

fn shout(name: &str) -> &str {            // returning a borrow: lifetime elision ties it to input
    name
}

Strings are UTF-8, so indexing is not allowed

let s = "héllo";
let c = s[0];              // error[E0277]: the type `str` cannot be indexed by `{integer}`

s[0] is ambiguous: byte 0? char 0? They differ for any non-ASCII text. Use:

let chars: Vec<char> = s.chars().collect();
let first = s.chars().next();            // Option<char>
let bytes = s.as_bytes();                // &[u8], safe to index
let sliced = &s[0..1];                   // panics if 1 is not a char boundary
let safe = s.get(0..1);                  // Option<&str>

This is not a wart — it is the reason Rust programs do not mangle names in Kannada, Tamil, or any non-ASCII text.

Compound types

let tup: (i32, f64, char) = (500, 6.4, 'x');
let (a, b, c) = tup;            // destructure
let first = tup.0;              // or index

let arr: [i32; 3] = [1, 2, 3];  // fixed size, on the stack
let zeros = [0u8; 1024];        // 1 KB of zeros
let len = arr.len();            // 3, known at compile time

Arrays are fixed-length and stack-allocated. Vec<T> is the growable, heap-allocated version — module 02.06.

Type inference, and where it stops

let v = Vec::new();             // error: type annotations needed
let v: Vec<i32> = Vec::new();   // ok
let v = Vec::<i32>::new();      // ok — turbofish
let v: Vec<_> = (0..3).map(|i| i * 2).collect();  // `_` = "you infer it"

Inference works backwards from later use:

let mut v = Vec::new();
v.push(1u8);            // now v is Vec<u8> — inference succeeded

Debug vs Display

#[derive(Debug)]
struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

println!("{:?}", Point { x: 1, y: 2 });   // Point { x: 1, y: 2 }
println!("{:#?}", Point { x: 1, y: 2 });  // pretty-printed, multi-line
println!("{}", Point { x: 1, y: 2 });     // error: `Point` doesn't implement Display

Display must be implemented by hand because there is no correct default format for a user-facing message.

Mutability, precisely

let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];

let a = &v;          // shared borrow
let b = &v;          // another shared borrow — fine, many allowed
println!("{a:?} {b:?}");

let c = &mut v;      // error if `a` or `b` still used afterwards
c.push(4);

Mutability is a property of the binding and of the borrow, and the compiler tracks both. That is module 02.03.

A worked example

Parsing a small config line, using shadowing and explicit types:

fn parse_line(line: &str) -> Option<(String, u32)> {
    let (key, raw) = line.split_once('=')?;   // `?` on Option
    let key = key.trim().to_string();
    let value: u32 = raw.trim().parse().ok()?; // `.ok()?` converts Result to Option
    Some((key, value))
}

fn main() {
    assert_eq!(parse_line("port = 8080"), Some(("port".into(), 8080)));
    assert_eq!(parse_line("no equals sign"), None);
    assert_eq!(parse_line("port = abc"), None);

    let input = "  workers=4  ";
    let (k, v) = parse_line(input).unwrap();
    println!("{k} -> {v}");
}

Note how ? on Option inside a function returning Option propagates None without any match arms.

Exercises

  1. Write fn describe(n: i64) -> String that returns "zero", "negative" or "positive" — then try n: i128 and explain the change needed.
  2. Demonstrate overflow: a u8 counter incremented in a loop. Run it with cargo run and cargo run --release. Explain the two behaviours.
  3. Convert "300" to a u8 three ways: as, parse::<u8>(), and u8::try_from. Which succeed and which lose data?
  4. Write fn initials(full_name: &str) -> String that works correctly for "आदित्य शर्मा" and "Ada Lovelace". (Hint: chars(), not bytes.)
  5. Predict the type of let x = 0..10;. Check with let _: () = x; and read the compiler's error.

02 · Functions and Control Flow

Rust control flow is expression-oriented: if, match, and blocks all produce values. This removes a whole category of ceremony.

Functions

fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
    a + b          // last expression is the return value — no semicolon
}

fn early(x: i32) -> i32 {
    if x < 0 {
        return 0;  // explicit return exits early
    }
    x * 2
}

Gotcha: a trailing semicolon turns the expression into a statement returning (). fn f() -> i32 { a + b; } fails with error[E0308]: mismatched types and a note "expected i32, found ()". This is the single most common beginner error in Rust.

Everything is an expression

let x = if true { 1 } else { 2 };        // if is an expression

let y = match x {
    1 => "one",
    _ => "other",
};                                       // match is an expression

let z = {
    let a = 2;
    let b = 3;
    a * b                                // block is an expression
};

let () = ();                             // unit

All arms of an if-expression must have the same type:

let x = if cond { 1 } else { "two" };    // error[E0308]

Functions that never return

fn fatal(msg: &str) -> ! {          // `!` = never type
    eprintln!("{msg}");
    std::process::exit(1);
}

! coerces to any type, which is why panic!() works in a match arm that must produce i32.

if / else if / else

let temp = 38;
if temp > 40 {
    println!("scorching");
} else if temp > 30 {
    println!("hot");
} else {
    println!("fine");
}

No parentheses around the condition, braces always required (even for one line).

Loops

// loop — infinite, can return a value
let mut n = 0;
let found = loop {
    n += 1;
    if n * n > 100 { break n; }     // break with a value
};

// while
let mut i = 3;
while i > 0 {
    println!("{i}");
    i -= 1;
}

// for — the idiomatic one
for i in 0..3 { println!("{i}"); }          // 0,1,2  (exclusive)
for i in 0..=3 { println!("{i}"); }         // 0,1,2,3 (inclusive)
for item in &vec { println!("{item}"); }    // iterate by reference
for (idx, item) in vec.iter().enumerate() { }
for _ in 0..10 { }                          // `_` = ignore the value

for works on anything implementing IntoIterator. Prefer it over while with an index — it cannot go out of bounds and it is faster (no bounds checks).

Loop labels

'outer: for i in 0..5 {
    for j in 0..5 {
        if i * j == 6 {
            break 'outer;      // break the outer loop, not the inner
        }
        if j == 3 { continue 'outer; }
    }
}

Labels are 'name: before the loop, break 'name / continue 'name inside.

match

let n = 7;
match n {
    0 => println!("zero"),
    1 | 2 => println!("small"),        // or-pattern
    3..=9 => println!("medium"),       // range pattern
    x if x < 0 => println!("negative {x}"),  // guard
    other => println!("big {other}"),  // binding catch-all
}

match is exhaustive: the compiler proves every case is handled. Forgetting a variant of an enum is a compile error, which means adding a variant to an enum shows you every place that needs updating. This is the single biggest maintainability win in the language.

Matching structs and tuples

struct Point { x: i32, y: i32 }

let p = Point { x: 0, y: 5 };
match p {
    Point { x: 0, y: 0 } => println!("origin"),
    Point { x: 0, y } => println!("on y-axis at {y}"),
    Point { x, y: 0 } => println!("on x-axis at {x}"),
    Point { x, y } => println!("({x}, {y})"),
}

let pair = (1, "a");
match pair {
    (1, s) => println!("one and {s}"),
    (n, _) => println!("{n}"),
}

@ bindings and ref

match 42 {
    n @ 1..=50 => println!("in range: {n}"),   // bind AND test
    _ => {}
}

// match on a reference does not move: match ergonomics handle it
let s = Some(String::from("hi"));
match &s {
    Some(v) => println!("{v}"),   // v: &String
    None => {}
}

match on Option and Result

let maybe: Option<i32> = Some(3);
match maybe {
    Some(n) if n > 2 => println!("big {n}"),
    Some(_) => println!("small"),
    None => println!("nothing"),
}

if let and let else

When you only care about one pattern:

if let Some(user) = find_user(id) {
    println!("{}", user.name);
}

// let-else: bind or bail — great for early returns
let Some(user) = find_user(id) else {
    return Err(Error::NotFound);
};
println!("{}", user.name);

// while let: drain a stack
while let Some(top) = stack.pop() {
    println!("{top}");
}

Rule of thumb: use match when you handle two or more cases, if let for one case with a fall-through, and let else when the fall-through is an early return. let else is usually the cleanest for validation.

The ? operator

Propagates errors (or None) and is by far the most-used piece of control flow in real Rust.

use std::fs;
use std::io;

fn read_config() -> Result<String, io::Error> {
    let s = fs::read_to_string("config.toml")?;   // return early on Err
    Ok(s.trim().to_string())
}

fn maybe_parse(s: &str) -> Option<u32> {
    let n: u32 = s.parse().ok()?;                 // Result -> Option -> early None
    Some(n)
}

Full treatment in Error handling.

Recursion and stack depth

fn fib(n: u64) -> u64 {
    if n < 2 { return n; }
    fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)      // exponential — do not ship this
}

Rust has no guaranteed tail-call optimisation. Deep recursion overflows the stack (default 8 MB main thread, 2 MB spawned threads). For deep structures, write an explicit loop with a Vec stack, or use the stacker crate.

A worked example: a tiny expression evaluator

Control flow, match, recursion and Result in 40 lines.

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Token { Num(i64), Plus, Minus, Star, LParen, RParen }

fn tokenize(src: &str) -> Result<Vec<Token>, String> {
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    let mut chars = src.chars().peekable();
    while let Some(c) = chars.next() {
        match c {
            '0'..='9' => {
                let mut n = c.to_digit(10).unwrap() as i64;
                while let Some(d) = chars.peek().and_then(|c| c.to_digit(10)) {
                    n = n * 10 + d as i64;
                    chars.next();
                }
                out.push(Token::Num(n));
            }
            '+' => out.push(Token::Plus),
            '-' => out.push(Token::Minus),
            '*' => out.push(Token::Star),
            '(' => out.push(Token::LParen),
            ')' => out.push(Token::RParen),
            ' ' | '\t' => {}
            other => return Err(format!("unexpected character {other:?}")),
        }
    }
    Ok(out)
}

struct Parser { toks: Vec<Token>, pos: usize }

impl Parser {
    fn peek(&self) -> Option<&Token> { self.toks.get(self.pos) }

    fn expr(&mut self) -> Result<i64, String> {
        let mut lhs = self.term()?;
        while let Some(op) = self.peek() {
            match op {
                Token::Plus => { self.pos += 1; lhs += self.term()?; }
                Token::Minus => { self.pos += 1; lhs -= self.term()?; }
                _ => break,
            }
        }
        Ok(lhs)
    }

    fn term(&mut self) -> Result<i64, String> {
        let mut lhs = self.atom()?;
        while matches!(self.peek(), Some(Token::Star)) {
            self.pos += 1;
            lhs *= self.atom()?;
        }
        Ok(lhs)
    }

    fn atom(&mut self) -> Result<i64, String> {
        match self.peek() {
            Some(Token::Num(n)) => { let n = *n; self.pos += 1; Ok(n) }
            Some(Token::LParen) => {
                self.pos += 1;
                let v = self.expr()?;
                match self.peek() {
                    Some(Token::RParen) => { self.pos += 1; Ok(v) }
                    _ => Err("expected ')'".into()),
                }
            }
            other => Err(format!("unexpected token {other:?}")),
        }
    }
}

fn eval(src: &str) -> Result<i64, String> {
    let toks = tokenize(src)?;
    let mut p = Parser { toks, pos: 0 };
    let v = p.expr()?;
    if p.pos != p.toks.len() { return Err("trailing input".into()); }
    Ok(v)
}

fn main() {
    assert_eq!(eval("2 + 3 * 4"), Ok(14));
    assert_eq!(eval("(2 + 3) * 4"), Ok(20));
    assert!(eval("2 +").is_err());
    println!("{}", eval("10 * (2 - 1) + 5").unwrap());
}

Two subtleties worth noting:

  • matches!(self.peek(), Some(Token::Star)) avoids borrowing problems that a match on self.peek() inside a &mut self method would create.
  • let n = *n; self.pos += 1; copies the number out before mutating self, because the borrow from peek() is still alive.

Style notes that matter in review

// instead of this
if x == true { }

// write
if x { }

// instead of
if let Some(v) = o { return v } else { return 0 }

// write
o.unwrap_or(0)

Clippy catches most of these. Run it (module 03.04).

Exercises

  1. Write fn classify(n: i32) -> &'static str returning "negative", "zero", "small", "large" using a match with guards and ranges.
  2. Rewrite the evaluator to support / with division-by-zero returning an error instead of panicking.
  3. Add unary minus so -3 + 4 evaluates to 1.
  4. Write a loop that reads lines from stdin until the user types quit, accumulating a running total. Use break with a value to return the total.
  5. Convert a match with Some(x) => Some(f(x)), None => None into .map(f). Then convert a chain of if let into ?.

03 · Ownership, Borrowing, Lifetimes

This is the heart of Rust. Everything else in the language follows from these three rules. Read this module twice.

The three rules

  1. Every value has exactly one owner.
  2. There can only be one owner at a time.
  3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped (its destructor runs, its memory is freed).

That is it. Memory safety, no garbage collector, no use-after-free, no double free — all of it falls out of these three rules plus the borrow rules below.

Move semantics

fn main() {
    let s1 = String::from("hello");
    let s2 = s1;                 // ownership MOVES to s2

    println!("{s1}");            // error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s1`
    println!("{s2}");            // fine
}

error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s1`
 --> src/main.rs:5:15
  |
3 |     let s1 = String::from("hello");
  |         -- move occurs because `s1` has type `String`,
  |            which does not implement the `Copy` trait
4 |     let s2 = s1;
  |              -- value moved here
5 |     println!("{s1}");
  |               ^^^^ value borrowed here after move

In C++, let s2 = s1 would be a copy (or a move that leaves s1 "valid but unspecified"). In Rust the compiler tracks it and rejects use after move.

Copy vs move

Types that are cheap to duplicate implement Copy and are copied instead:

let a = 5;
let b = a;          // i32 is Copy — both valid
println!("{a} {b}");

let t = (1, 2.0, 'c');   // tuples of Copy types are Copy
let u = t;               // copied
Copy Not Copy
all integers, floats, bool, char String, Vec<T>, Box<T>
&T (shared references) &mut T
tuples/arrays of Copy types most structs by default 
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct Point { x: f64, y: f64 }   // now Point is copied, not moved

Rule of thumb: derive Copy only for small, plain-data types (≤ 4 words). A Copy struct containing a 1 KB array silently copies on every assignment, and you will not see it in the code.

Cloning is explicit

let s1 = String::from("hello");
let s2 = s1.clone();       // deep copy, allocates
println!("{s1} {s2}");     // both valid

Clone is visible at the call site. That is the point: allocation costs are never hidden.

Ownership and functions

Passing a value to a function moves it (unless it is Copy):

fn consume(s: String) {
    println!("{s}");
}   // s dropped here

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("hi");
    consume(s);
    consume(s);      // error[E0382]: use of moved value
}

Returning a value transfers ownership out:

fn make() -> String {
    String::from("new")
}
let s = make();      // we own it now

Borrowing

Moving everything in and out of functions would be unbearable. Instead, borrow:

fn length(s: &String) -> usize {   // & = shared reference
    s.len()
}

fn main() {
    let s = String::from("hello");
    let n = length(&s);      // lend it
    println!("{s} is {n}");  // still ours
}

The borrow rules

At any point in time, for a given value, you may have either:

  • any number of shared borrows (&T), or
  • exactly one mutable borrow (&mut T),

but never both at once. And references must always be valid (no dangling).

let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];

let a = &v;
let b = &v;              // ok — two shared borrows
println!("{a:?} {b:?}"); // last use of a, b

let c = &mut v;          // ok — a and b are no longer used
c.push(4);

Violating it:

let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
let a = &v;
let c = &mut v;          // error[E0502]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable
                         // because it is also borrowed as immutable
println!("{a:?}");
c.push(4);

Why this rule exists

It eliminates data races at compile time. A data race requires two threads accessing the same memory, at least one writing, without synchronisation. If a &mut T cannot coexist with any other reference, that situation cannot be expressed. Send/Sync (module 02.10) extend the same argument across threads.

Non-lexical lifetimes (NLL)

Borrows end at their last use, not at the end of the block:

let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
let a = &v;
println!("{a:?}");       // last use of `a` here
v.push(4);               // fine — the shared borrow already ended

This is why Rust code from 2015 looked so contorted and modern Rust does not.

&mut is not "mutable reference" in the C++ sense

&mut T means exclusive access. It is a guarantee to the compiler that nobody else can see this value, which is why the optimiser can do so much.

fn add_one(x: &mut i32) { *x += 1; }   // note the deref

let mut n = 5;
add_one(&mut n);
assert_eq!(n, 6);

Method receivers

struct Counter { n: u32 }

impl Counter {
    fn get(&self) -> u32 { self.n }              // shared borrow
    fn bump(&mut self) { self.n += 1; }          // exclusive borrow
    fn into_n(self) -> u32 { self.n }            // consumes
}

Pick the weakest receiver that works: &self unless you must mutate, self only when the type is a one-shot builder or converter.

Lifetimes

A lifetime is how long a reference is valid. You mostly do not write them — the compiler infers them via elision rules. You write them when the compiler cannot tell which input a returned reference came from.

The problem

fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {   // error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
    if a.len() > b.len() { a } else { b }
}

The compiler asks: the returned reference — is it tied to a or to b? It cannot know, so it refuses.

fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() > b.len() { a } else { b }
}

Read 'a as: "there is some region 'a such that both inputs live at least that long, and the output lives no longer than that." The returned reference is valid for the shorter of the two inputs.

let s1 = String::from("long string");
{
    let s2 = String::from("xy");
    let r = longest(&s1, &s2);
    println!("{r}");     // ok
}
// println!("{r}");      // error if r were still used here — s2 is gone

Elision rules

The compiler applies three rules, in order:

  1. Each elided input lifetime becomes its own parameter.
  2. If there is exactly one input lifetime, it is assigned to all elided outputs.
  3. If there is a &self or &mut self parameter, its lifetime is assigned to all elided outputs.
fn first_word(s: &str) -> &str          // rule 2 → &'a str
fn name(&self) -> &str                  // rule 3 → tied to self
fn pair(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str       // rules do not apply → error, must annotate

Lifetimes in structs

A struct holding a reference needs a lifetime parameter:

struct Excerpt<'a> {
    text: &'a str,
}

impl<'a> Excerpt<'a> {
    fn announce(&self, msg: &str) -> &str {
        // rule 3: returned ref tied to &self, not to msg
        self.text
    }
}

Rule of thumb: if you find yourself adding lifetimes to a struct, ask whether it should own the data (String instead of &str). Structs with lifetimes propagate that parameter into every type that uses them. For domain types, owning is almost always simpler.

'static

'static means "valid for the entire program". String literals are 'static. A 'static bound on a trait object or thread also means "contains no borrows":

let s: &'static str = "in the binary";
let v: Vec<Box<dyn std::error::Error + 'static>> = vec![];

Gotcha: 'static does not mean "leaked" or "lives forever in RAM". It means "no shorter lifetime could invalidate it". Box::leak gives you one, but so do all literals, and neither costs anything at runtime.

'_ and anonymous lifetimes

struct Parser<'a> { input: &'a str }
impl Parser<'_> { }        // "_ = infer the lifetime here"

Higher-ranked trait bounds (HRTB), briefly

When you accept a closure that takes a reference of any lifetime:

fn apply<F>(f: F) -> String
where
    F: for<'a> Fn(&'a str) -> String,   // for<'a> = HRTB
{
    f("hello")
}

You will meet for<'a> mostly in error messages about closures and Fn traits. It means "this works for every lifetime, not one particular one".

Common borrow-checker fights, and the real fix

1. Mutating while iterating

let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
for x in &v {
    if *x == 2 { v.push(4); }   // error[E0499]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable
}

Fixes, in order of preference:

// a) collect what to do, then do it
let to_add: Vec<i32> = v.iter().filter(|&&x| x == 2).map(|_| 4).collect();
v.extend(to_add);

// b) index-based, if you must mutate in place
for i in 0..v.len() {
    if v[i] == 2 { v[i] = 4; }
}

// c) retain / drain / split_at_mut for structural edits
v.retain(|&x| x != 2);

2. Returning a reference to a local

fn bad() -> &String {          // error[E0515]: returns a value referencing
    let s = String::from("x"); // data owned by the current function
    &s
}

Fix: return owned (String), or take the storage as a parameter (fn fill(buf: &mut String)).

3. Two &mut into the same Vec

let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4];
let (a, b) = v.split_at_mut(2);   // two disjoint &mut slices — legal
a[0] = 10;
b[0] = 30;

splice_at_mut, iter_mut, chunks_mut, split_at_mut exist precisely to express "two disjoint mutable pieces".

4. Self-referential structs

struct Bad {
    data: String,
    slice: &str,   // needs a lifetime; and it would point into `data`,
}                  // which moves when the struct moves

Do not build these. Options: store indices instead of slices, use owning_ref/yoke/self_cell, or restructure so the borrow is local.

5. Storing a borrow in a struct that outlives the source

Symptom: error[E0597]: does not live long enough. The fix is nearly always "make the struct own a String/Arc<str>".

Interior mutability: the escape hatch

When you need to mutate through a shared reference, use Cell/RefCell (single-threaded) or Mutex/RwLock/atomics (multi-threaded). The borrow rules are then checked at runtime instead of compile time. Details in Smart pointers.

A worked example: a text buffer with borrowed views

/// Splits a line into (key, value) without allocating.
fn split_kv(line: &str) -> Option<(&str, &str)> {
    let (k, v) = line.split_once('=')?;
    Some((k.trim(), v.trim()))
}

/// A view over a document: borrows, never copies.
struct Line<'a> {
    number: usize,
    text: &'a str,
}

fn lines_with<'a>(doc: &'a str, needle: &str) -> Vec<Line<'a>> {
    doc.lines()
        .enumerate()
        .filter(|(_, l)| l.contains(needle))
        .map(|(i, l)| Line { number: i + 1, text: l })
        .collect()
}

fn main() {
    let doc = "a=1\nb=2\n# note\nc=3";
    for l in lines_with(doc, "=") {
        let (k, v) = split_kv(l.text).unwrap();
        println!("line {}: {k} -> {v}", l.number);
    }
}

lines_with returns Vec<Line<'a>> where 'a is the lifetime of doc. The compiler proves the vector cannot outlive the document. Zero copies, zero allocation beyond the Vec itself.

Exercises

  1. Write fn longest_word(s: &str) -> &str. Why does this compile without an explicit lifetime? Which elision rule applies?
  2. Write fn first_of(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str returning whichever is non-empty. Add the lifetime annotation. Then call it where b is a temporary and observe the error.
  3. Explain why this fails, then fix it without cloning: rust let mut v = vec![String::from("a")]; let first = &v[0]; v.push(String::from("b")); println!("{first}");
  4. Write a struct WordIndex<'a> holding Vec<&'a str> of unique words. Then rewrite it to own Vec<String> and compare the API ergonomics.
  5. Implement fn split_twice(s: &mut Vec<i32>) -> (&mut [i32], &mut [i32]) using split_at_mut. Call it and mutate both halves.

04 · Structs, Enums, Pattern Matching

Rust has no classes and no inheritance. It has structs (data), enums (data that is one of several shapes), traits (shared behaviour, module 02.05) and composition. This combination is why Rust code tends to have small, obvious types.

Structs

Named fields

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct User {
    id: u64,
    email: String,
    active: bool,
}

let u = User {
    id: 1,
    email: String::from("a@example.com"),
    active: true,
};

println!("{}", u.email);      // field access

Field init shorthand and struct update

fn new_user(id: u64, email: String) -> User {
    User { id, email, active: true }    // `id` and `email` shorthand
}

let u2 = User { id: 2, ..u.clone() };   // remaining fields from u

..base moves non-Copy fields out of base. After that, base is partially moved and cannot be used as a whole.

Tuple structs

struct Meters(f64);
struct UserId(u64);

fn distance(a: Meters, b: Meters) -> Meters {
    Meters((a.0 - b.0).abs())
}

The newtype pattern: a one-field tuple struct that gives a distinct type to a primitive. It prevents passing a UserId where a u64 order id is expected, at zero runtime cost.

// newtype with validation — the "smart constructor"
struct Email(String);

impl Email {
    pub fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<Self, &'static str> {
        if s.contains('@') { Ok(Email(s.to_lowercase())) }
        else { Err("missing @") }
    }
    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &str { &self.0 }
}

Now any function taking Email is guaranteed a validated address. This is the single most valuable pattern in Rust application code.

Unit structs

struct Marker;               // no data, zero size

Used for type-state and as trait impl targets.

impl blocks

impl User {
    // associated function (no self) — the constructor convention
    pub fn new(id: u64, email: impl Into<String>) -> Self {
        Self { id, email: email.into(), active: true }
    }

    // method
    pub fn is_active(&self) -> bool { self.active }

    // mutating method
    pub fn deactivate(&mut self) { self.active = false; }

    // consuming method
    pub fn into_email(self) -> String { self.email }
}

Self is an alias for the type being implemented. impl Into<String> accepts both &str and String without a generic parameter at the call site.

Multiple impl blocks

Legal and useful: keep inherent methods separate from trait impls, or split by feature flag.

impl User { /* inherent */ }
impl std::fmt::Display for User { /* trait */ }

Builder pattern

Rust has no named/default arguments, so builders are the idiomatic answer for anything with more than ~4 fields.

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
pub struct ServerConfig {
    host: String,
    port: u16,
    workers: usize,
    tls: bool,
}

#[derive(Default)]
pub struct ServerConfigBuilder {
    inner: ServerConfig,
}

impl ServerConfigBuilder {
    pub fn host(mut self, host: impl Into<String>) -> Self {
        self.inner.host = host.into(); self
    }
    pub fn port(mut self, port: u16) -> Self {
        self.inner.port = port; self
    }
    pub fn workers(mut self, n: usize) -> Self {
        self.inner.workers = n; self
    }
    pub fn tls(mut self, on: bool) -> Self {
        self.inner.tls = on; self
    }
    pub fn build(self) -> Result<ServerConfig, String> {
        if self.inner.host.is_empty() { return Err("host required".into()); }
        Ok(self.inner)
    }
}

let cfg = ServerConfigBuilder::default()
    .host("0.0.0.0")
    .port(8080)
    .workers(4)
    .build()?;

Taking mut self and returning Self makes the chain work by value. The derive(Default) on the builder means every field has a sane starting point.

Gotcha: if the builder's build() validates, do not also offer Default on the built type — two ways to construct an invalid value defeats the point.

Enums

An enum is a type that is exactly one of a fixed set of variants, and each variant may carry data. This replaces the C "tag + union" pattern and makes illegal states unrepresentable.

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Shape {
    Circle { radius: f64 },
    Rect { w: f64, h: f64 },
    Triangle(f64, f64),        // tuple variant
    Empty,                     // unit variant
}

impl Shape {
    fn area(&self) -> f64 {
        match self {
            Shape::Circle { radius } => std::f64::consts::PI * radius * radius,
            Shape::Rect { w, h } => w * h,
            Shape::Triangle(b, h) => 0.5 * b * h,
            Shape::Empty => 0.0,
        }
    }
}

match self on &self binds radius: &f64 — match ergonomics dereference automatically. No * needed to read it.

Option<T> and Result<T, E> are ordinary enums

enum Option<T> { Some(T), None }
enum Result<T, E> { Ok(T), Err(E) }

There is no null in Rust. Option<T> costs nothing extra when T is a non-nullable pointer (Option<Box<T>> is pointer-sized), because the niche optimisation stores None in the null bit pattern.

Making illegal states unrepresentable

Before:

struct Connection {
    connected: bool,
    socket: Option<TcpStream>,
    last_error: Option<String>,
}   // 8 valid-looking combinations, 3 of them nonsense

After:

enum Connection {
    Connected(TcpStream),
    Disconnected { last_error: String },
    Connecting,
}

Now every combination is meaningful and match forces you to handle each.

Pattern matching in depth

let point = (3, -7);
match point {
    (0, 0) => println!("origin"),
    (x, 0) => println!("on x at {x}"),
    (0, y) => println!("on y at {y}"),
    (x, y) if x == y => println!("diagonal at {x}"),
    (x, y) => println!("({x}, {y})"),
}

Patterns everywhere

let (a, b) = (1, 2);                       // let
fn f((x, y): (i32, i32)) -> i32 { x + y }  // function parameters
for (i, v) in vec.iter().enumerate() { }   // for
if let Some(v) = o { }                     // if let
while let Some(v) = it.next() { }          // while let
let Some(v) = o else { return };           // let-else
match x { Some(v) => v, None => 0 }        // match

Pattern syntax reference

Pattern Matches
_ anything, binds nothing
x anything, binds to x
1 / 'a' / "s" a literal
1..=5 / 'a'..='z' a range (integers, chars)
A \| B either
Some(x) a variant, binding its payload
Point { x, y: 0 } a struct with a field pattern
Point { x, .. } a struct, ignoring the rest
[a, b, ..] a slice with at least two elements
(a, b) a tuple
ref x / &x bind by reference / destructure a reference
x @ 1..=9 bind and test
NAME a unit struct or const — not a new binding

Gotcha: a bare identifier in a pattern binds, it does not compare. This compiles and always matches: rust const MAX: i32 = 10; let MAX = 5; // new binding, shadows the const — warning match 7 { MAX => println!("ten"), _ => {} } // matches anything! Use a path (Self::MAX) or a literal to compare. Clippy warns about bindings_with_variant_name.

Destructuring with .. and nested patterns

struct Order { id: u64, items: Vec<Item>, total: f64 }

match order {
    Order { id, items, .. } if items.is_empty() => println!("{id} empty"),
    Order { total, .. } => println!("total {total}"),
}

matches! macro

if matches!(status, Status::Active | Status::Trial) { }

Much cleaner than if let ... { true } else { false }.

Methods on enums: the state machine pattern

#[derive(Debug)]
enum State { Idle, Running { since: u64 }, Failed(String) }

impl State {
    fn tick(self) -> State {
        match self {
            State::Idle => State::Running { since: 0 },
            State::Running { since } if since > 100 => State::Failed("timeout".into()),
            State::Running { since } => State::Running { since: since + 1 },
            s @ State::Failed(_) => s,
        }
    }
}

Taking self and returning State makes transitions explicit and total.

Default, From, TryFrom

#[derive(Default)]
struct Config { port: u16, debug: bool }

impl From<&str> for Meters {
    fn from(s: &str) -> Self { Meters(s.parse().unwrap_or(0.0)) }
}

impl TryFrom<i64> for Meters {
    type Error = &'static str;
    fn try_from(v: i64) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
        if v < 0 { Err("negative") } else { Ok(Meters(v as f64)) }
    }
}

From/TryFrom give you .into() / .try_into() for free, and they compose with generic APIs.

Debugging output

#[derive(Debug)]
#[debug("{id}")]
struct User { id: u64 }

{:?} is derived; {:#?} pretty-prints. For custom user-facing output, implement Display by hand:

impl std::fmt::Display for Shape {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        match self {
            Shape::Circle { radius } => write!(f, "circle r={radius}"),
            Shape::Rect { w, h } => write!(f, "rect {w}x{h}"),
            Shape::Triangle(b, h) => write!(f, "triangle b={b} h={h}"),
            Shape::Empty => write!(f, "empty"),
        }
    }
}

A worked example: a config parser with typed values

use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Value { Int(i64), Float(f64), Bool(bool), Text(String) }

#[derive(Debug, Default)]
struct Config(HashMap<String, Value>);

impl Config {
    fn parse(src: &str) -> Result<Self, String> {
        let mut map = HashMap::new();
        for (n, line) in src.lines().enumerate() {
            let line = line.trim();
            if line.is_empty() || line.starts_with('#') { continue; }
            let (k, v) = line.split_once('=')
                .ok_or_else(|| format!("line {}: missing '='", n + 1))?;
            let k = k.trim().to_string();
            let v = v.trim();
            let val = if let Ok(i) = v.parse::<i64>() {
                Value::Int(i)
            } else if let Ok(f) = v.parse::<f64>() {
                Value::Float(f)
            } else if v == "true" || v == "false" {
                Value::Bool(v == "true")
            } else {
                Value::Text(v.trim_matches('"').to_string())
            };
            map.insert(k, val);
        }
        Ok(Config(map))
    }

    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> Option<&Value> { self.0.get(key) }
}

fn main() {
    let cfg = Config::parse("port = 8080\nratio = 0.5\n# comment\ndebug = true\nname = \"api\"")
        .unwrap();
    assert_eq!(cfg.get("port"), Some(&Value::Int(8080)));
    assert_eq!(cfg.get("debug"), Some(&Value::Bool(true)));
    assert_eq!(cfg.get("name"), Some(&Value::Text("api".into())));
    println!("{cfg:#?}");
}

Exercises

  1. Add a Scale(f64) variant to Shape that scales every other shape. Decide whether Scale should be a variant or a method — justify it.
  2. Implement Email as a validated newtype and use it in a User struct. Confirm no code path can construct an invalid Email.
  3. Write fn classify(input: &str) -> Token with at least five variants including one carrying data, and a Display impl.
  4. Build a ServerConfigBuilder with a build() that rejects port 0. Add a test for the rejection.
  5. Rewrite this without match: rust let msg = match opt { Some(n) => format!("{n}"), None => "none".into() };

PreviousOwnership, Borrowing, LifetimesNextTraits and Generics

05 · Traits and Generics

Traits are Rust's answer to interfaces. Generics are its answer to templates. Together they give you polymorphism with zero runtime cost — but they also generate the error messages that Rust is famous for. This module teaches you to read them.

Defining a trait

trait Summary {
    fn summarize(&self) -> String;                 // required

    fn preview(&self) -> String {                  // provided, overridable
        format!("{}...", &self.summarize()[..10.min(self.summarize().len())])
    }
}

struct Article { title: String, body: String }

impl Summary for Article {
    fn summarize(&self) -> String {
        format!("{}: {}", self.title, self.body)
    }
}

A trait is a set of guarantees. Any function that takes impl Summary can rely on all of them and knows nothing else about the concrete type.

Generic functions

fn largest<T: PartialOrd + Copy>(list: &[T]) -> T {
    let mut max = list[0];
    for &item in list {
        if item > max { max = item; }
    }
    max
}

T: PartialOrd + Copy is a bound: T must support comparison and copying. Without it, item > max does not compile because the compiler cannot assume anything about T.

// equivalent, with a where clause — better for long bounds
fn largest<T>(list: &[T]) -> T
where
    T: PartialOrd + Copy,
{ /* ... */ }

Monomorphisation, and its cost

Generic functions are compiled once per concrete type. largest::<i32> and largest::<f64> are two separate functions in the binary. That is why generics are as fast as hand-written code, and why they increase binary size and compile time.

Use dyn Trait (below) instead when binary size or compile time dominates, or when the set of types is open.

impl Trait in argument position

fn notify(item: &impl Summary) {
    println!("{}", item.summarize());
}

Sugar for fn notify<T: Summary>(item: &T). Use it for one generic parameter; use explicit <T> when you need two parameters of the same type.

fn compare(a: &impl Summary, b: &impl Summary) { }        // may be different types
fn compare<T: Summary>(a: &T, b: &T) { }                  // must be the same type

impl Trait in return position

fn evens() -> impl Iterator<Item = u32> {
    (0..).filter(|n| n % 2 == 0).take(10)
}

The concrete type (Filter<Take<RangeFrom<u32>>, ...>) is unnameable, so impl Trait lets you return it without boxing. This is the standard way to return iterators and futures.

Trait objects: dyn Trait

fn render_all(items: &[Box<dyn Summary>]) {
    for item in items {
        println!("{}", item.summarize());
    }
}
impl Trait / <T: Trait> dyn Trait
Dispatch static (inlined, monomorphised) dynamic (vtable)
Cost per call zero one indirect call
Binary size grows per type one
Heterogeneous collections no yes
Compile time higher lower

Rule of thumb: generics by default; dyn when you need a collection of mixed types, a plugin boundary, or you are fighting compile time.

Object safety

Not every trait can become dyn Trait. A trait is object-safe only if it has no generic methods, no Self: Sized requirements, and no associated constants or methods returning Self.

trait NotObjectSafe {
    fn clone_me(&self) -> Self;     // returns Self → not object-safe
}

trait ObjectSafe {
    fn name(&self) -> &str;         // fine
}

Fix: add where Self: Sized to the offending method so it is excluded from the vtable.

Common standard traits

Trait Method Gives you
Clone .clone() explicit deep copy
Copy — implicit copy semantics
Debug {:?} developer output
Display {} user output
PartialEq / Eq == comparison (Eq = total equality)
PartialOrd / Ord <, .sort() ordering
Hash — usable as HashMap key
Default T::default() zero/empty value
From / Into .into() infallible conversion
TryFrom / TryInto .try_into() fallible conversion
AsRef / Borrow .as_ref() cheap re-interpretation
Iterator for, .map() iteration
Deref *x, auto-deref smart pointer behaviour
Drop — destructor
Send / Sync — thread safety markers

Deriving

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Default)]
struct Id(u64);

Derive is a procedural macro that writes the impl. For Hash + Eq pairs, both are needed for HashMap keys. Ord requires PartialOrd + Eq.

Implementing Display and Error

use std::fmt;

#[derive(Debug)]
struct ParseError { line: usize, msg: String }

impl fmt::Display for ParseError {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        write!(f, "line {}: {}", self.line, self.msg)
    }
}

impl std::error::Error for ParseError {}

Once Display + Debug + Error exist, the type works with ?, Box<dyn Error>, anyhow, thiserror, and every logging crate.

Supertraits

trait Repository: Send + Sync {
    fn get(&self, id: u64) -> Option<&Record>;
}

// any T: Repository is also Send + Sync
fn spawn_worker<R: Repository + 'static>(repo: R) { }

Send + Sync supertraits are the standard way to say "this abstraction is usable from async tasks".

Associated types vs generic parameters

trait Iterator {
    type Item;                       // associated type — ONE impl per type
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;
}

trait Add<Rhs = Self> {
    type Output;                     // generic parameter — MANY impls allowed
    fn add(self, rhs: Rhs) -> Self::Output;
}

Use an associated type when there is exactly one sensible choice per implementation (Item). Use a generic parameter when a type could sensibly implement it several ways (Add<i32> and Add<f64>).

Static dispatch across a plugin boundary

trait Storage {
    fn put(&self, key: &str, val: &[u8]) -> std::io::Result<()>;
    fn get(&self, key: &str) -> std::io::Result<Vec<u8>>;
}

struct Memory(HashMap<String, Vec<u8>>);
struct Disk { root: PathBuf }

impl Storage for Memory { /* ... */ }
impl Storage for Disk { /* ... */ }

// generic: zero-cost, one copy of the handler per storage type
fn save<S: Storage>(s: &S) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    s.put("k", b"v")
}

Trait objects at runtime: a plugin registry

trait Handler: Send + Sync {
    fn name(&self) -> &'static str;
    fn handle(&self, input: &str) -> String;
}

struct Registry { handlers: HashMap<&'static str, Box<dyn Handler>> }

impl Registry {
    fn new() -> Self { Self { handlers: HashMap::new() } }
    fn register(&mut self, h: impl Handler + 'static) {
        self.handlers.insert(h.name(), Box::new(h));
    }
    fn dispatch(&self, name: &str, input: &str) -> Option<String> {
        self.handlers.get(name).map(|h| h.handle(input))
    }
}

This is how routers, CLI subcommands and migration runners are structured internally.

Blanket implementations

trait Describe {
    fn describe(&self) -> String;
}

// anything that is Display gets Describe, for free
impl<T: std::fmt::Display> Describe for T {
    fn describe(&self) -> String { format!("value: {self}") }
}

Powerful and dangerous: a blanket impl blocks anyone else from implementing Describe for their own type. The standard library uses this for impl<T: Display> ToString for T.

Extension traits

Adding methods to a type you do not own:

trait StrExt {
    fn title_case(&self) -> String;
}

impl StrExt for str {
    fn title_case(&self) -> String {
        self.split_whitespace()
            .map(|w| {
                let mut c = w.chars();
                match c.next() {
                    Some(f) => f.to_uppercase().collect::<String>() + c.as_str(),
                    None => String::new(),
                }
            })
            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
            .join(" ")
    }
}

assert_eq!("hello world".title_case(), "Hello World");

This is how itertools, tower, axum and sqlx add ergonomics without touching upstream types.

Reading generic error messages

fn largest<T: PartialOrd>(list: &[T]) -> T { ... }

error[E0507]: cannot move out of index of `[T]`
  |
  |     let mut max = list[0];
  |                   ^^^^^^^ move occurs because value has type `T`,
  |                           which does not implement the `Copy` trait
help: consider borrowing here
  |
  |     let mut max = &list[0];

The fix is to add Copy (as we did) or to work with &T. Reading these messages: the help: block is usually the correct fix; the note: block explains why.

The Sized bound

fn by_value<T>(t: T) { }            // implicit T: Sized
fn by_ref<T: ?Sized>(t: &T) { }     // opt out — accepts str, [u8], dyn Trait

?Sized means "may not have a known size at compile time" — required for &str and dyn Trait parameters.

A worked example: a generic repository with a trait object fallback

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
struct User { id: u64, email: String }

trait Repo {
    type Error;
    fn find(&self, id: u64) -> Result<Option<User>, Self::Error>;
    fn save(&mut self, user: User) -> Result<(), Self::Error>;
}

struct InMemory { rows: Vec<User> }

impl Repo for InMemory {
    type Error = std::convert::Infallible;

    fn find(&self, id: u64) -> Result<Option<User>, Self::Error> {
        Ok(self.rows.iter().find(|u| u.id == id).cloned())
    }

    fn save(&mut self, user: User) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
        match self.rows.iter_mut().find(|u| u.id == user.id) {
            Some(existing) => *existing = user,
            None => self.rows.push(user),
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

// generic in, so it monomorphises per backend and inlines
fn upsert<R: Repo>(repo: &mut R, user: User) -> Result<(), R::Error> {
    repo.save(user)
}

fn main() {
    let mut repo = InMemory { rows: Vec::new() };
    upsert(&mut repo, User { id: 1, email: "a@x.com".into() }).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(repo.find(1).unwrap().unwrap().email, "a@x.com");
}

Exercises

  1. Write trait Area { fn area(&self) -> f64; }, implement it for three shapes, then write fn total(shapes: &[Box<dyn Area>]) -> f64.
  2. Convert total to a generic fn total<A: Area>(shapes: &[A]) -> f64. What can you no longer pass it, and why?
  3. Implement From<&str> for Meters and confirm "5".into() works.
  4. Write an extension trait VecExt adding .second() returning Option<&T>. Apply it to Vec<i32> and Vec<String>.
  5. Take a trait with a method returning Self and make it object-safe using where Self: Sized.
  6. Explain why impl<T: Display> MyTrait for T prevents you from also writing impl MyTrait for MyStruct.
