02 · The Library Tour

The crates that do the heavy lifting. Every entry states what it is for, the version line to add, and a snippet that compiles.

Serialisation

serde + serde_json

The universal (de)serialisation framework. Almost every other crate integrates with it.

serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct User {
    id: u64,
    email: String,
    #[serde(rename = "createdAt")]
    created_at: String,
    #[serde(default)]
    active: bool,
    #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    avatar: Option<String>,
}

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let json = r#"{"id":1,"email":"a@x.com","createdAt":"2026-01-01"}"#;
    let u: User = serde_json::from_str(json)?;
    println!("{}", serde_json::to_string_pretty(&u)?);
    Ok(())
}

Useful attributes: rename_all = "camelCase", tag = "type" (internally tagged enums), flatten (merge a nested struct), deny_unknown_fields, skip, with (custom module for a field).

Alternatives: rkyv (zero-copy, very fast), bincode/postcard (compact binary), toml, serde_yaml, quick-xml.

Async runtime

tokio

The default async runtime. Hyper, Axum, SQLx, reqwest and tonic all build on it.

tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt-multi-thread", "macros", "time", "sync", "net"] }

Alternatives: async-std (simpler, less used now), smol (tiny), embassy (embedded, no_std).

Web

axum

HTTP framework by the Tokio team. Built on tower, so every middleware is a tower layer. Ergonomic extractors, no macro DSL.

axum = "0.8"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }

use axum::{routing::get, Router, Json, extract::Path};
use serde::Serialize;

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Health { ok: bool }

async fn health() -> Json<Health> { Json(Health { ok: true }) }

async fn user(Path(id): Path<u64>) -> String { format!("user {id}") }

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/health", get(health))
        .route("/users/{id}", get(user));   // 0.8 uses {id}, not :id
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await.unwrap();
    axum::serve(listener, app).await.unwrap();
}
Framework Style Notes
axum extractors, tower default choice, huge ecosystem
actix-web actor-ish, macros very fast, older design
rocket macros, batteries included nice DX, slower release cadence
poem, warp, salvo variants niche

tower / tower-http

Middleware: timeouts, rate limits, compression, tracing, CORS, static files.

tower-http = { version = "0.6", features = ["trace", "cors", "compression-gzip"] }

use tower_http::{trace::TraceLayer, cors::CorsLayer, compression::CompressionLayer};

let app = Router::new()
    .route("/", get(|| async { "ok" }))
    .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http())
    .layer(CompressionLayer::new())
    .layer(CorsLayer::permissive());

reqwest

HTTP client, sync or async.

reqwest = { version = "0.12", features = ["json", "rustls-tls"] }

let resp = reqwest::Client::new()
    .get("https://api.github.com/repos/rust-lang/rust")
    .header("User-Agent", "my-app")
    .send()
    .await?
    .error_for_status()?
    .json::<serde_json::Value>()
    .await?;

Reuse one Client for the whole process — it owns the connection pool. Creating one per request destroys keep-alive and TLS session reuse.

Databases

sqlx

Async SQL with compile-time checked queries. No DSL, no hidden queries.

sqlx = { version = "0.8", features = ["runtime-tokio", "postgres", "macros", "chrono", "uuid", "migrate"] }

let user: Option<User> = sqlx::query_as::<_, User>("SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = $1")
    .bind(id)
    .fetch_optional(&pool)
    .await?;

With DATABASE_URL set at build time, sqlx::query_as! validates the SQL and infers types. Runtime-checked query_as needs no build-time DB.

Option Style Notes
sqlx async, raw SQL, checked best default
diesel sync, typed DSL, ORM excellent compile-time safety, no async
sea-orm async ORM on sqlx entity generation
rusqlite sync SQLite simple, embedded

CLI

clap

clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive", "env"] }

use clap::{Parser, Subcommand};

#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(name = "mytool", version, about = "Does useful things")]
struct Cli {
    /// Verbose logging
    #[arg(short, long, global = true)]
    verbose: bool,

    /// Config file
    #[arg(short, long, env = "MYTOOL_CONFIG", default_value = "mytool.toml")]
    config: String,

    #[command(subcommand)]
    cmd: Command,
}

#[derive(Subcommand, Debug)]
enum Command {
    /// Import a file
    Import {
        #[arg(value_name = "FILE")]
        path: std::path::PathBuf,
        #[arg(long, default_value_t = false)]
        dry_run: bool,
    },
    /// Print statistics
    Stats {
        #[arg(long, value_parser = clap::value_parser!(u32).range(1..=100))]
        top: u32,
    },
}

Free from the derive: --help, --version, shell completions (with clap_complete), validation and error messages.

Alternatives: argh (smaller), bpaf, lexopt (minimal, no deps).

Terminal output

anyhow = "1"
indicatif = "0.17"        # progress bars
console = "0.15"          # colours, terminal width
dialoguer = "0.11"        # interactive prompts
owo-colors = "4"          # simple colours

Errors and logging

thiserror = "2"           # libraries
anyhow = "1"              # applications
tracing = "0.1"           # structured logging
tracing-subscriber = { version = "0.3", features = ["env-filter", "json"] }

use tracing::{info, instrument, warn};

#[instrument(skip(pool), fields(user_id = id))]
async fn load(id: u64, pool: &sqlx::PgPool) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    info!("loading user");
    warn!(retries = 2, "retrying");
    Ok(())
}

tracing beats log because it carries structured fields and spans, which becomes real traces when you add tracing-opentelemetry.

Time and IDs

chrono = { version = "0.4", features = ["serde"] }     # datetime, timezone-aware
time = "0.3"                                            # alternative
uuid = { version = "1", features = ["v4", "serde"] }   # UUIDs
ulid = "1"                                              # sortable IDs

use chrono::{DateTime, Utc, Duration};
let now: DateTime<Utc> = Utc::now();
let later = now + Duration::hours(1);
let id = uuid::Uuid::new_v4();

Prefer Utc everywhere internally; convert at the edges.

Concurrency and parallelism

rayon = "1"                # data parallelism
crossbeam = "0.8"          # channels, scoped threads, lock-free structures
parking_lot = "0.12"       # faster Mutex/RwLock
dashmap = "6"              # concurrent HashMap
flume = "0.11"             # mpsc/MPMC channels

Data and text

regex = "1"
glob = "0.3"
walkdir = "2"
memchr = "2"
csv = "1"
quick-xml = "0.36"
polars = { version = "0.4x", features = ["lazy"] }   # dataframes
arrow = "5x"

Observability

prometheus = "0.13"
opentelemetry = "0.27"
opentelemetry-otlp = "0.27"
metrics = "0.24"

Validation and config

validator = { version = "0.19", features = ["derive"] }
config = "0.14"
dotenvy = "0.15"
figment = "0.10"

Testing

[dev-dependencies]
proptest = "1"
insta = "1"                # snapshot testing
mockall = "0.13"
wiremock = "0.6"           # mock HTTP servers
criterion = "0.5"
rstest = "0.23"            # fixtures and parametrised tests

Utilities you will reach for constantly

itertools = "0.13"         # extra iterator adapters
once_cell = "1"            # Lazy / OnceCell (std has LazyLock now)
indexmap = "2"             # insertion-ordered HashMap
smallvec = "1"             # inline small vectors
bytes = "1"                # cheap byte buffers (axum/tokio use it)
humantime = "2"            # parse/format durations
tempfile = "3"             # temp dirs in tests
rand = "0.8"

Picking a crate: a checklist

  1. Maintenance — commits in the last 6 months? Issues answered?
  2. Downloads — cargo add shows popularity; check the crates.io page.
  3. Dependency weight — cargo tree -p <crate> | wc -l. A 200-crate tree for a small job is a red flag.
  4. Unsafe usage — check cargo geiger; a parser with lots of unsafe deserves scrutiny.
  5. License — most Rust is MIT/Apache-2.0 dual. cargo deny checks this in CI (module 03.04).
  6. Bus factor — one maintainer with no releases for two years is a risk you are taking on.

Exercises

  1. Add serde with rename_all = "camelCase" and skip_serializing_if to a struct; verify with serde_json::to_string.
  2. Stand up a two-route Axum server and hit it with curl.
  3. Write a clap CLI with two subcommands and a --verbose global flag.
  4. Use sqlx against SQLite to insert and query one row.
  5. Replace a log-style println! with tracing::info! and add tracing-subscriber with EnvFilter.
  6. Run cargo tree -p regex | wc -l and cargo tree -p clap | wc -l. Compare dependency weight.

03 · Testing and Benchmarking

Rust's test story is unusually good: tests live in the same file, they are just functions, and the doc examples in your comments are tests too.

Unit tests

// src/lib.rs
pub fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }

pub fn divide(a: f64, b: f64) -> Result<f64, &'static str> {
    if b == 0.0 { Err("division by zero") } else { Ok(a / b) }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn adds() {
        assert_eq!(add(2, 2), 4);
    }

    #[test]
    fn divide_rejects_zero() {
        assert!(divide(1.0, 0.0).is_err());
    }

    #[test]
    #[should_panic(expected = "boom")]
    fn panics_with_message() {
        panic!("boom");
    }

    #[test]
    fn result_returning_test() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
        let v: i32 = "42".parse()?;      // `?` works in tests
        assert_eq!(v, 42);
        Ok(())
    }

    #[test]
    #[ignore = "requires a database"]
    fn needs_db() { }
}

#[cfg(test)] means the module is only compiled for cargo test, so it costs nothing in release builds. use super::* gives access to the parent module's items — including private ones, which is why unit tests can test internals.

Assertions

assert!(cond);
assert_eq!(a, b);                          // needs Debug + PartialEq
assert_ne!(a, b);
assert_eq!(a, b, "custom message: {a}");

// float comparison — never use ==
let (x, y) = (0.1 + 0.2, 0.3);
assert!((x - y).abs() < 1e-9);

// Option / Result helpers
assert!(result.is_ok());
assert_eq!(result.unwrap(), 5);
assert!(matches!(value, Some(1..=9)));

Integration tests

tests/ is a separate crate. It can only use your public API — which is exactly the check you want for a library.

// tests/api.rs
use mylib::{add, divide};

#[test]
fn public_api_works() {
    assert_eq!(add(1, 1), 2);
    assert!(divide(1.0, 0.0).is_err());
}

$ cargo test --test api       # one integration test file
$ cargo test --lib            # only unit tests

Shared helpers

tests/
├── common/
│   └── mod.rs        # NOT compiled as its own test binary
└── users.rs          # uses `mod common;`

// tests/users.rs
mod common;

#[tokio::test]
async fn creates_user() {
    let app = common::spawn_test_app().await;
    // ...
}

Any .rs file directly in tests/ becomes a test binary; a subdirectory does not.

Async tests

[dev-dependencies]
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }

#[tokio::test]
async fn fetches() {
    let v = async { 1 + 1 }.await;
    assert_eq!(v, 2);
}

#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 4)]
async fn concurrent() { }

Doc tests

/// Multiplies two numbers.
///
/// ```
/// use mylib::mul;
/// assert_eq!(mul(3, 4), 12);
/// ```
///
/// Failing examples can be marked:
///
/// ```should_panic
/// mylib::mul(1, 0);   // this does not panic — this block FAILS
/// ```
///
/// ```no_run
/// mylib::mul(1, 2);   // compiled but not executed
/// ```
///
/// ```ignore
/// // neither compiled nor run
/// ```
///
/// ```compile_fail
/// let x: i32 = "string";
/// ```
pub fn mul(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a * b }

Doc tests are why Rust's documentation is trustworthy: every example on docs.rs was executed on the author's machine.

Gotcha: doc tests link against your crate as an external user would, so they can only see public items. And they are slow to compile in bulk — cargo test --lib skips them when you are iterating fast.

Test organisation that scales

src/
├── lib.rs
├── domain/
│   ├── mod.rs
│   ├── user.rs          # #[cfg(test)] mod tests inline
│   └── order.rs
tests/
├── integration/
│   ├── mod.rs
│   ├── api_users.rs
│   └── api_orders.rs
└── e2e.rs
benches/
└── parse.rs

Rule: unit tests next to the code (they test internals), integration tests in tests/ (they test the API), end-to-end tests as a separate crate or a shell script against a running service.

Test doubles

Hand-written traits (preferred)

pub trait Clock: Send + Sync {
    fn now(&self) -> chrono::DateTime<chrono::Utc>;
}

pub struct SystemClock;
impl Clock for SystemClock {
    fn now(&self) -> chrono::DateTime<chrono::Utc> { chrono::Utc::now() }
}

#[cfg(test)]
pub struct FixedClock(pub chrono::DateTime<chrono::Utc>);
#[cfg(test)]
impl Clock for FixedClock {
    fn now(&self) -> chrono::DateTime<chrono::Utc> { self.0 }
}

Time, randomness, and I/O are the three things worth abstracting. Everything else can usually be tested directly.

mockall

mockall = "0.13"

#[cfg_attr(test, mockall::automock)]
pub trait Mailer {
    fn send(&self, to: &str, body: &str) -> Result<(), String>;
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use mockall::predicate::*;

    #[test]
    fn sends_welcome() {
        let mut m = MockMailer::new();
        m.expect_send()
            .with(eq("a@x.com"), contains("welcome"))
            .times(1)
            .returning(|_, _| Ok(()));
        notify(&m, "a@x.com");
    }
}

Property-based testing with proptest

Instead of one example, generate hundreds and shrink failures to a minimal case.

[dev-dependencies]
proptest = "1"

use proptest::prelude::*;

fn encode(s: &str) -> String { s.chars().map(|c| c as u32).map(|n| format!("{n:x}")).collect() }

proptest! {
    #[test]
    fn roundtrip(s in ".*") {
        let enc = encode(&s);
        let dec: String = enc.split('-').filter(|p| !p.is_empty())
            .map(|p| char::from_u32(u32::from_str_radix(p, 16).unwrap()).unwrap())
            .collect();
        prop_assert_eq!(dec, s);
    }

    #[test]
    fn sort_is_idempotent(mut v in prop::collection::vec(any::<i32>(), 0..100)) {
        v.sort();
        let once = v.clone();
        v.sort();
        prop_assert_eq!(v, once);
    }
}

The value is in the shrunk counter-example: instead of [1, 2, 3] you get the exact minimal input that breaks the invariant.

Snapshot testing with insta

[dev-dependencies]
insta = { version = "1", features = ["json"] }

#[test]
fn renders_report() {
    let report = build_report(&sample_data());
    insta::assert_json_snapshot!(report);
}

First run writes .snap.new files; cargo insta review shows a diff and lets you accept. Ideal for CLI output, HTML rendering, and JSON API responses.

Benchmarking with criterion

[dev-dependencies]
criterion = { version = "0.5", features = ["html_reports"] }

[[bench]]
name = "parse"
harness = false

// benches/parse.rs
use criterion::{black_box, criterion_group, criterion_main, Criterion, BenchmarkId};

fn parse_baseline(input: &str) -> usize { input.len() }

fn bench_parse(c: &mut Criterion) {
    let input = "a=1;b=2;c=3;".repeat(100);

    c.bench_function("baseline", |b| {
        b.iter(|| parse_baseline(black_box(&input)))
    });

    let mut group = c.benchmark_group("sizes");
    for size in [10, 100, 1000] {
        let data = "x".repeat(size);
        group.bench_with_input(BenchmarkId::from_parameter(size), &data, |b, d| {
            b.iter(|| parse_baseline(black_box(d)))
        });
    }
    group.finish();
}

criterion_group!(benches, bench_parse);
criterion_main!(benches);

$ cargo bench
$ cargo bench -- --save-baseline before
$ # make a change
$ cargo bench -- --baseline before

black_box stops the optimiser from constant-folding your benchmark into nothing. Criterion does statistical analysis, detects regressions, and writes HTML reports with plots to target/criterion/.

Gotcha: benchmarking a debug build measures nothing useful. Criterion uses the bench profile (release-like) automatically — but cargo run does not.

Running tests fast: cargo-nextest

$ cargo install cargo-nextest --locked
$ cargo nextest run
$ cargo nextest run --workspace --no-fail-fast

Nextest runs each test in its own process (so a segfault or a leaked global does not poison the suite), parallelises better than cargo test, and has a cleaner output format. On large suites it is 2–5× faster.

Coverage

$ cargo install cargo-llvm-cov
$ cargo llvm-cov --html --open
$ cargo llvm-cov --workspace --lcov --output-path lcov.info

Do not chase 100%. Aim for coverage of decision points — every match arm, every Err path — not every line.

A worked example: testing an HTTP handler

use axum::{routing::get, Router, Json};
use serde::Serialize;

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct Pong { pong: bool }

async fn ping() -> Json<Pong> { Json(Pong { pong: true }) }

pub fn app() -> Router { Router::new().route("/ping", get(ping)) }

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use axum::body::Body;
    use axum::http::{Request, StatusCode};
    use http_body_util::BodyExt;
    use tower::ServiceExt;          // for `oneshot`

    #[tokio::test]
    async fn ping_returns_pong() {
        let response = app()
            .oneshot(Request::builder().uri("/ping").body(Body::empty()).unwrap())
            .await
            .unwrap();

        assert_eq!(response.status(), StatusCode::OK);

        let body = response.into_body().collect().await.unwrap().to_bytes();
        let v: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_slice(&body).unwrap();
        assert_eq!(v["pong"], true);
    }
}

oneshot runs the router without binding a port. That is the fastest and most reliable way to test HTTP handlers.

CI gate

- run: cargo fmt --all -- --check
- run: cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
- run: cargo nextest run --workspace
- run: cargo test --doc --workspace

Exercises

  1. Add a unit test module to a module with a private helper, and assert on the private function directly.
  2. Write an integration test that uses only the public API, then make the function private and confirm it fails to compile.
  3. Write a doc test that is should_panic and one that is compile_fail.
  4. Introduce a Clock trait, implement SystemClock and FixedClock, and test a function that uses it.
  5. Write a proptest for fn reverse(s: &str) -> String asserting reverse(reverse(s)) == s.
  6. Benchmark two implementations of the same string parser with criterion and report the ratio.

Next: Tooling and CI

PreviousThe Library TourNextTooling and CI

04 · Tooling and CI

The Rust toolchain ships with the two tools that matter most (fmt, clippy), and the community has built excellent ones for everything else. This module is the "make it production-grade" checklist.

rustfmt — formatting

$ cargo fmt                  # format everything
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check # CI: fail if not formatted

rustfmt.toml — note that most options are nightly-only:

# rustfmt.toml  (stable options)
edition = "2021"
max_width = 100

# nightly-only — run with `cargo +nightly fmt`
imports_granularity = "Module"
group_imports = "StdExternalCrate"

Rule of thumb: do not fight rustfmt. Its default output is what every Rust developer reads fluently, and diff noise from manual formatting is a real cost in review.

clippy — the linter

$ cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
$ cargo clippy --fix --allow-dirty     # auto-apply machine-applicable lints

Clippy has ~750 lints in groups:

Group Meaning
correctness almost certainly a bug (on by default)
suspicious probably a bug
style idiomatic alternative
complexity needlessly convoluted
perf a faster way exists
pedantic stricter, sometimes noisy
nursery unstable, experimental
cargo manifest problems 
# Cargo.toml
[lints.clippy]
all = { level = "warn", priority = -1 }
pedantic = { level = "warn", priority = -1 }
module_name_repetitions = "allow"
must_use_candidate = "allow"
missing_errors_doc = "allow"

Start with all, add pedantic selectively. Enabling all of pedantic on a real codebase produces hundreds of module_name_repetitions warnings and people start ignoring clippy, which is the worst outcome.

Lints worth knowing by name

  • unwrap_used, expect_used — ban panics in library code
  • todo, unimplemented — never ship these
  • dbg_macro, print_stdout — ban debug output in a server
  • arithmetic_side_effects — catch overflow risks
  • cast_possible_truncation — catch lossy as
  • large_enum_variant — a variant 10× bigger than the others
  • redundant_clone — an unnecessary allocation

cargo-deny — supply chain policy

$ cargo install cargo-deny

# deny.toml
[advisories]
vulnerability = "deny"
unmaintained = "warn"

[licenses]
allow = ["MIT", "Apache-2.0", "BSD-3-Clause", "ISC", "Unicode-3.0"]

[bans]
multiple-versions = "warn"
deny = [
    { name = "openssl-sys" },   # force rustls instead
]

[sources]
unknown-registry = "deny"
unknown-git = "deny"

$ cargo deny check

This is the one CI step that stops a compromised or GPL-licensed dependency from reaching production.

cargo-audit — known vulnerabilities

$ cargo install cargo-audit
$ cargo audit
$ cargo audit --json

Reads the RustSec advisory database. Run it on a schedule in CI, not just on push — new CVEs appear for dependencies you did not change.

cargo-mutants — does your test suite actually test?

$ cargo install cargo-mutants
$ cargo mutants

It mutates your source (flips < to <=, replaces a return value) and checks whether a test fails. A surviving mutant is an untested behaviour. This finds the "tests that assert nothing" problem better than coverage does.

miri — undefined behaviour detection

$ rustup +nightly component add miri
$ cargo +nightly miri test

An interpreter for Rust's MIR that catches UB your tests would miss: out-of-bounds reads, use of uninitialised memory, data races, invalid unsafe. Slow — run it on the unsafe-heavy crates only.

cargo-geiger — unsafe usage audit

$ cargo install cargo-geiger
$ cargo geiger

Counts unsafe in your code and your dependency tree. Useful when evaluating a new crate.

cargo-semver-checks

$ cargo install cargo-semver-checks
$ cargo semver-checks check-release

Detects breaking changes in your public API that a version bump does not declare. Essential for a library.

cargo-release and cargo-dist

$ cargo install cargo-release
$ cargo release patch --execute

Bumps versions, tags, publishes, and pushes — across a workspace, in dependency order. cargo-dist generates cross-platform release binaries and installers (shell script, Homebrew formula, MSI) from a GitHub Actions workflow.

Editor and IDE

Tool Purpose
rust-analyzer LSP: completion, inline errors, refactors
CodeLLDB (VS Code) debugger
rust-gdb / rust-lldb pretty-printers for Vec, String
RustRover / IntelliJ Rust full IDE with refactoring

Worth enabling in settings.json:

{
  "rust-analyzer.check.command": "clippy",
  "rust-analyzer.cargo.allFeatures": true,
  "rust-analyzer.inlayHints.lifetimeElisionHints.enable": "skip_trivial",
  "rust-analyzer.inlayHints.closureReturnTypeHints.enable": "with_block"
}

Lifetime inlay hints are genuinely helpful while learning module 02.03.

A complete CI workflow

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request:

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always
  RUSTFLAGS: "-D warnings"

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
        ports: ["5432:5432"]
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s --health-retries 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with:
          components: rustfmt, clippy
      - uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@v2

      - name: Format
        run: cargo fmt --all -- --check

      - name: Clippy
        run: cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings

      - name: Test
        run: cargo nextest run --workspace
        env:
          DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost/test

      - name: Doc tests
        run: cargo test --doc --workspace

      - name: Security
        run: |
          cargo install cargo-audit cargo-deny --locked
          cargo audit
          cargo deny check

  msrv:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.75.0
      - run: cargo check --workspace

  cross:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        target: [x86_64-unknown-linux-musl, aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable
        with: { targets: "${{ matrix.target }}" }
      - run: cargo build --release --target ${{ matrix.target }}

Three jobs worth having that people skip: MSRV (proves your rust-version is honest), cross (proves the cfg blocks compile), and deny (supply chain).

Pre-commit hooks

$ cargo install cargo-husky

// in dev-dependencies
cargo-husky = { version = "1", default-features = false, features = ["precommit-hook", "run-cargo-fmt", "run-cargo-clippy"] }

Or with lefthook / pre-commit:

# lefthook.yml
pre-commit:
  commands:
    fmt:
      run: cargo fmt --all -- --check
    clippy:
      run: cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings

The order to fix things in

When you inherit a messy Rust repo, do this in order — each step makes the next cheaper:

  1. cargo fmt — one huge diff, then never again.
  2. cargo clippy --fix — automatic, safe.
  3. cargo clippy -D warnings in CI.
  4. cargo deny check in CI.
  5. cargo nextest for speed.
  6. Coverage or cargo-mutants to find untested code.
  7. cargo-audit on a schedule.

Exercises

  1. Add [lints.clippy] to a project with all = "warn" and unwrap_used = "warn", then fix the fallout.
  2. Run cargo clippy --fix on a project with a few style lints and review the diff before committing.
  3. Write a deny.toml that allows only MIT/Apache-2.0/BSD-3-Clause and bans duplicate major versions of any crate as an error.
  4. Run cargo audit and, if it reports anything, evaluate whether it applies to your usage.
  5. Add the three-job CI workflow above to a real repo and get it green.
  6. Explain why RUSTFLAGS: "-D warnings" in CI is both useful and dangerous.

PreviousTesting and BenchmarkingNextPerformance and Profiling

05 · Performance and Profiling

Rust is fast by default, but "fast by default" is not the same as "fast in your program". This module is about measuring first and changing second.

The rule

Never optimise without a measurement. Every section below assumes you have a profile or a benchmark in hand. Intuition about performance is wrong often enough that guessing is a waste of time.

Step 1: build for measurement

$ cargo build --release
$ cargo bench                      # criterion (module 03.03)

[profile.release]
debug = true        # keep symbols so profilers show function names

Then strip for the shipped binary (strip = "symbols" in a separate profile).

Step 2: profile

Linux: perf

$ perf record -g --call-graph dwarf ./target/release/myapp
$ perf report
$ perf stat ./target/release/myapp      # cache misses, branch misses, IPC

--call-graph dwarf needs debug = true and gives readable stacks.

Flame graphs

$ cargo install flamegraph
$ cargo flamegraph --bin myapp -- --args
# opens flamegraph.svg

Wide bars are where the time goes. Look for the widest leaf frame — that is actual work, not the call chain above it.

macOS: Instruments, samply

$ cargo install samply
$ samply record ./target/release/myapp

samply opens a Firefox Profiler UI with a timeline — better than flame graphs for async code, because it shows idle time separately.

Async profiling

Flame graphs of async code show the executor, not your tasks. For tokio, enable tokio-console:

tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full", "tracing"] }
console-subscriber = "0.4"

console_subscriber::init();

$ cargo install tokio-console
$ tokio-console

You get per-task poll counts, busy time, wakeups, and — most importantly — tasks that are blocked for a long time.

Step 3: the usual wins, in order

1. Algorithm and data structure

Nothing else competes. A HashMap lookup instead of a linear scan inside a loop is a 1000× win; no compiler flag comes close.

// O(n²) — 10,000 items = 100M comparisons
for a in &items { if other.contains(a) { } }

// O(n) with a HashSet
let set: HashSet<_> = other.iter().collect();
for a in &items { if set.contains(a) { } }

2. Allocations

Every String/Vec/format! allocates. In a hot loop this dominates.

// allocations: 1 per iteration
for row in rows { out.push(format!("{},{}", row.a, row.b)); }

// one allocation, reused buffer
use std::fmt::Write;
let mut buf = String::with_capacity(1024);
for row in rows {
    buf.clear();
    write!(buf, "{},{}", row.a, row.b).unwrap();
    out.push_str(&buf);
}

// pre-size collections you know the length of
let mut v = Vec::with_capacity(rows.len());
let mut m = HashMap::with_capacity(rows.len());

Consider SmallVec<[T; 8]> when most vectors stay small — it avoids the heap entirely for ≤ 8 items.

3. Cloning

// clones the whole struct per call
fn handle(user: User) -> String { user.name.clone() }

// borrows instead
fn handle(user: &User) -> &str { &user.name }

cargo clippy flags some of these with redundant_clone; the rest you find in a profile.

4. I/O buffering

// one syscall per line — 100× slower
let f = File::create("out.txt")?;
for line in lines { writeln!(f, "{line}")?; }

// buffered
use std::io::BufWriter;
let mut w = BufWriter::new(File::create("out.txt")?);
for line in lines { writeln!(w, "{line}")?; }
w.flush()?;

Same for reading: BufReader. For very large files, memmap2 avoids copying altogether.

5. Bounds checks

Iterators usually eliminate them:

// bounds check per iteration
let mut sum = 0;
for i in 0..v.len() { sum += v[i]; }

// no bounds check — the compiler proves the iterator stays in range
let sum: i64 = v.iter().sum();

When you genuinely need indexed access and have proven safety, get_unchecked in an unsafe block removes the check — but measure first; modern CPUs predict bounds checks almost perfectly and the win is often zero.

6. String building

// quadratic: reallocates and copies each time
let mut s = String::new();
for part in parts { s = s + part; }

// linear
let mut s = String::with_capacity(total_len);
for part in parts { s.push_str(part); }

7. Hashing

The default SipHash in HashMap is DoS-resistant and slow. For trusted, internal keys, ahash or rustc-hash is 2–3× faster:

ahash = "0.8"

use ahash::AHashMap;
let mut m: AHashMap<u64, String> = AHashMap::new();

Do not do this for a map keyed by untrusted input — you lose hash-flooding protection.

8. Vec growth patterns

// repeated removal from the front is O(n) each time
while !v.is_empty() { v.remove(0); }

// O(1)
let mut dq = std::collections::VecDeque::from(v);
while let Some(_) = dq.pop_front() { }

9. Compile flags

[profile.release]
lto = "fat"
codegen-units = 1
panic = "abort"

$ RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo build --release

target-cpu=native enables AVX2/AVX-512 and is worth 5–20% on numeric code — but the binary then may not run on older CPUs. In containers, build with an explicit target-cpu=x86-64-v3 instead.

10. Parallelism

After everything else, use rayon:

use rayon::prelude::*;
let total: u64 = data.par_iter().map(|x| heavy(x)).sum();

Only after the single-threaded version is tight. Parallelising a slow algorithm just makes it slow in parallel.

Reading perf stat

  1,234,567,890      cycles
    987,654,321      instructions     #  0.80  insn per cycle
     45,678,901      branches
      1,234,567      branch-misses    #  2.70% of all branches
     12,345,678      cache-misses     # 15.2% of all cache refs
  • IPC < 1.0 — usually memory-bound or branch-heavy, not compute-bound. Look at data layout.
  • High branch-misses — unpredictable branches. Sorting input first, or branchless code, helps.
  • High cache-misses — the working set does not fit in cache. Restructure to arrays of structs → struct of arrays.

Struct of arrays vs array of structs

// AoS — good for "process one entity at a time"
struct Particle { x: f32, y: f32, vx: f32, vy: f32 }
let particles: Vec<Particle>;

// SoA — good for "process one field across all entities"
struct Particles { x: Vec<f32>, y: Vec<f32>, vx: Vec<f32>, vy: Vec<f32> }

SoA vectorises: for x in &p.x { *x += 1.0 } is a clean SIMD loop. AoS forces gather/scatter. This is a 2–10× difference in numeric kernels.

Zero-cost abstractions: what is actually free

Free (compiled away):

  • iterators and closures (after inlining)
  • generics and monomorphisation
  • newtypes
  • Option<&T> (niche optimisation)
  • #[inline] on small functions

Not free:

  • dyn Trait dispatch (one indirect call, blocks inlining)
  • Box/Rc/Arc (allocation and counting)
  • format! (allocation)
  • RefCell (runtime borrow flag)
  • clone() (obvious, but easy to miss inside a chain)

A worked example: profiling a real bottleneck

Start with a slow function:

fn count_words(text: &str) -> HashMap<String, usize> {
    let mut m = HashMap::new();
    for w in text.split_whitespace() {
        *m.entry(w.to_string()).or_insert(0) += 1;   // allocates per word
    }
    m
}

Profile says: to_string and HashMap::entry dominate. Three changes:

fn count_words_fast(text: &str) -> HashMap<String, usize> {
    // 1. borrow instead of allocating — keys point into `text`
    let mut m: HashMap<&str, usize> = HashMap::with_capacity(256);
    for w in text.split_whitespace() {
        *m.entry(w).or_insert(0) += 1;              // no allocation
    }
    // 2. convert once at the end, if you need owned keys
    m.into_iter().map(|(k, v)| (k.to_string(), v)).collect()
}

Measured on a 10 MB corpus: ~4× faster, and the first version's allocation count (~1.2M) drops to ~30k (the final conversion only).

Benchmarks that lie

Trap Fix
Debug build Always --release / criterion
Optimiser removes the work black_box(input) and black_box(result)
One run, cold cache criterion runs many iterations and reports statistics
Unrealistic input Benchmark with production-sized, production-shaped data
Benchmarking the setup Hoist setup out of the timed closure
Comparing micro-opts with no profile Measure end-to-end first

Exercises

  1. Generate a flame graph for a program with an obvious hot loop. Identify the widest leaf frame.
  2. Take count_words and measure both versions with criterion. Report the ratio and the allocation count (use a counting allocator).
  3. Convert an AoS Vec<Particle> to SoA and benchmark a physics step.
  4. Run perf stat on a hot loop and report IPC. Is it compute- or memory-bound?
  5. Replace HashMap with AHashMap in a benchmark and measure the difference.
  6. Add BufWriter to a file-writing loop and measure the speedup on 1M lines.

PreviousTooling and CINextObservability: Logs, Metrics, Traces

06 · Observability: Logs, Metrics, Traces

A service you cannot see inside is a service you cannot operate. Rust's answer is tracing for structured events, metrics/prometheus for numbers, and OpenTelemetry for distributed traces.

Why tracing, not log

log gives you a string. tracing gives you an event with fields and a span context:

log::info!("user 42 loaded in 12ms");        // a string you must parse later
tracing::info!(user_id = 42, ms = 12, "user loaded");   // structured

Structured fields are what let you query "p99 latency by user_id" without regex-parsing logs.

Setup

tracing = "0.1"
tracing-subscriber = { version = "0.3", features = ["env-filter", "json", "time"] }

use tracing_subscriber::{fmt, prelude::*, EnvFilter};

pub fn init() {
    let filter = EnvFilter::try_from_default_env()
        .unwrap_or_else(|_| EnvFilter::new("info,my_app=debug,axum=info,sqlx=warn"));

    tracing_subscriber::registry()
        .with(filter)
        .with(fmt::layer().with_target(true).with_thread_ids(true))
        .init();
}

$ RUST_LOG=debug cargo run
$ RUST_LOG=my_app::db=trace,info cargo run

RUST_LOG filters by target (module path) and level. my_app::db=trace,info means "trace for that module, info for everything else".

JSON output in production

.with(fmt::layer().json().flatten_event(true))

One JSON object per line — what Loki, Elasticsearch and CloudWatch expect.

Levels

Level Use for
error something failed and a human must look
warn degraded but handled (retry, fallback, slow query)
info lifecycle events: started, connected, job finished
debug diagnostic detail, off in production
trace per-item detail, almost never on

Rule of thumb: if it fires per request, it is debug, not info. A service logging info! per request produces gigabytes a day and buries the events that matter.

Spans

A span is a unit of work with a start, an end, and fields. Events inside a span inherit its context.

use tracing::{info, instrument, warn};

#[instrument(skip(db), fields(order_id = %order.id))]
async fn process_order(order: Order, db: &PgPool) -> Result<()> {
    info!("validating");
    db.save(&order).await?;         // errors are recorded automatically
    info!(total = order.total, "processed");
    Ok(())
}

#[instrument] creates a span named after the function, records each argument as a field (use skip for anything not Debug or too large), and records the returned Err at ERROR level with the error's Display.

Manual spans:

let span = tracing::info_span!("batch", size = items.len());
let _guard = span.enter();          // or span.in_scope(|| { ... })

// async-safe: hold the guard across awaits with .instrument()
use tracing::Instrument;
async fn work() { }.instrument(tracing::info_span!("work")).await;

Gotcha: span.enter() returns a guard tied to the thread, not the task. In async code, holding it across an .await attributes the wrong events when the task migrates threads. Use .instrument(span) instead — it is correct by construction.

Metrics with metrics + Prometheus

metrics = "0.24"
metrics-exporter-prometheus = "0.16"

use metrics::{counter, gauge, histogram};

counter!("http_requests_total", "route" => "/users", "status" => "200").increment(1);
gauge!("queue_depth").set(42.0);
histogram!("http_request_duration_seconds").record(elapsed.as_secs_f64());

use metrics_exporter_prometheus::PrometheusBuilder;

let handle = PrometheusBuilder::new()
    .install_recorder()
    .expect("install prometheus recorder");

// axum: expose /metrics
let app = Router::new()
    .route("/metrics", get(move || async move { handle.render() }));

The four golden signals

Signal Metric
Latency histogram of request duration
Traffic counter of requests
Errors counter of responses by status
Saturation gauge of queue depth, pool usage, memory

If you instrument only four things, instrument these.

Naming conventions

http_requests_total{method,route,status}          counter — ends in _total
http_request_duration_seconds{route}              histogram — ends in _seconds
db_pool_connections_in_use                        gauge — no suffix

Never put an unbounded value (user id, request id, raw URL) in a label. That creates one time series per user and kills the metrics backend.

Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry

opentelemetry = "0.27"
opentelemetry-otlp = "0.27"
tracing-opentelemetry = "0.28"

use opentelemetry_otlp::WithExportConfig;

pub fn init_tracing() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let exporter = opentelemetry_otlp::SpanExporter::builder()
        .with_tonic()
        .with_endpoint("http://localhost:4317")
        .build()?;

    let provider = opentelemetry_sdk::trace::SdkTracerProvider::builder()
        .with_batch_exporter(exporter)
        .build();

    use opentelemetry::trace::TracerProvider;
    let tracer = provider.tracer("my_app");

    tracing_subscriber::registry()
        .with(tracing_opentelemetry::layer().with_tracer(tracer))
        .with(tracing_subscriber::fmt::layer())
        .init();
    Ok(())
}

Now every #[instrument] span becomes a span in Jaeger/Tempo/Honeycomb, and tracing propagates the trace context over HTTP if you add the header propagation layer.

Health and readiness endpoints

use axum::{routing::get, Router, Json, http::StatusCode};

async fn live() -> StatusCode { StatusCode::OK }

async fn ready(State(pool): State<PgPool>) -> (StatusCode, Json<serde_json::Value>) {
    match sqlx::query("SELECT 1").execute(&pool).await {
        Ok(_) => (StatusCode::OK, Json(serde_json::json!({"db": "ok"}))),
        Err(e) => {
            tracing::error!(error = %e, "readiness check failed");
            (StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, Json(serde_json::json!({"db": "down"})))
        }
    }
}

let app = Router::new()
    .route("/healthz", get(live))       // liveness: is the process alive?
    .route("/readyz", get(ready))       // readiness: can it serve traffic?
    .with_state(pool);

The distinction matters: a failing liveness probe restarts the pod; a failing readiness probe only removes it from the load balancer. Getting these backwards causes restart storms.

Panic and error reporting

sentry = "0.35"

let _guard = sentry::init(("https://key@sentry.io/1", sentry::ClientOptions {
    release: sentry::release_name!(),
    traces_sample_rate: 0.1,
    ..Default::default()
}));

For a Rust service, also install a panic hook that logs before unwinding:

std::panic::set_hook(Box::new(|info| {
    tracing::error!(panic = %info, "thread panicked");
}));

Structured logging in practice

#[instrument(skip(pool), fields(user.id = id))]
async fn load_user(id: u64, pool: &PgPool) -> anyhow::Result<User> {
    let user = sqlx::query_as::<_, User>("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1")
        .bind(id)
        .fetch_optional(pool)
        .await?
        .ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("user {id} not found"))?;

    tracing::info!(email = %user.email, "loaded user");
    Ok(user)
}

The JSON line this produces:

{"timestamp":"2026-11-25T10:12:33Z","level":"INFO","fields":{"message":"loaded user","email":"a@x.com","user.id":1},"target":"my_app::users","span":{"name":"load_user"}}

Everything you need to correlate, filter and alert on.

Checklist for a new service

  • [ ] tracing_subscriber initialised once, at startup, before anything else
  • [ ] RUST_LOG respected; default info
  • [ ] JSON output when LOG_FORMAT=json
  • [ ] #[instrument] on every handler and every DB/HTTP call boundary
  • [ ] /healthz (liveness) and /readyz (readiness)
  • [ ] /metrics with the four golden signals
  • [ ] Request-id propagation into logs and outbound calls
  • [ ] Panic hook that logs at error
  • [ ] No println! anywhere in library code (clippy print_stdout)

Exercises

  1. Replace every println! in a small service with tracing::info! and add an EnvFilter that turns on debug only for your crate.
  2. Add #[instrument] to a handler with one field skipped, and confirm the field appears in the JSON output.
  3. Expose /metrics with a request counter and a latency histogram; scrape it with curl.
  4. Add /healthz and /readyz, with readiness checking the database.
  5. Explain why span.enter() across an .await is a bug and show the .instrument() fix.
  6. Name three label values you must never use in a Prometheus metric, and why.

PreviousPerformance and ProfilingNextCommand-Line Tools

01 · Command-Line Tools

CLI tools are Rust's home turf: a single static binary, no runtime, startup in microseconds, and a dependency ecosystem built for exactly this.

The stack

[package]
name = "mytool"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"
rust-version = "1.75"

[dependencies]
clap = { version = "4", features = ["derive", "env", "wrap_help"] }
anyhow = "1"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
toml = "0.8"
indicatif = "0.17"
console = "0.15"
walkdir = "2"
regex = "1"
tracing = "0.1"
tracing-subscriber = { version = "0.3", features = ["env-filter"] }

[dev-dependencies]
assert_cmd = "2"
predicates = "3"
tempfile = "3"
Crate Role
clap argument parsing, help, completions
anyhow error reporting at the top level
indicatif progress bars
console colours, terminal width, spinners
assert_cmd + predicates end-to-end CLI testing
tempfile isolated test directories

Full example: a file search tool

// src/main.rs
use anyhow::{Context, Result};
use clap::{Parser, Subcommand, ValueEnum};
use std::path::PathBuf;
use std::process::ExitCode;
use walkdir::WalkDir;

#[derive(Parser, Debug)]
#[command(
    name = "findstr",
    version,
    about = "Search files for a pattern",
    long_about = None,
    arg_required_else_help = true
)]
struct Cli {
    /// Print more detail
    #[arg(short, long, global = true, action = clap::ArgAction::Count)]
    verbose: u8,

    /// Disable coloured output
    #[arg(long, global = true, env = "NO_COLOR")]
    no_color: bool,

    #[command(subcommand)]
    cmd: Command,
}

#[derive(Subcommand, Debug)]
enum Command {
    /// Search for a pattern in files
    Search {
        /// Regular expression
        pattern: String,

        /// Directory to search
        #[arg(default_value = ".")]
        dir: PathBuf,

        /// File extensions to include (repeatable)
        #[arg(short = 'e', long = "ext")]
        extensions: Vec<String>,

        /// Skip files larger than this many bytes
        #[arg(long, default_value_t = 10 * 1024 * 1024)]
        max_size: u64,

        /// Output format
        #[arg(long, value_enum, default_value_t = Format::Text)]
        format: Format,
    },
}

#[derive(ValueEnum, Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq)]
enum Format {
    Text,
    Json,
}

#[derive(serde::Serialize)]
struct Hit {
    path: String,
    line: usize,
    text: String,
}

fn main() -> ExitCode {
    let cli = Cli::parse();

    let level = match cli.verbose {
        0 => "warn",
        1 => "info",
        _ => "debug",
    };
    tracing_subscriber::fmt()
        .with_env_filter(level)
        .with_target(false)
        .without_time()
        .init();

    match run(cli) {
        Ok(found) if found == 0 => ExitCode::from(1),   // like grep: 1 = no match
        Ok(_) => ExitCode::SUCCESS,
        Err(e) => {
            eprintln!("error: {e:#}");
            ExitCode::from(2)
        }
    }
}

fn run(cli: Cli) -> Result<usize> {
    match cli.cmd {
        Command::Search { pattern, dir, extensions, max_size, format } => {
            let re = regex::Regex::new(&pattern)
                .with_context(|| format!("invalid regex `{pattern}`"))?;

            let mut hits = 0usize;
            let bar = indicatif::ProgressBar::new_spinner();
            bar.enable_steady_tick(std::time::Duration::from_millis(100));

            for entry in WalkDir::new(&dir)
                .follow_links(false)
                .into_iter()
                .filter_map(Result::ok)
                .filter(|e| e.file_type().is_file())
            {
                let path = entry.path();

                if !extensions.is_empty() {
                    let ok = path
                        .extension()
                        .and_then(|e| e.to_str())
                        .is_some_and(|e| extensions.iter().any(|x| x == e));
                    if !ok { continue; }
                }

                let meta = entry.metadata()?;
                if meta.len() > max_size { continue; }

                let Ok(text) = std::fs::read_to_string(path) else { continue };

                for (i, line) in text.lines().enumerate() {
                    if re.is_match(line) {
                        hits += 1;
                        match format {
                            Format::Text => {
                                println!("{}:{}: {}", path.display(), i + 1, line.trim());
                            }
                            Format::Json => {
                                let hit = Hit {
                                    path: path.display().to_string(),
                                    line: i + 1,
                                    text: line.trim().to_string(),
                                };
                                println!("{}", serde_json::to_string(&hit)?);
                            }
                        }
                    }
                }
            }

            bar.finish_and_clear();
            Ok(hits)
        }
    }
}

Note the exit codes: 0 found, 1 not found, 2 error. That is the convention every shell script and CI system expects, and getting it wrong breaks pipelines silently.

Argument parsing patterns

Env var fallback

#[arg(long, env = "MYTOOL_TOKEN", hide_env_values = true)]
token: Option<String>,

hide_env_values keeps secrets out of --help output and error messages.

Mutually exclusive flags

#[arg(long, conflicts_with = "json")]
yaml: bool,

Validation at parse time

#[arg(long, value_parser = clap::value_parser!(u16).range(1..=65535))]
port: u16,

Reading from stdin when no file is given

use std::io::{self, Read};

fn read_input(path: Option<PathBuf>) -> anyhow::Result<String> {
    match path {
        Some(p) => Ok(std::fs::read_to_string(p)?),
        None if !io::stdin().is_terminal() => {
            let mut s = String::new();
            io::stdin().read_to_string(&mut s)?;
            Ok(s)
        }
        None => anyhow::bail!("no input file and stdin is a terminal"),
    }
}

This is what makes a tool composable in a pipeline: cat x | mytool.

Shell completions

use clap::CommandFactory;
use clap_complete::{generate, Shell};

fn print_completions(shell: Shell, cmd: &mut clap::Command) {
    generate(shell, cmd, cmd.get_name().to_string(), &mut std::io::stdout());
}

$ mytool completions bash > /etc/bash_completion.d/mytool

Progress and output

use indicatif::{ProgressBar, ProgressStyle};

let bar = ProgressBar::new(files.len() as u64);
bar.set_style(
    ProgressStyle::with_template("{spinner:.green} [{bar:40.cyan/blue}] {pos}/{len} {msg}")
        .unwrap()
        .progress_chars("=>-"),
);
for f in &files {
    bar.set_message(f.display().to_string());
    process(f)?;
    bar.inc(1);
}
bar.finish_with_message("done");

use console::style;
println!("{} {}", style("ok").green().bold(), path.display());
println!("{} {}", style("error").red(), msg);

Gotcha: write progress to stderr and data to stdout. Otherwise mytool > out.json fills the file with progress bar escape codes.

Detect whether colour is appropriate:

use std::io::IsTerminal;
let colour = std::io::stdout().is_terminal() && std::env::var("NO_COLOR").is_err();

Respect the NO_COLOR convention — it is a real standard and users expect it.

Signal handling and clean shutdown

tokio = { version = "1", features = ["signal", "macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    tokio::select! {
        r = run() => r,
        _ = tokio::signal::ctrl_c() => {
            eprintln!("interrupted");
            Ok(())
        }
    }
}

For long-running work, write output atomically: write to out.tmp then fs::rename — a rename is atomic on POSIX, so a Ctrl-C never leaves a half-written file.

Testing a CLI

// tests/cli.rs
use assert_cmd::Command;
use predicates::prelude::*;

#[test]
fn prints_help() {
    Command::cargo_bin("mytool").unwrap()
        .arg("--help")
        .assert()
        .success()
        .stdout(predicate::str::contains("Search files"));
}

#[test]
fn exits_1_when_no_match() {
    let dir = tempfile::tempdir().unwrap();
    std::fs::write(dir.path().join("a.txt"), "hello").unwrap();

    Command::cargo_bin("mytool").unwrap()
        .args(["search", "zzz", dir.path().to_str().unwrap()])
        .assert()
        .code(1);
}

#[test]
fn finds_a_match() {
    let dir = tempfile::tempdir().unwrap();
    std::fs::write(dir.path().join("a.txt"), "hello world").unwrap();

    Command::cargo_bin("mytool").unwrap()
        .args(["search", "world", dir.path().to_str().unwrap()])
        .assert()
        .success()
        .stdout(predicate::str::contains("hello world"));
}

assert_cmd runs the real binary — the only way to test exit codes, stdout and stderr together.

Distribution

# static Linux binary that runs anywhere
$ cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl

# Homebrew tap
$ cargo install --path .

# crates.io
$ cargo publish

For cross-platform releases, cargo-dist generates the GitHub Actions workflow and installers:

$ cargo install cargo-dist
$ cargo dist init
$ cargo dist build

Real-world Rust CLIs worth reading

Tool Why read it
ripgrep the benchmark for fast, correct CLI design
fd simple, excellent clap usage
bat output formatting and terminal handling
hyperfine benchmarking with good UX
zoxide shell integration done well
starship performance under a strict startup budget

Exercises

  1. Build the findstr tool above and add a --count flag that prints only the number of matches.
  2. Add --json output that emits one array instead of JSONL. Which is better for jq? For streaming?
  3. Make it respect .gitignore using the ignore crate (the one ripgrep uses).
  4. Add a progress bar on stderr and verify mytool > out.txt produces clean output.
  5. Add a --exclude glob flag and tests for it with assert_cmd.
  6. Add Ctrl-C handling that leaves no partial output file.

PreviousObservability: Logs, Metrics, TracesNextWeb APIs with Axum

02 · Web APIs with Axum

Axum is the default choice for new Rust services: built on hyper and tower, maintained by the Tokio team, and free of macro DSLs.

Why Axum

  • Extractors instead of macros — a handler is a plain async fn whose arguments are typed requests.
  • tower middleware — the same layer works on any tower service, so timeouts, retries and load balancing compose.
  • No hidden magic — no #[get("/x")] attributes, no global router.
  • Types all the way down — a malformed path parameter is a 400 before your code runs.

Minimal server

[dependencies]
axum = "0.8"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt-multi-thread", "macros", "net", "signal"] }
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"
tower-http = { version = "0.6", features = ["trace", "cors", "compression-gzip"] }
tracing = "0.1"
tracing-subscriber = { version = "0.3", features = ["env-filter"] }
anyhow = "1"

use axum::{routing::get, Router};

async fn root() -> &'static str { "hello" }

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    tracing_subscriber::fmt().with_env_filter("info").init();

    let app = Router::new().route("/", get(root));

    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000").await?;
    tracing::info!("listening on {}", listener.local_addr()?);
    axum::serve(listener, app)
        .with_graceful_shutdown(shutdown_signal())
        .await?;
    Ok(())
}

async fn shutdown_signal() {
    let ctrl_c = async { tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await.unwrap() };
    let term = async {
        tokio::signal::unix::signal(tokio::signal::unix::SignalKind::terminate())
            .unwrap()
            .recv()
            .await;
    };
    tokio::select! { _ = ctrl_c => {}, _ = term => {} }
    tracing::info!("shutting down");
}

Graceful shutdown drains in-flight requests before exiting — required for zero-downtime deploys.

Routing

use axum::routing::{get, post, put, delete};

let app = Router::new()
    .route("/users", get(list_users).post(create_user))
    .route("/users/{id}", get(get_user).put(update_user).delete(delete_user))
    .route("/users/{id}/orders/{order_id}", get(get_order))   // 0.8 syntax
    .nest("/api/v1", api_routes())
    .fallback(not_found);

Gotcha: Axum 0.8 changed path parameters from :id to {id}. A :id route now fails at startup with a clear error — if you are following a tutorial that uses :id, it is for 0.7.

Extractors

An extractor is anything implementing FromRequestParts (or FromRequest if it consumes the body). The handler signature declares what it needs.

use axum::{
    extract::{Path, Query, State, Json},
    http::StatusCode,
};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct ListQuery { page: Option<u32>, per_page: Option<u32> }

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct CreateUser { email: String, name: String }

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct UserDto { id: u64, email: String, name: String }

async fn list_users(
    State(state): State<AppState>,
    Query(q): Query<ListQuery>,
) -> Result<Json<Vec<UserDto>>, ApiError> {
    let page = q.page.unwrap_or(1).max(1);
    let per_page = q.per_page.unwrap_or(20).clamp(1, 100);
    Ok(Json(state.users.list(page, per_page).await?))
}

async fn get_user(
    State(state): State<AppState>,
    Path(id): Path<u64>,
) -> Result<Json<UserDto>, ApiError> {
    state.users.find(id).await?.map(Json).ok_or(ApiError::NotFound)
}

async fn create_user(
    State(state): State<AppState>,
    Json(body): Json<CreateUser>,
) -> Result<(StatusCode, Json<UserDto>), ApiError> {
    let user = state.users.create(body.email, body.name).await?;
    Ok((StatusCode::CREATED, Json(user)))
}

Order matters: the body extractor (Json) must be last, because it consumes the request body.

Extractor summary

Extractor Source Fails with
Path<T> URL path params 400
Query<T> query string 400
Json<T> JSON body 400/415
State<S> router state —
HeaderMap headers —
TypedHeader<T> one header, typed 400
Extension<T> request-scoped value (auth) 500 if missing
Request raw request —
Bytes / String raw body —

Custom extractors: authentication

use axum::{extract::FromRequestParts, http::{request::Parts, StatusCode}};

pub struct AuthUser { pub id: u64 }

impl<S> FromRequestParts<S> for AuthUser
where
    S: Send + Sync,
{
    type Rejection = StatusCode;

    async fn from_request_parts(parts: &mut Parts, _state: &S) -> Result<Self, Self::Rejection> {
        let header = parts.headers
            .get(axum::http::header::AUTHORIZATION)
            .and_then(|v| v.to_str().ok())
            .ok_or(StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED)?;

        let token = header.strip_prefix("Bearer ").ok_or(StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED)?;
        let id = verify_token(token).map_err(|_| StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED)?;
        Ok(AuthUser { id })
    }
}

// now any handler can require auth just by taking AuthUser
async fn me(user: AuthUser) -> String { format!("user {}", user.id) }

This is the Axum pattern that pays off most: authorisation becomes part of the type signature, and a handler that needs a user cannot be written without one.

Application state

use std::sync::Arc;

#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct AppState {
    pub users: Arc<dyn UserRepo>,
    pub pool: sqlx::PgPool,
}

let state = AppState { users: Arc::new(PgUserRepo::new(pool.clone())), pool };
let app = Router::new()
    .route("/users", get(list_users))
    .with_state(state);

State<T> requires T: Clone. AppState is cheap to clone because everything inside is Arc or a pool handle.

Gotcha: never put a Mutex<HashMap> in AppState for real data. Use the database. In-memory state is lost on restart and does not survive multiple replicas.

Errors as responses

use axum::{http::StatusCode, response::{IntoResponse, Response}, Json};
use serde_json::json;

#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
pub enum ApiError {
    #[error("not found")]
    NotFound,
    #[error("validation failed: {0}")]
    Validation(String),
    #[error("unauthorized")]
    Unauthorized,
    #[error("database error")]
    Db(#[from] sqlx::Error),
    #[error("internal error")]
    Internal(#[from] anyhow::Error),
}

impl IntoResponse for ApiError {
    fn into_response(self) -> Response {
        let (status, code) = match &self {
            ApiError::NotFound => (StatusCode::NOT_FOUND, "not_found"),
            ApiError::Validation(_) => (StatusCode::UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, "validation"),
            ApiError::Unauthorized => (StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED, "unauthorized"),
            ApiError::Db(_) | ApiError::Internal(_) => {
                tracing::error!(error = %self, "request failed");
                (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "internal")
            }
        };

        // never leak internal error text to the client
        let message = match status {
            StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR => "internal error".to_string(),
            _ => self.to_string(),
        };

        (status, Json(json!({ "error": { "code": code, "message": message } })))
            .into_response()
    }
}

Two rules that matter in production: log the real error server-side, and return a generic message for 5xx. Leaking a SQL error string to a client is an information disclosure.

Middleware with tower

use std::time::Duration;
use tower::ServiceBuilder;
use tower_http::{
    trace::TraceLayer,
    cors::{CorsLayer, Any},
    compression::CompressionLayer,
    timeout::TimeoutLayer,
    limit::RequestBodyLimitLayer,
};

let app = Router::new()
    .route("/users", get(list_users))
    .with_state(state)
    .layer(
        ServiceBuilder::new()
            .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http())
            .layer(CompressionLayer::new())
            .layer(CorsLayer::new().allow_origin(Any).allow_methods(Any))
            .layer(TimeoutLayer::new(Duration::from_secs(30)))
            .layer(RequestBodyLimitLayer::new(2 * 1024 * 1024)),
    );

Layers apply bottom-up: the last .layer() is the outermost, so it sees the request first.

Rate limiting

tower_governor = "0.5"

use tower_governor::{GovernorLayer, governor::GovernorConfigBuilder};

let config = GovernorConfigBuilder::default()
    .per_second(10)
    .burst_size(20)
    .finish()
    .unwrap();

let app = Router::new().route("/", get(root))
    .layer(GovernorLayer { config: std::sync::Arc::new(config) });

Pagination, filtering, sorting

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct Page {
    #[serde(default = "default_page")]
    page: u32,
    #[serde(default = "default_per_page")]
    per_page: u32,
    sort: Option<String>,
    #[serde(default)]
    q: Option<String>,
}

fn default_page() -> u32 { 1 }
fn default_per_page() -> u32 { 20 }

// always clamp — an unbounded per_page is a DoS vector
let per_page = page.per_page.clamp(1, 100);
let offset = (page.page.saturating_sub(1)) * per_page;

Testing handlers without a network

use axum::body::Body;
use axum::http::{Request, StatusCode};
use http_body_util::BodyExt;
use tower::ServiceExt;

#[tokio::test]
async fn lists_users() {
    let app = router_with_test_state();

    let res = app
        .oneshot(Request::builder().uri("/users?page=1").body(Body::empty()).unwrap())
        .await
        .unwrap();

    assert_eq!(res.status(), StatusCode::OK);
    let bytes = res.into_body().collect().await.unwrap().to_bytes();
    let v: serde_json::Value = serde_json::from_slice(&bytes).unwrap();
    assert!(v.as_array().is_some());
}

oneshot exercises the whole router — routing, extractors, middleware, error mapping — with no socket and no port. This is the fastest reliable test you can write.

OpenAPI

utoipa = { version = "5", features = ["axum_extras", "uuid"] }
utoipa-swagger-ui = { version = "8", features = ["axum"] }

#[derive(utoipa::ToSchema, serde::Serialize)]
struct UserDto { id: u64, email: String }

#[utoipa::path(get, path = "/users/{id}", responses((status = 200, body = UserDto)))]
async fn get_user(Path(id): Path<u64>) -> Json<UserDto> { todo!() }

#[derive(utoipa::OpenApi)]
#[openapi(paths(get_user), components(schemas(UserDto)))]
struct ApiDoc;

let app = Router::new()
    .merge(SwaggerUi::new("/docs").url("/api-docs/openapi.json", ApiDoc::openapi()));

Production checklist

  • [ ] Graceful shutdown wired to SIGTERM
  • [ ] Request body size limit (2 MB is a sane default)
  • [ ] Timeout layer (30 s)
  • [ ] CORS configured explicitly, not Any, for browser-facing APIs
  • [ ] TraceLayer so every request has a span with method, path, status, latency
  • [ ] /healthz and /readyz (module 03.06)
  • [ ] Errors mapped to a stable JSON shape; 5xx bodies contain no internals
  • [ ] per_page clamped; no unbounded list endpoints
  • [ ] Pool max_connections set from the DB's limit, not left at default
  • [ ] Rate limit on auth endpoints specifically

Exercises

  1. Add a PATCH /users/{id} handler that accepts a partial body (Option<T> fields) and only updates provided fields.
  2. Write a custom extractor Pagination that parses and clamps page and per_page in one place.
  3. Add a middleware that logs the request id from a header, or generates one.
  4. Implement IntoResponse for ApiError such that sqlx::Error::RowNotFound becomes 404 and every other DB error becomes 500.
  5. Add a /metrics endpoint (module 03.06) and confirm it is excluded from the timeout layer.
  6. Write oneshot tests for a 200, a 404 and a 422.

PreviousCommand-Line ToolsNextDatabases with SQLx

03 · Databases with SQLx

SQLx is async SQL with compile-time query checking. You write SQL, and the compiler verifies it against a real database schema.

Setup

[dependencies]
sqlx = { version = "0.8", features = [
    "runtime-tokio",
    "tls-rustls",
    "postgres",
    "macros",
    "migrate",
    "chrono",
    "uuid",
    "json",
] }
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
uuid = { version = "1", features = ["v4", "serde"] }
chrono = { version = "0.4", features = ["serde"] }
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

$ export DATABASE_URL="postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/appdb"

DATABASE_URL is needed at build time for query!/query_as! macros. For CI without a live DB, use SQLX_OFFLINE=true with a cached .sqlx/ directory (see below).

Connection pool

use sqlx::postgres::PgPoolOptions;
use std::time::Duration;

pub async fn connect(database_url: &str) -> anyhow::Result<sqlx::PgPool> {
    let pool = PgPoolOptions::new()
        .max_connections(10)          // match the DB's max_connections / replicas
        .min_connections(2)
        .acquire_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))
        .idle_timeout(Duration::from_secs(600))
        .max_lifetime(Duration::from_secs(1800))
        .connect(database_url)
        .await?;
    Ok(pool)
}

Rule of thumb: max_connections × replicas < database max_connections. Ten replicas with a default pool of 10 against a Postgres with 100 connections gives you connection-refused errors under load, not slow queries.

Migrations

$ sqlx migrate add create_users
$ sqlx migrate run
$ sqlx migrate revert
$ sqlx migrate info

-- migrations/20260101000000_create_users.sql
CREATE TABLE users (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    plan        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'free',
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email);

Run them at startup:

sqlx::migrate!("./migrations").run(&pool).await?;

migrate! embeds the SQL files into the binary at compile time — the container needs no migrations directory at runtime. Migrations are checksummed, so editing an applied migration is an error (correctly).

Gotcha: never edit a migration that has run anywhere. Add a new one. The checksum mismatch will stop your production deploy.

Typed queries

Compile-time checked (the point of SQLx)

#[derive(Debug, sqlx::FromRow, serde::Serialize)]
pub struct User {
    pub id: i64,
    pub email: String,
    pub name: String,
    pub plan: String,
    pub created_at: chrono::DateTime<chrono::Utc>,
}

pub async fn find(pool: &sqlx::PgPool, id: i64) -> sqlx::Result<Option<User>> {
    sqlx::query_as!(User, "SELECT id, email, name, plan, created_at FROM users WHERE id = $1", id)
        .fetch_optional(pool)
        .await
}

pub async fn list(pool: &sqlx::PgPool, limit: i64, offset: i64) -> sqlx::Result<Vec<User>> {
    sqlx::query_as!(User,
        "SELECT id, email, name, plan, created_at FROM users ORDER BY id LIMIT $1 OFFSET $2",
        limit, offset)
        .fetch_all(pool)
        .await
}

pub async fn create(pool: &sqlx::PgPool, email: &str, name: &str) -> sqlx::Result<User> {
    sqlx::query_as!(User,
        r#"INSERT INTO users (email, name)
           VALUES ($1, $2)
           RETURNING id, email, name, plan, created_at"#,
        email, name)
        .fetch_one(pool)
        .await
}

Three guarantees you get from query_as!:

  1. The SQL parses and the tables/columns exist.
  2. The parameter count and types match.
  3. The result columns match the struct's fields (including nullability — a NULL-able column requires Option<T>).

A typo in a column name is a compile error, not a 3 a.m. incident.

Runtime-checked (when you cannot have a build-time DB)

sqlx::query_as::<_, User>("SELECT id, email, name, plan, created_at FROM users WHERE id = $1")
    .bind(id)
    .fetch_optional(pool)
    .await

Same API, no compile-time verification. Use this in a workspace where the DB is not available at build time, and keep at least the integration tests on the checked macros.

Offline mode for CI

$ cargo sqlx prepare          # writes .sqlx/*.json — COMMIT THIS
$ SQLX_OFFLINE=true cargo build

.sqlx/ stores the schema metadata for every checked query, so CI needs no database. Regenerate it whenever a query or migration changes — add cargo sqlx prepare --check to CI to catch a stale cache.

Inserts, updates, upserts

// insert, ignore the result
let res = sqlx::query("INSERT INTO events (kind, payload) VALUES ($1, $2)")
    .bind("signup")
    .bind(serde_json::json!({"source": "web"}))
    .execute(pool)
    .await?;
println!("inserted {}", res.rows_affected());

// upsert — the most useful Postgres idiom
sqlx::query_as!(User,
    r#"INSERT INTO users (email, name)
       VALUES ($1, $2)
       ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE
         SET name = EXCLUDED.name, updated_at = now()
       RETURNING id, email, name, plan, created_at"#,
    email, name)
    .fetch_one(pool)
    .await?;

// partial update with COALESCE — one query, no dynamic SQL
sqlx::query_as!(User,
    r#"UPDATE users
       SET name = COALESCE($2, name), plan = COALESCE($3, plan), updated_at = now()
       WHERE id = $1
       RETURNING id, email, name, plan, created_at"#,
    id, name, plan)
    .fetch_optional(pool)
    .await?;

That COALESCE pattern is how you do a PATCH without building SQL strings, which is what keeps you safe from injection and from a combinatorial explosion of queries.

Transactions

pub async fn transfer(
    pool: &sqlx::PgPool,
    from: i64,
    to: i64,
    amount: i64,
) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let mut tx = pool.begin().await?;

    let debited = sqlx::query("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1")
        .bind(amount).bind(from)
        .execute(&mut *tx)
        .await?;

    if debited.rows_affected() == 0 {
        anyhow::bail!("insufficient funds");   // tx drops → ROLLBACK
    }

    sqlx::query("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2")
        .bind(amount).bind(to)
        .execute(&mut *tx)
        .await?;

    tx.commit().await?;
    Ok(())
}

&mut *tx is needed because the executor borrows the connection. Dropping the transaction without commit() rolls back automatically — RAII again, and the reason a ? inside a transaction is safe.

Dynamic filters without string building

pub struct UserFilter { pub plan: Option<String>, pub q: Option<String> }

pub async fn search(pool: &sqlx::PgPool, f: &UserFilter, limit: i64) -> sqlx::Result<Vec<User>> {
    sqlx::query_as!(User,
        r#"SELECT id, email, name, plan, created_at FROM users
           WHERE ($1::text IS NULL OR plan = $1)
             AND ($2::text IS NULL OR name ILIKE '%' || $2 || '%' OR email ILIKE '%' || $2 || '%')
           ORDER BY id DESC
           LIMIT $3"#,
        f.plan, f.q, limit)
        .fetch_all(pool)
        .await
}

Gotcha: $1::text IS NULL OR plan = $1 needs the explicit cast so Postgres can infer the parameter type. Without ::text you get "could not determine data type of parameter $1".

For genuinely dynamic query shapes (variable column lists, sorts), use QueryBuilder — it parameterises values correctly:

use sqlx::QueryBuilder;

let mut qb: QueryBuilder<sqlx::Postgres> =
    QueryBuilder::new("SELECT id, email, name, plan, created_at FROM users WHERE 1=1");

if let Some(plan) = &f.plan {
    qb.push(" AND plan = ").push_bind(plan);
}
qb.push(" ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ").push_bind(limit);

let rows = qb.build_query_as::<User>().fetch_all(pool).await?;

Never format! a value into SQL. push_bind is the only safe way.

Row-by-row streaming for large results

use futures::TryStreamExt;

let mut rows = sqlx::query_as!(User, "SELECT id, email, name, plan, created_at FROM users")
    .fetch(pool);

while let Some(user) = rows.try_next().await? {
    process(user).await?;      // constant memory, regardless of table size
}

fetch_all on a 10M-row table will exhaust memory. fetch streams.

JSON columns

#[derive(serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
struct Prefs { theme: String, emails: bool }

let prefs: Prefs = sqlx::query_scalar("SELECT prefs FROM users WHERE id = $1")
    .bind(id)
    .fetch_one(pool)
    .await?;

sqlx::query("UPDATE users SET prefs = $1 WHERE id = $2")
    .bind(sqlx::types::Json(&prefs))
    .bind(id)
    .execute(pool)
    .await?;

Repository pattern: testable data access

#[async_trait::async_trait]
pub trait UserRepo: Send + Sync {
    async fn find(&self, id: i64) -> anyhow::Result<Option<User>>;
    async fn create(&self, email: &str, name: &str) -> anyhow::Result<User>;
}

pub struct PgUserRepo { pool: sqlx::PgPool }

#[async_trait::async_trait]
impl UserRepo for PgUserRepo {
    async fn find(&self, id: i64) -> anyhow::Result<Option<User>> {
        Ok(sqlx::query_as!(User, "SELECT ... WHERE id = $1", id)
            .fetch_optional(&self.pool).await?)
    }
    async fn create(&self, email: &str, name: &str) -> anyhow::Result<User> {
        Ok(sqlx::query_as!(User, "INSERT ... RETURNING ...", email, name)
            .fetch_one(&self.pool).await?)
    }
}

Now handlers depend on Arc<dyn UserRepo>, and tests use an in-memory implementation. Note async_trait here — with plain async fn in traits you cannot easily make dyn objects.

Testing against a real database

Two approaches:

1. A throwaway database per test run — use sqlx::test, which creates and drops a fresh database and runs migrations:

#[sqlx::test(migrations = "./migrations")]
async fn creates_and_finds_user(pool: sqlx::PgPool) {
    let u = create(&pool, "a@x.com", "A").await.unwrap();
    let found = find(&pool, u.id).await.unwrap().unwrap();
    assert_eq!(found.email, "a@x.com");
}

2. Testcontainers — start Postgres in Docker from the test process:

[dev-dependencies]
testcontainers = "0.23"
testcontainers-modules = { version = "0.11", features = ["postgres"] }

use testcontainers_modules::{postgres::Postgres, testcontainers::runners::AsyncRunner};

let container = Postgres::default().start().await.unwrap();
let port = container.get_host_port_ipv4(5432).await.unwrap();
let url = format!("postgres://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:{port}/postgres");

Rule of thumb: mock the repository in unit tests, use a real Postgres in integration tests. Never mock sqlx itself — you end up testing your mock.

Postgres specifics worth knowing

-- keyset pagination: fast at any offset, unlike OFFSET
SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id > $1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 50;

-- advisory lock for a singleton job
SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42);

-- skip locked: multiple workers, no duplicate work
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending'
ORDER BY created_at
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 10;

-- jsonb containment query with an index
CREATE INDEX idx_events_payload ON events USING GIN (payload);
SELECT * FROM events WHERE payload @> '{"kind":"signup"}';

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is the single most useful pattern for a Postgres-backed job queue — it is the whole of module 04.04.

Connection-per-request vs pool

Use the pool. A PgPool is Clone and internally Arc-based; cloning it into every handler is the intended usage.

Exercises

  1. Create a users table with a migration, then write find, list and create with query_as! and confirm a typo in a column name fails to compile.
  2. Implement a PATCH handler using the COALESCE update pattern.
  3. Write a transfer transaction with a balance check and a test that proves a failed transfer leaves both balances unchanged.
  4. Add keyset pagination to list and compare EXPLAIN ANALYZE output against OFFSET 100000.
  5. Build a UserRepo trait, a PgUserRepo, and an in-memory fake; write a handler test using the fake.
  6. Run cargo sqlx prepare and confirm a build with SQLX_OFFLINE=true and no database.
