04 · Background Jobs and Queues

Anything that takes longer than a request should not happen inside the request. This module covers the four ways to run work in the background in Rust, from a spawned task to a durable queue.

The four options

Approach Durability Complexity Use when
tokio::spawn none — lost on restart trivial fire-and-forget, e.g. cache warm
In-process channel + worker none low burst smoothing, low value
Postgres table + SKIP LOCKED full low you already have Postgres
Redis / SQS / RabbitMQ full medium high volume, cross-language

Rule of thumb: start with tokio::spawn. Move to a Postgres queue the day losing a job would cost money. Do not add Redis on day one.

Option 1: tokio::spawn

async fn handle_signup(State(state): State<AppState>, Json(body): Json<Signup>) -> StatusCode {
    let user = state.users.create(body.email).await.unwrap();

    // do not await — the response goes out immediately
    let mailer = state.mailer.clone();
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        if let Err(e) = mailer.send_welcome(&user.email).await {
            tracing::warn!(error = %e, "welcome email failed");
        }
    });

    StatusCode::CREATED
}

Two things to be careful about:

  • A panicking task is silent. The JoinHandle is dropped, so nothing observes the panic. Log inside the task.
  • An aborted process loses the work. If the pod restarts mid-email, the email never happens.

For a small number of known-at-startup tasks, keep the handles and supervise them:

let mut handles = Vec::new();
for i in 0..4 {
    handles.push(tokio::spawn(worker(i, state.clone())));
}

// if any worker dies, restart it (or fail loudly)
for h in handles {
    if let Err(e) = h.await {
        tracing::error!(error = ?e, "worker crashed");
    }
}

Option 2: bounded channel + worker pool

use tokio::sync::mpsc;

#[derive(Debug)]
enum Job {
    SendEmail { to: String },
    Reindex { id: i64 },
}

pub struct Queue { tx: mpsc::Sender<Job> }

impl Queue {
    pub fn new(capacity: usize) -> (Self, mpsc::Receiver<Job>) {
        let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel(capacity);
        (Queue { tx }, rx)
    }

    pub async fn submit(&self, job: Job) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
        self.tx.send(job).await?;      // awaits when full → backpressure
        Ok(())
    }
}

pub async fn run_workers(mut rx: mpsc::Receiver<Job>, n: usize, state: AppState) {
    let rx = std::sync::Arc::new(tokio::sync::Mutex::new(rx));
    for i in 0..n {
        let rx = rx.clone();
        let state = state.clone();
        tokio::spawn(async move {
            loop {
                let job = { rx.lock().await.recv().await };
                let Some(job) = job else { break };
                if let Err(e) = process(job, &state).await {
                    tracing::error!(worker = i, error = %e, "job failed");
                }
            }
        });
    }
}

A bounded channel gives you backpressure: when workers are saturated, submit awaits instead of growing memory without limit. That is the whole point of mpsc::channel(1000) rather than unbounded_channel().

Option 3: a Postgres-backed queue (the workhorse)

One table, one index, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. No extra infrastructure.

CREATE TABLE jobs (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    kind        TEXT NOT NULL,
    payload     JSONB NOT NULL,
    status      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',   -- pending|running|done|failed
    attempts    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    max_attempts INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 5,
    run_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    locked_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
    locked_by   TEXT,
    last_error  TEXT,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_pending ON jobs (run_at) WHERE status = 'pending';

Enqueue

pub async fn enqueue(pool: &PgPool, kind: &str, payload: serde_json::Value) -> sqlx::Result<i64> {
    sqlx::query_scalar(
        "INSERT INTO jobs (kind, payload) VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING id",
    )
    .bind(kind)
    .bind(payload)
    .fetch_one(pool)
    .await
}

Because it is a normal table, enqueuing can happen inside the same transaction as the business write. That is the killer feature: the job and the row it refers to commit or roll back together. No dual-write problem.

let mut tx = pool.begin().await?;
let user_id: i64 = sqlx::query_scalar("INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ($1) RETURNING id")
    .bind(&email).fetch_one(&mut *tx).await?;
sqlx::query("INSERT INTO jobs (kind, payload) VALUES ('send_welcome', $1)")
    .bind(serde_json::json!({ "user_id": user_id }))
    .execute(&mut *tx).await?;
tx.commit().await?;

Claim

#[derive(Debug, sqlx::FromRow)]
pub struct ClaimedJob {
    pub id: i64,
    pub kind: String,
    pub payload: serde_json::Value,
    pub attempts: i32,
}

pub async fn claim(pool: &PgPool, worker: &str, limit: i64) -> sqlx::Result<Vec<ClaimedJob>> {
    sqlx::query_as::<_, ClaimedJob>(
        r#"UPDATE jobs SET
             status = 'running',
             attempts = attempts + 1,
             locked_at = now(),
             locked_by = $1
           WHERE id IN (
             SELECT id FROM jobs
             WHERE status = 'pending' AND run_at <= now()
             ORDER BY run_at
             FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
             LIMIT $2
           )
           RETURNING id, kind, payload, attempts"#,
    )
    .bind(worker)
    .bind(limit)
    .fetch_all(pool)
    .await
}

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED means N workers never claim the same row and never block each other. This is the entire trick.

Complete / fail

pub async fn complete(pool: &PgPool, id: i64) -> sqlx::Result<()> {
    sqlx::query("UPDATE jobs SET status = 'done', locked_at = NULL WHERE id = $1")
        .bind(id).execute(pool).await?;
    Ok(())
}

pub async fn fail(pool: &PgPool, id: i64, err: &str, attempts: i32, max: i32) -> sqlx::Result<()> {
    if attempts >= max {
        sqlx::query("UPDATE jobs SET status = 'failed', last_error = $2 WHERE id = $1")
            .bind(id).bind(err).execute(pool).await?;
    } else {
        // exponential backoff: 2^attempts seconds, capped at 1 hour
        let delay = (1i64 << attempts.min(12)).min(3600);
        sqlx::query(
            r#"UPDATE jobs SET status = 'pending', last_error = $2,
                 run_at = now() + make_interval(secs => $3),
                 locked_at = NULL, locked_by = NULL
               WHERE id = $1"#,
        )
        .bind(id).bind(err).bind(delay as f64)
        .execute(pool).await?;
    }
    Ok(())
}

The worker loop

pub async fn run(pool: PgPool, worker: String) {
    let mut tick = tokio::time::interval(std::time::Duration::from_secs(1));
    loop {
        tick.tick().await;
        let jobs = match claim(&pool, &worker, 10).await {
            Ok(j) => j,
            Err(e) => { tracing::error!(error = %e, "claim failed"); continue; }
        };
        if jobs.is_empty() { continue; }

        for job in jobs {
            let span = tracing::info_span!("job", id = job.id, kind = %job.kind);
            let result = handle(&job, &pool).instrument(span).await;
            match result {
                Ok(()) => { let _ = complete(&pool, job.id).await; }
                Err(e) => {
                    tracing::error!(id = job.id, error = %e, "job failed");
                    let _ = fail(&pool, job.id, &e.to_string(), job.attempts, 5).await;
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

Reclaiming stuck jobs

A worker that dies mid-job leaves a row in running forever. Add a reaper:

pub async fn reap(pool: &PgPool, stale_after_secs: i64) -> sqlx::Result<u64> {
    let res = sqlx::query(
        r#"UPDATE jobs SET status = 'pending', locked_at = NULL, locked_by = NULL
           WHERE status = 'running' AND locked_at < now() - make_interval(secs => $1)"#,
    )
    .bind(stale_after_secs as f64)
    .execute(pool)
    .await?;
    Ok(res.rows_affected())
}

Run it from the same worker loop every 60 s with stale_after_secs = 300. Without this, one crashed pod silently stops processing a subset of your jobs.

Gotcha: the reaper can resurrect a job that is genuinely still running (a long task, not a dead worker). Either set stale_after above your longest job, or have handlers be idempotent. Idempotency is the real answer.

Idempotency

Every handler should tolerate running twice:

async fn handle_send_welcome(payload: &serde_json::Value, pool: &PgPool) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let user_id = payload["user_id"].as_i64().ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("bad payload"))?;

    // claim the effect exactly once
    let inserted = sqlx::query(
        "INSERT INTO sent_emails (user_id, kind) VALUES ($1, 'welcome')
         ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING",
    )
    .bind(user_id)
    .execute(pool)
    .await?
    .rows_affected();

    if inserted == 0 {
        tracing::info!(user_id, "welcome already sent, skipping");
        return Ok(());
    }

    send_email(user_id).await
}

A unique constraint plus ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING gives you exactly-once semantics on top of at-least-once delivery. This pattern works for emails, webhooks, invoices and payments.

Scheduling: cron in Rust

tokio-cron-scheduler = "0.13"

use tokio_cron_scheduler::{Job, JobScheduler};

let sched = JobScheduler::new().await?;
sched.add(Job::new_async("0 0 * * * *", |_uuid, _l| Box::pin(async {
    tracing::info!("hourly task");
}))?).await?;
sched.start().await?;

For a single-replica scheduler this is fine. With multiple replicas, every pod runs it — use a Postgres advisory lock to elect one:

let acquired: bool = sqlx::query_scalar("SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(12345)")
    .fetch_one(pool).await?;
if !acquired { return; }   // someone else is running it

Observability for jobs

Emit these four metrics per queue (module 03.06):

metrics::gauge!("jobs_pending").set(pending as f64);
metrics::gauge!("jobs_running").set(running as f64);
metrics::counter!("jobs_completed_total", "kind" => kind.clone()).increment(1);
metrics::histogram!("job_duration_seconds", "kind" => kind).record(elapsed);

Alert on jobs_pending growing monotonically for 10 minutes — that is the signature of a stuck consumer, and it is invisible without a metric.

Exercises

  1. Implement the Postgres queue: schema, enqueue, claim, complete, fail.
  2. Run three worker processes concurrently and prove no job is processed twice (count rows in a processed table).
  3. Add exponential backoff and verify run_at increases on repeated failures.
  4. Write the reaper and test it by inserting a running job with an old locked_at.
  5. Make the welcome-email handler idempotent with a unique constraint.
  6. Add a /admin/jobs endpoint returning counts by status.

05 · WebAssembly in the Browser

Rust compiles to WebAssembly: near-native speed in the browser, a small binary, and the same language on both sides of the wire.

When it is worth it

Use WASM Do not use WASM
CPU-heavy work: parsing, codecs, crypto, simulation ordinary UI and forms
Reusing an existing Rust library in the browser anything the DOM does well
Image/video/audio processing a page that is mostly text
Games and graphics CRUD apps
Running untrusted code in a sandbox when bundle size dominates

WASM's real win is sharing logic: the same validation, parser or pricing engine running on the server and in the browser, with no reimplementation and no drift.

Toolchain

$ rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown
$ cargo install wasm-pack          # build + npm packaging
$ cargo install trunk              # dev server + bundler for web apps
$ cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli

The smallest useful module

[package]
name = "wasm-lib"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]

[dependencies]
wasm-bindgen = "0.2"

[profile.release]
opt-level = "s"        # optimise for size
lto = true

use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn slugify(input: &str) -> String {
    input
        .to_lowercase()
        .chars()
        .map(|c| if c.is_alphanumeric() { c } else { '-' })
        .collect::<String>()
        .trim_matches('-')
        .to_string()
}

$ wasm-pack build --target web --release

That produces pkg/ with a .wasm, a JS glue file, and TypeScript types.

<script type="module">
  import init, { add, slugify } from './pkg/wasm_lib.js';
  await init();
  console.log(add(2, 3));              // 5
  console.log(slugify('Hello, World!')); // hello-world
</script>

crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"] matters: cdylib for the wasm artifact, rlib so you can still unit-test the crate natively with cargo test.

Working with JS values

use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Order { pub id: u64, pub total: f64, pub items: Vec<String> }

#[wasm_bindgen]
pub fn total_of(orders: JsValue) -> Result<f64, JsValue> {
    let orders: Vec<Order> = serde_wasm_bindgen::from_value(orders)
        .map_err(|e| JsValue::from_str(&e.to_string()))?;
    Ok(orders.iter().map(|o| o.total).sum())
}

serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde-wasm-bindgen = "0.6"

Gotcha: passing complex data across the boundary costs. Every JsValue conversion copies. For hot paths, keep the data on the Rust side and pass handles (integers) instead of structures.

Calling the browser

[dependencies]
wasm-bindgen = "0.2"
web-sys = { version = "0.3", features = ["Window", "Document", "HtmlElement", "console"] }
js-sys = "0.3"

use wasm_bindgen::prelude::*;
use web_sys::window;

#[wasm_bindgen(start)]           // runs automatically on module init
pub fn main() -> Result<(), JsValue> {
    let doc = window().unwrap().document().unwrap();
    let el = doc.get_element_by_id("app").unwrap();
    el.set_inner_html("<h1>Hello from Rust</h1>");
    web_sys::console::log_1(&"wasm started".into());
    Ok(())
}

Panics and logging

[dependencies]
console_error_panic_hook = "0.1"

#[wasm_bindgen(start)]
pub fn start() {
    console_error_panic_hook::set_once();   // panic messages in the browser console
}

Without this, a Rust panic in WASM shows up as unreachable executed with no information. Set the hook first, always.

A real app: the Yew framework

[dependencies]
yew = { version = "0.21", features = ["csr"] }
wasm-bindgen = "0.2"

use yew::prelude::*;

#[function_component(App)]
fn app() -> Html {
    let count = use_state(|| 0);

    let onclick = {
        let count = count.clone();
        Callback::from(move |_| count.set(*count + 1))
    };

    html! {
        <main class="p-4">
            <h1>{ "Counter" }</h1>
            <p>{ format!("Clicked {} times", *count) }</p>
            <button {onclick}>{ "Increment" }</button>
        </main>
    }
}

fn main() { yew::Renderer::<App>::new().render(); }
Framework Model Notes
leptos fine-grained signals fastest, closest to SolidJS
yew React-like components mature, familiar
dioxus React-like, multi-target also desktop/mobile/TUI
sycamore signals smaller community

Trunk: the build tool

# Trunk.toml
[build]
target = "index.html"

[serve]
port = 8080

<!-- index.html -->
<link data-trunk rel="rust" data-wasm-opt="s" />

$ trunk serve --open
$ trunk build --release

Trunk compiles the Rust, runs wasm-bindgen, runs wasm-opt, hashes assets and serves with hot reload. It removes the whole npm layer for a pure-Rust frontend.

Size and speed

$ wasm-opt -Oz -o out.wasm in.wasm

[profile.release]
opt-level = "s"     # or "z" for minimum size
lto = true
codegen-units = 1
panic = "abort"     # much smaller, no unwinding
strip = true
Setting Rough effect
opt-level = "s" −10–20% size vs 3
lto = true −10%
panic = "abort" −10–15%
wasm-opt -Oz −10–20%
No std formatting −30% (big)

format! and Display pull in a large chunk of std. In a size-sensitive WASM build, avoid them in hot paths — or go no_std.

Enable gzip/brotli on the server: WASM compresses to about 30% of its size, and the browser caches it.

Threads and SIMD (advanced)

$ RUSTFLAGS="-C target-feature=+simd128" cargo build --target wasm32-unknown-unknown

SIMD is widely supported. Threads require SharedArrayBuffer, which needs cross-origin isolation headers:

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp

Without those two headers, SharedArrayBuffer is undefined and any thread-based WASM fails.

WASM outside the browser

The same .wasm runs in:

  • Cloudflare Workers / Fastly Compute — edge functions.
  • WASI (wasm32-wasip1) — server-side sandboxing, plugins.
  • Extism — a plugin system for any host language.
  • Wasmtime — an embeddable runtime.

A plugin architecture where untrusted customer code runs in a WASM sandbox with explicit host functions is one of the genuinely great uses of this technology.

// host side with wasmtime
let engine = wasmtime::Engine::default();
let module = wasmtime::Module::from_file(&engine, "plugin.wasm")?;
let mut store = wasmtime::Store::new(&engine, ());
let instance = wasmtime::Instance::new(&mut store, &module, &[])?;
let run = instance.get_typed_func::<(), i32>(&mut store, "run")?;
let result = run.call(&mut store, ())?;

Exercises

  1. Build the slugify module with wasm-pack and call it from a plain HTML page.
  2. Add console_error_panic_hook and trigger a panic; read the message in the console.
  3. Pass a Vec<Order> from JS to Rust as JsValue and return the total.
  4. Build a Yew counter, then a Leptos counter, and compare bundle sizes.
  5. Take a WASM build and shrink it with opt-level = "s", lto, panic = "abort" and wasm-opt -Oz. Report each step's size.
  6. Explain why crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"] is needed to keep cargo test working.

Next: Embedded and IoT

PreviousBackground Jobs and QueuesNextEmbedded and IoT

06 · Embedded and IoT

Rust on microcontrollers: no OS, no allocator required, and the same ownership rules that make systems code safe make firmware safe. Memory errors in firmware are bricked devices, so this is where Rust's guarantees pay off most.

The stack

Layer Crate Role
Language #![no_std] no standard library
HAL traits embedded-hal standard interfaces (GPIO, SPI, I2C)
Async HAL embedded-hal-async async versions
Chip support cortex-m, cortex-m-rt ARM Cortex-M runtime
PAC stm32f4xx-hal etc. register-level access
HAL embassy-stm32, rp2040-hal ergonomic per-chip drivers
Async runtime embassy-executor no-alloc async executor
Logging defmt deferred formatting, tiny binary size
Flashing probe-rs debug probe flashing + RTT logging
RTOS-ish rtic real-time scheduling with priorities

no_std vs std

#![no_std]
#![no_main]

use cortex_m_rt::entry;
use panic_halt as _;        // what to do on panic

#[entry]
fn main() -> ! {
    loop {}                  // embedded main never returns
}

You lose std's String, Vec (unless you add alloc with a heap), threads, files and networking. You gain a binary that fits in 16 KB and boots in microseconds.

panic_halt on panic: an infinite loop. Alternatives: panic_abort, panic_probe (prints over RTT then halts — the useful one while developing).

Blinky: the "hello world"

[package]
name = "blinky"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
cortex-m = "0.7"
cortex-m-rt = "0.7"
panic-probe = { version = "0.3", features = ["print-defmt"] }
defmt = "0.3"
defmt-rtt = "0.4"
embassy-executor = { version = "0.6", features = ["arch-cortex-m", "executor-thread", "integrated-timers"] }
embassy-time = { version = "0.3", features = ["tick-hz-32_768"] }
embassy-stm32 = { version = "0.1", features = ["stm32f411ce", "time-driver-any", "exti"] }

[profile.release]
debug = 2
lto = true
opt-level = "s"

#![no_std]
#![no_main]

use defmt_rtt as _;
use embassy_executor::Spawner;
use embassy_stm32::gpio::{Level, Output, Speed};
use embassy_time::Timer;
use panic_probe as _;

#[embassy_executor::main]
async fn main(_spawner: Spawner) {
    let p = embassy_stm32::init(Default::default());
    let mut led = Output::new(p.PC13, Level::Low, Speed::Low);

    defmt::info!("blinky started");
    loop {
        led.set_high();
        Timer::after_millis(500).await;
        led.set_low();
        Timer::after_millis(500).await;
    }
}

$ cargo run --release       # requires .cargo/config.toml with `runner = "probe-rs run"`

Gotcha: async on a microcontroller is not an OS. Timer::after(...).await suspends the task and the executor runs something else; there is no thread and no stack switch. Stack usage per task is fixed at compile time and a deep call chain in one task can still overflow the 2–8 KB you gave it.

embedded-hal: driver code that works everywhere

The reason the ecosystem is healthy: a driver written against embedded-hal traits works on every chip.

use embedded_hal::digital::OutputPin;
use embedded_hal::delay::DelayNs;

pub struct Led<P: OutputPin> { pin: P }

impl<P: OutputPin> Led<P> {
    pub fn new(pin: P) -> Self { Led { pin } }
    pub fn on(&mut self) -> Result<(), P::Error> { self.pin.set_high() }
    pub fn off(&mut self) -> Result<(), P::Error> { self.pin.set_low() }
}

pub fn blink<P: OutputPin, D: DelayNs>(led: &mut Led<P>, delay: &mut D, times: u32) {
    for _ in 0..times {
        let _ = led.on();
        delay.delay_ms(200);
        let _ = led.off();
        delay.delay_ms(200);
    }
}

That function compiles for an STM32, an nRF52, an ESP32 and an RP2040 without change. This is what "traits instead of inheritance" buys you.

Reading a sensor over I2C

use embedded_hal::i2c::I2c;

const ADDR: u8 = 0x76;      // BME280

pub fn read_chip_id<I: I2c>(i2c: &mut I) -> Result<u8, I::Error> {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 1];
    i2c.write_read(ADDR, &[0xD0], &mut buf)?;
    Ok(buf[0])
}

pub fn read_temp_raw<I: I2c>(i2c: &mut I) -> Result<i32, I::Error> {
    let mut buf = [0u8; 3];
    i2c.write_read(ADDR, &[0xFA], &mut buf)?;    // temp registers
    Ok(((buf[0] as i32) << 12) | ((buf[1] as i32) << 4) | ((buf[2] as i32) >> 4))
}

No allocation, no dynamic dispatch, fixed-size buffers on the stack. Everything is proven at compile time.

RTIC: real-time scheduling

#[rtic::app(device = stm32f4xx_hal::pac, peripherals = true)]
mod app {
    use stm32f4xx_hal::prelude::*;

    #[shared]
    struct Shared { counter: u32 }

    #[local]
    struct Local { led: stm32f4xx_hal::gpio::Pin<'C', 13, Output> }

    #[init]
    fn init(cx: init::Context) -> (Shared, Local) {
        let dp = cx.device;
        let gpio = dp.GPIOC.split();
        let led = gpio.pc13.into_push_pull_output();
        (Shared { counter: 0 }, Local { led })
    }

    #[task(binds = TIM2, local = [led], shared = [counter])]
    fn tick(mut cx: tick::Context) {
        *cx.shared.counter.lock() += 1;
        cx.local.led.toggle();
    }
}

RTIC gives you compile-time-verified interrupt priorities with no data races: the borrow checker enforces that two tasks cannot access a shared resource at conflicting priorities.

Firmware update (OTA) considerations

The parts people get wrong:

  1. A/B partitions. Flash two slots; write the new image to the inactive one, verify a checksum, flip a boot flag. Never overwrite the running image.
  2. Power loss mid-write must leave a bootable device. Write-then-verify-then- flip-flag is the only safe order.
  3. Signature verification before boot. An unsigned OTA endpoint is remote code execution for anyone who can reach the server.
  4. Rollback. Keep the previous image until the new one has run for N minutes.

Practical reality check

Concern Reality
Binary size Rust firmware is 5–20% larger than C, shrinking with opt-level="s" + LTO
Toolchain maturity excellent on Cortex-M and RISC-V; ESP32 and Xtensa also work
Debugging probe-rs + defmt is better than most C setups
Libraries fewer than C, but embedded-hal unifies what exists
Hiring fewer embedded Rust engineers, but they tend to be strong

Where Rust embedded is actually used

  • Espressif ships official Rust support for ESP32.
  • Microsoft Azure Sphere uses Rust for secure MCU apps.
  • Nordic supports Rust on nRF52/nRF53.
  • Automotive and industrial gateways: RTIC and embassy on Cortex-M.
  • Raspberry Pi Pico has first-class embassy-rp support.

Exercises

  1. Get blinky running on any dev board with probe-rs. If you have no hardware, run it under qemu-system-arm with the lm3s6965evb machine.
  2. Write a generic blink against embedded-hal traits and compile it for two different chips.
  3. Read a sensor's chip-id over I2C and print it with defmt::info!.
  4. Convert a polling loop into an embassy task with Timer::after.
  5. Explain why #![no_main] is required and what cortex_m_rt::entry provides.
  6. Design (on paper) an A/B OTA scheme with power-loss safety, and list the failure points.

07 · Game Development with Bevy

Bevy is the most active Rust game engine. Its defining idea is ECS (Entity Component System): data lives in components, behaviour lives in systems, and the engine schedules systems to run in parallel wherever they do not conflict.

Version note: Bevy's API changes quickly (roughly quarterly). The examples below target the 0.15/0.16 era (Camera2d and Sprite as components, required components instead of *Bundle). If something does not compile, check the migration guide for your version — that is normal in Bevy, not a mistake on your part.

Setup

[package]
name = "my_game"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
bevy = "0.16"

# Much faster builds during development
[profile.dev]
opt-level = 1

[profile.dev.package."*"]
opt-level = 3

$ cargo run

The first build compiles ~400 crates and takes several minutes. After that, incremental builds are seconds.

The smallest game

use bevy::prelude::*;

fn main() {
    App::new()
        .add_plugins(DefaultPlugins)
        .add_systems(Startup, setup)
        .add_systems(Update, spin)
        .run();
}

#[derive(Component)]
struct Spinner;

fn setup(mut commands: Commands, asset_server: Res<AssetServer>) {
    commands.spawn(Camera2d);

    commands.spawn((
        Sprite::from_image(asset_server.load("player.png")),
        Transform::from_xyz(0.0, 0.0, 0.0),
        Spinner,
    ));
}

fn spin(time: Res<Time>, mut query: Query<&mut Transform, With<Spinner>>) {
    for mut transform in &mut query {
        transform.rotate_z(1.0 * time.delta_secs());
    }
}

Read that as: "on startup, create a camera and an entity with a sprite and a Spinner marker; every frame, rotate everything with a Spinner."

Query<&mut Transform, With<Spinner>> is a system parameter — Bevy uses the type to decide which entities match and, because the types declare access, it can run non-conflicting systems in parallel on different threads.

ECS in one page

Concept Meaning
Entity an ID. Nothing else. Cheap to create and destroy
Component a plain struct of data attached to an entity
System a function that reads/writes components
Resource a singleton, like Time or your Score
Query a typed filter over entities and their components
Schedule an ordered set of systems (Startup, Update, FixedUpdate) 
#[derive(Component)] struct Health { current: f32, max: f32 }
#[derive(Component)] struct Player;
#[derive(Component)] struct Enemy;
#[derive(Resource)] struct Score(u32);

Movement and input

use bevy::input::keyboard::KeyCode;

fn move_player(
    keys: Res<ButtonInput<KeyCode>>,
    time: Res<Time>,
    mut q: Query<&mut Transform, With<Player>>,
) {
    const SPEED: f32 = 300.0;
    let mut dir = Vec2::ZERO;
    if keys.pressed(KeyCode::KeyW) { dir.y += 1.0; }
    if keys.pressed(KeyCode::KeyS) { dir.y -= 1.0; }
    if keys.pressed(KeyCode::KeyA) { dir.x -= 1.0; }
    if keys.pressed(KeyCode::KeyD) { dir.x += 1.0; }

    if dir != Vec2::ZERO {
        let dir = dir.normalize();
        for mut t in &mut q {
            t.translation += (dir * SPEED * time.delta_secs()).extend(0.0);
        }
    }
}

Spawning and despawning

fn spawn_enemy(mut commands: Commands, asset_server: Res<AssetServer>) {
    commands.spawn((
        Sprite::from_image(asset_server.load("enemy.png")),
        Transform::from_xyz(400.0, 0.0, 0.0),
        Enemy,
        Health { current: 30.0, max: 30.0 },
    ));
}

fn cleanup(mut commands: Commands, q: Query<(Entity, &Health)>) {
    for (entity, health) in &q {
        if health.current <= 0.0 {
            commands.entity(entity).despawn();     // deferred to end of stage
        }
    }
}

commands are deferred: they apply at a synchronisation point, not immediately. That is why you can despawn an entity you are still iterating over.

Combat: a system that touches two queries

#[derive(Event)]
struct Hit { target: Entity, damage: f32 }

fn apply_hits(
    mut events: EventReader<Hit>,
    mut q: Query<&mut Health>,
) {
    for hit in events.read() {
        if let Ok(mut health) = q.get_mut(hit.target) {
            health.current -= hit.damage;
        }
    }
}

// registration
app.add_event::<Hit>();
app.add_systems(Update, apply_hits);

UI: text and score

#[derive(Component)]
struct ScoreText;

fn setup_ui(mut commands: Commands, asset_server: Res<AssetServer>) {
    commands.spawn((
        Text::new("Score: 0"),
        TextFont { font: asset_server.load("fonts/FiraSans-Bold.ttf"), font_size: 32.0, ..default() },
        TextColor(Color::WHITE),
        Node { position_type: PositionType::Absolute, top: Val::Px(12.0), left: Val::Px(12.0), ..default() },
        ScoreText,
    ));
}

fn update_score(score: Res<Score>, mut q: Query<&mut Text, With<ScoreText>>) {
    if !score.is_changed() { return; }
    for mut text in &mut q {
        **text = format!("Score: {}", score.0);
    }
}

Res<T>::is_changed() is the cheap way to skip work when nothing happened — Bevy tracks change detection per component and per resource.

Fixed timestep for physics

app.add_systems(FixedUpdate, physics_step);

// FixedUpdate runs at a fixed rate regardless of frame rate
// configure once:
// app.insert_resource(Time::<Fixed>::from_hz(60.0));

Use FixedUpdate for physics and game logic that must be deterministic; use Update for input, animation and UI. Mixing them causes the classic "jumps higher on a fast machine" bug.

Assets and hot reload

let texture: Handle<Image> = asset_server.load("sprites/player.png");

Assets are loaded by path and return a Handle. In debug builds Bevy watches the assets directory and hot-reloads on save — a large quality-of-life win.

Performance notes

Symptom Cause Fix
Low FPS with few entities per-frame allocation reuse buffers, avoid format! in Update
Frame spikes asset loading on the main thread preload in Startup, use AssetServer states
Systems not parallel one system queries &mut everything split into narrower queries
Huge binary default features default-features = false, enable only what you need 
bevy = { version = "0.16", default-features = false, features = [
    "bevy_sprite", "bevy_text", "bevy_ui", "bevy_winit", "png", "x11"
] }

Ecosystem

Crate Purpose
bevy_rapier2d / bevy_rapier3d physics
avian2d / avian3d ECS-native physics (newer alternative)
bevy_egui immediate-mode debug UI
bevy-inspector-egui live entity inspector — invaluable
bevy_asset_loader declarative asset loading states
leafwing-input-manager action-mapped input
bevy_kira_audio audio
iyes_progress loading screens

Install bevy-inspector-egui on day one. Being able to see and edit every component live saves hours.

Honest assessment

Good: data-oriented architecture, hot reload, excellent 2D, no GC pauses, strong community momentum, compiles to WASM and native.

Costs: API churn between versions, compile times, a smaller asset store than Unity, and 3D is less mature than 2D.

When to pick it: a 2D game, a prototype where you want determinism and no engine licence, or a game whose logic you want to unit test.

When not to: a large 3D title on a deadline, or a team of artists who need Unity/Unreal tooling.

Exercises

  1. Build the spinning-sprite example and add WASD movement.
  2. Add a Score resource, an Hit event, and a system that increments the score when an enemy's health reaches zero.
  3. Move physics into FixedUpdate at 60 Hz and verify behaviour is frame-rate-independent by capping the frame rate to 30.
  4. Add a bevy_egui debug window showing entity count.
  5. Split one fat &mut Transform system into two narrower systems and check with the inspector that they run in parallel.
  6. Disable default features and enable only 2D + UI; measure the binary size difference.

PreviousEmbedded and IoTNextData Pipelines and Stream Processing

08 · Data Pipelines and Stream Processing

Rust's role in data is the runtime, not the notebook: ingestion services, stream processors, and batch jobs where memory and latency are predictable.

The two halves

Batch Streaming
Process a file or table Process an endless event stream
polars, arrow, parquet rdkafka, tokio, serde
Memory-bound, throughput-bound Latency-bound, backpressure-bound
Runs to completion Runs forever

Batch: Polars

Polars is a Rust dataframe library with a lazy query engine. It is the reason "do it in Python with pandas" is no longer automatically right.

polars = { version = "0.4x", features = ["lazy", "csv", "parquet", "json", "temporal"] }

use polars::prelude::*;

fn main() -> PolarsResult<()> {
    let lf = LazyCsvReader::new("orders.csv")
        .with_has_header(true)
        .finish()?
        .filter(col("status").eq(lit("paid")))
        .with_columns([
            (col("qty") * col("price")).alias("amount"),
            col("created_at").str().to_datetime(
                Some(TimeUnit::Microseconds),
                None,
                StrptimeOptions::default(),
                lit("raise"),
            )?,
        ])
        .group_by([col("customer_id")])
        .agg([
            col("amount").sum().alias("total"),
            col("amount").mean().alias("avg"),
            col("order_id").count().alias("orders"),
        ])
        .sort(["total"], SortMultipleOptions::default().with_order_descending(true))
        .limit(100);

    let mut df = lf.collect()?;
    println!("{}", df.head(Some(10)));

    // write parquet — columnar, compressed, fast to re-read
    let mut file = std::fs::File::create("top_customers.parquet")?;
    ParquetWriter::new(&mut file).finish(&mut df)?;
    Ok(())
}

Key difference from pandas: LazyFrame builds a plan and the engine optimises it — predicate pushdown, projection pushdown, common subexpression elimination — before reading a single row. On a 10 GB parquet file that is the difference between reading 200 MB and 10 GB.

Streaming a file larger than memory

let q = LazyFrame::scan_parquet("huge.parquet", ScanArgsParquet::default())?
    .filter(col("country").eq(lit("IN")))
    .group_by([col("city")])
    .agg([col("amount").sum()]);

let df = q.collect()?;    // polars streams internally for scan_* sources

scan_parquet / scan_csv are lazy sources; read_parquet loads eagerly. Use scan_* for anything big.

Polars vs pandas

Polars pandas
Multi-threaded yes, by default mostly single-threaded
Memory model Arrow, zero-copy numpy + object columns
Nulls first-class NaN workarounds
Strings fast, Arrow-backed slow object columns
Ecosystem smaller enormous

Streaming: Kafka with rdkafka

rdkafka = { version = "0.36", features = ["cmake-build", "ssl", "sasl"] }

use rdkafka::consumer::{Consumer, StreamConsumer};
use rdkafka::message::Message;
use rdkafka::ClientConfig;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let consumer: StreamConsumer = ClientConfig::new()
        .set("group.id", "enricher")
        .set("bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092")
        .set("enable.auto.commit", "false")        // commit AFTER processing
        .set("auto.offset.reset", "earliest")
        .create()?;

    consumer.subscribe(&["orders"])?;

    loop {
        let msg = consumer.recv().await?;
        let payload = msg.payload().unwrap_or_default();

        match serde_json::from_slice::<Order>(payload) {
            Ok(order) => {
                if let Err(e) = handle(&order).await {
                    tracing::error!(error = %e, "failed to handle order");
                    continue;                       // do not commit — retry
                }
                consumer.commit_message(&msg, rdkafka::consumer::CommitMode::Async)?;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                tracing::warn!(error = %e, "poison message, skipping");
                consumer.commit_message(&msg, rdkafka::consumer::CommitMode::Async)?;
            }
        }
    }
}

Two rules that matter more than the code:

  1. enable.auto.commit = false. With auto-commit you acknowledge messages before processing them, so a crash silently loses data.
  2. Distinguish poison messages from transient failures. A malformed message should go to a dead-letter topic, not block the partition forever. A database timeout should retry.

A typed event envelope

use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct Event<T> {
    pub id: uuid::Uuid,
    pub kind: String,
    pub version: u16,
    pub occurred_at: chrono::DateTime<chrono::Utc>,
    pub payload: T,
}

#[derive(Debug, Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct OrderPlaced {
    pub order_id: u64,
    pub customer_id: u64,
    pub amount: i64,          // paise, not rupees — never floats for money
    pub currency: String,
}

version in the envelope lets consumers handle schema evolution. Money as integer minor units is non-negotiable — floating point money bugs are real and expensive.

Backpressure

A pipeline with no backpressure is a memory leak that runs at the speed of the slowest stage. Three mechanisms:

// 1. bounded channel between stages
let (tx, mut rx) = tokio::sync::mpsc::channel::<Batch>(64);

// 2. bounded concurrency for outbound calls
let sem = std::sync::Arc::new(tokio::sync::Semaphore::new(32));

// 3. batch by size or time, whichever comes first
struct Batcher { buf: Vec<Event>, max: usize, flush_at: tokio::time::Instant }

use futures::stream::{self, StreamExt};

let results: Vec<_> = stream::iter(items)
    .map(|item| async move { process(item).await })
    .buffer_unordered(16)          // at most 16 in flight
    .collect()
    .await;

buffer_unordered(16) is the single most useful line in a data pipeline: it keeps throughput high without opening 100,000 connections.

Exactly-once vs at-least-once

True exactly-once is expensive and rare. The practical approach:

  1. At-least-once delivery — retry on failure, accept duplicates.
  2. Idempotent processing — a unique key plus ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.
  3. Deterministic output keys — write to a path or row keyed by event id.
let inserted = sqlx::query(
    "INSERT INTO processed_events (event_id) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING",
)
.bind(event.id)
.execute(&pool)
.await?
.rows_affected();

if inserted == 0 {
    tracing::debug!(id = %event.id, "duplicate, skipping");
    return Ok(());
}

This gives you the effect of exactly-once on top of at-least-once delivery. It is what every mature pipeline actually does.

A worked example: CSV → validate → aggregate → Parquet

use polars::prelude::*;
use std::fs::File;

fn etl(input: &str, output: &str) -> PolarsResult<()> {
    let lf = LazyCsvReader::new(input)
        .with_has_header(true)
        .with_try_parse_dates(true)
        .finish()?
        // drop rows that fail validation, keep the count separately
        .filter(col("amount").gt(lit(0)).and(col("currency").is_in(lit(
            Series::new("c".into(), ["INR", "USD", "EUR"]),
        ))))
        .with_columns([
            (col("amount").cast(DataType::Float64) / lit(100.0)).alias("amount_major"),
            col("ts").dt().truncate("1d").alias("day"),
        ])
        .group_by([col("day"), col("currency")])
        .agg([
            col("amount_major").sum().alias("gross"),
            col("amount_major").count().alias("txns"),
        ])
        .sort(["day"], SortMultipleOptions::default());

    let mut df = lf.collect()?;
    let mut file = File::create(output)?;
    ParquetWriter::new(&mut file)
        .with_compression(ParquetCompression::Zstd(None))
        .finish(&mut df)?;

    println!("wrote {} rows to {output}", df.height());
    Ok(())
}

Note the filter happens before the aggregation, so the optimizer never materialises the rejected rows.

When Rust beats Python here, and when it does not

Rust wins: long-running ingestion services, per-event latency under a millisecond, memory predictability, deploying a single binary with no interpreter, and pipelines processing terabytes where pandas would OOM.

Python wins: exploratory analysis, notebook iteration, the ML ecosystem, and anything where the library you need only exists in Python.

The common professional split: prototype in Python, then rewrite the hot path — or just the production job — in Rust once the shape of the problem is known.

Exercises

  1. Write a Polars pipeline that reads a CSV, filters, aggregates by day and writes Zstd-compressed Parquet.
  2. Compare read_csv + collect against scan_csv + collect on a 1 GB file. Measure peak RSS.
  3. Consume from a Kafka topic with manual commits and prove a restart does not lose messages.
  4. Add a dead-letter topic for messages that fail to deserialise.
  5. Add buffer_unordered(16) to a sequential enrichment loop and measure the throughput change.
  6. Implement idempotent processing with a processed_events table and prove a duplicate event is a no-op.

01 · Capstone Brief and Architecture

The capstone is Pulse: a small but complete SaaS usage-analytics product. It exercises everything in this course — a Rust API, a Postgres schema, a background worker, and a Next.js dashboard with HeroUI.

What it does

A customer signs up, gets an API key, and their application sends usage events (api_call, storage_write, job_run). Pulse:

  1. Ingests events at high volume (POST /v1/events).
  2. Aggregates them per tenant per day.
  3. Serves a dashboard: MRR, active users, plan breakdown, usage this month, recent invoices.
  4. Emails a monthly usage summary (background job).

Small enough to finish, real enough to be instructive.

Architecture

        ┌──────────────┐
        │  Customer    │
        │  SDK / curl  │
        └──────┬───────┘
               │  POST /v1/events  (API key)
               ▼
      ┌────────────────────┐
      │   Rust API (axum)  │──────┐
      │  auth · validate   │      │
      │  enqueue           │      │
      └────────┬───────────┘      │
               │                  │
               ▼                  ▼
      ┌────────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
      │  Postgres      │◄──│   Worker     │
      │  events        │   │  aggregate   │
      │  aggregates    │   │  email       │
      │  jobs          │   │  reaper      │
      └────────┬───────┘   └──────────────┘
               │
               │  GET /v1/dashboard  (session)
               ▼
      ┌────────────────────────┐
      │  Next.js + HeroUI      │
      │  sticky header · nav   │
      │  cards · table · chart │
      └────────────────────────┘

The four pieces

Piece Tech Module
API Rust, axum 0.8, sqlx, tokio 04.02, 04.03
Worker Rust, tokio, Postgres queue 04.04
Database Postgres 16 + migrations 04.03
Dashboard Next.js App Router, Tailwind v4, HeroUI v3 05.03

Schema

-- tenants and users
CREATE TABLE tenants (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name        TEXT NOT NULL,
    plan        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'free',   -- free|pro|scale
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE api_keys (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id   BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    key_hash    TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,           -- store a HASH, never the key
    prefix      TEXT NOT NULL,                  -- first 8 chars, for display
    revoked_at  TIMESTAMPTZ,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- events: high volume, append-only
CREATE TABLE events (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id   BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    kind        TEXT NOT NULL,
    quantity    BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    occurred_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    meta        JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb
);

CREATE INDEX idx_events_tenant_time ON events (tenant_id, occurred_at DESC);

-- daily rollups: what the dashboard reads
CREATE TABLE usage_daily (
    tenant_id   BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    day         DATE NOT NULL,
    kind        TEXT NOT NULL,
    total       BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, day, kind)
);

-- jobs: the queue from module 04.04
CREATE TABLE jobs (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    kind        TEXT NOT NULL,
    payload     JSONB NOT NULL,
    status      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    attempts    INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    run_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    locked_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
    locked_by   TEXT,
    last_error  TEXT,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_pending ON jobs (run_at) WHERE status = 'pending';

-- invoices: what the dashboard table shows
CREATE TABLE invoices (
    id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id   BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    number      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    amount_paise BIGINT NOT NULL,               -- integers for money
    status      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',   -- open|paid|void
    period_start DATE NOT NULL,
    period_end   DATE NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

Three decisions worth defending:

  • amount_paise BIGINT — money as integer minor units. No floats, ever.
  • key_hash, not the key — a leaked database must not leak credentials. Hash the key with SHA-256 on ingest and look it up by hash.
  • usage_daily rollups — the dashboard must never COUNT(*) over a billion events. Aggregate once per day, read the rollup.

API surface

Method Path Auth Purpose
POST /v1/events API key ingest one or many events
GET /v1/dashboard session everything the dashboard needs
GET /v1/tenants/{id}/usage session usage by day and kind
GET /v1/invoices session invoice list
POST /v1/invoices/{id}/pay session mark paid (demo)
GET /healthz none liveness
GET /readyz none readiness (checks DB)
GET /metrics none Prometheus

GET /v1/dashboard returns one payload so the UI makes one request:

{
  "mrr_paise": 4820000,
  "mrr_change_pct": 12.4,
  "active_users": 1842,
  "active_users_change_pct": 3.1,
  "churn_pct": 1.8,
  "plans": [
    { "name": "Free",  "count": 1200, "mrr_paise": 0 },
    { "name": "Pro",   "count": 540,  "mrr_paise": 2700000 },
    { "name": "Scale", "count": 102,  "mrr_paise": 2120000 }
  ],
  "usage": [
    { "day": "2026-11-19", "api_calls": 41200, "storage_writes": 8300, "job_runs": 1200 }
  ],
  "invoices": [
    { "id": 91, "number": "INV-2026-091", "amount_paise": 499000,
      "status": "paid", "period": "2026-10" }
  ],
  "quota": { "used": 412000, "limit": 500000 }
}

The quota object drives a ProgressBar in the UI.

Workspace layout

pulse/
├── Cargo.toml                 # workspace
├── crates/
│   ├── domain/                # types, no I/O — fully unit-testable
│   ├── api/                   # axum server
│   └── worker/                # background jobs
├── migrations/
├── .env.example
└── web/                       # Next.js dashboard
    ├── app/
    │   ├── layout.tsx
    │   ├── page.tsx
    │   └── globals.css
    └── components/

The domain crate has no database, no HTTP and no async — so its tests run in microseconds and its API is the contract everything else builds on.

Milestones

# Milestone Done when
1 Schema + migrations sqlx migrate run succeeds on a fresh DB
2 Ingest endpoint curl with an API key inserts an event
3 Dashboard endpoint returns the JSON above from seeded data
4 Worker rollups usage_daily fills for yesterday
5 Next.js dashboard renders real data with HeroUI
6 Deploy container runs, /readyz green, migrations on boot

Build them in this order. Each one is independently demonstrable, which matters when you are learning: a half-finished milestone is still a working system.

// crates/domain/src/lib.rs

// crates/domain/src/money.rs
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

/// An amount in paise (1 INR = 100 paise). Never use floats for money.
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(transparent)]
pub struct Paise(pub i64);

impl Paise {
    pub const ZERO: Paise = Paise(0);

    pub fn rupees(&self) -> f64 {
        self.0 as f64 / 100.0
    }

    pub fn checked_add(self, other: Paise) -> Option<Paise> {
        self.0.checked_add(other.0).map(Paise)
    }

    /// Percentage change from `self` to `next`, rounded to one decimal.
    pub fn pct_change(self, next: Paise) -> f64 {
        if self.0 == 0 {
            return 0.0;
        }
        let raw = (next.0 - self.0) as f64 / self.0 as f64 * 100.0;
        (raw * 10.0).round() / 10.0
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn converts_to_rupees() {
        assert_eq!(Paise(499_000).rupees(), 4990.0);
    }

    #[test]
    fn computes_percentage_change() {
        assert_eq!(Paise(1000).pct_change(Paise(1120)), 12.0);
        assert_eq!(Paise(0).pct_change(Paise(500)), 0.0);
    }
}

// crates/domain/src/events.rs
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use thiserror::Error;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "snake_case")]
pub enum EventKind {
    ApiCall,
    StorageWrite,
    JobRun,
}

impl EventKind {
    pub fn as_str(self) -> &'static str {
        match self {
            EventKind::ApiCall => "api_call",
            EventKind::StorageWrite => "storage_write",
            EventKind::JobRun => "job_run",
        }
    }

    pub fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<Self, DomainError> {
        match s {
            "api_call" => Ok(EventKind::ApiCall),
            "storage_write" => Ok(EventKind::StorageWrite),
            "job_run" => Ok(EventKind::JobRun),
            other => Err(DomainError::UnknownEventKind(other.to_string())),
        }
    }
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize)]
pub struct IngestEvent {
    pub kind: String,
    #[serde(default = "one")]
    pub quantity: i64,
    #[serde(default)]
    pub meta: serde_json::Value,
}

fn one() -> i64 { 1 }

#[derive(Debug, Error, PartialEq)]
pub enum DomainError {
    #[error("unknown event kind `{0}`")]
    UnknownEventKind(String),
    #[error("quantity must be between 1 and 1,000,000 (got {0})")]
    BadQuantity(i64),
    #[error("event metadata must be a JSON object")]
    BadMeta,
}

impl IngestEvent {
    pub fn validate(&self) -> Result<(EventKind, i64), DomainError> {
        let kind = EventKind::parse(&self.kind)?;
        if !(1..=1_000_000).contains(&self.quantity) {
            return Err(DomainError::BadQuantity(self.quantity));
        }
        if !self.meta.is_null() && !self.meta.is_object() {
            return Err(DomainError::BadMeta);
        }
        Ok((kind, self.quantity))
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;

    #[test]
    fn rejects_unknown_kind() {
        let e = IngestEvent { kind: "nope".into(), quantity: 1, meta: serde_json::json!({}) };
        assert!(e.validate().is_err());
    }

    #[test]
    fn rejects_zero_quantity() {
        let e = IngestEvent { kind: "api_call".into(), quantity: 0, meta: serde_json::json!({}) };
        assert_eq!(e.validate(), Err(DomainError::BadQuantity(0)));
    }

    #[test]
    fn accepts_valid_event() {
        let e = IngestEvent { kind: "job_run".into(), quantity: 5, meta: serde_json::json!({}) };
        assert_eq!(e.validate().unwrap(), (EventKind::JobRun, 5));
    }
}

crates/api — the server

// crates/api/src/main.rs
use std::process::ExitCode;
use pulse_api::{config::Config, AppState, router};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> ExitCode {
    if let Err(e) = run().await {
        eprintln!("fatal: {e:#}");
        return ExitCode::FAILURE;
    }
    ExitCode::SUCCESS
}

async fn run() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    pulse_api::telemetry::init();

    let cfg = Config::from_env()?;
    let pool = pulse_api::db::connect(&cfg.database_url).await?;

    sqlx::migrate!("../../migrations").run(&pool).await?;
    tracing::info!("migrations applied");

    let state = AppState::new(pool, cfg.clone());
    let app = router(state);

    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind(&cfg.bind_addr).await?;
    tracing::info!(addr = %listener.local_addr()?, "listening");

    axum::serve(listener, app)
        .with_graceful_shutdown(shutdown_signal())
        .await?;
    Ok(())
}

async fn shutdown_signal() {
    let ctrl_c = async { tokio::signal::ctrl_c().await.ok(); };
    let term = async {
        tokio::signal::unix::signal(tokio::signal::unix::SignalKind::terminate())
            .expect("install SIGTERM handler")
            .recv()
            .await;
    };
    tokio::select! { _ = ctrl_c => {}, _ = term => {} }
    tracing::info!("shutdown signal received");
}

// crates/api/src/lib.rs
pub mod auth;
pub mod config;
pub mod db;
pub mod error;
pub mod handlers;
pub mod telemetry;

use std::sync::Arc;
use axum::{routing::{get, post}, Router};
use sqlx::PgPool;

#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct AppState {
    pub pool: PgPool,
    pub cfg: config::Config,
}

impl AppState {
    pub fn new(pool: PgPool, cfg: config::Config) -> Arc<Self> {
        Arc::new(Self { pool, cfg })
    }
}

pub fn router(state: Arc<AppState>) -> Router {
    use tower_http::{compression::CompressionLayer, timeout::TimeoutLayer, trace::TraceLayer};

    Router::new()
        .route("/healthz", get(handlers::health::live))
        .route("/readyz", get(handlers::health::ready))
        .route("/v1/events", post(handlers::events::ingest))
        .route("/v1/dashboard", get(handlers::dashboard::get))
        .route("/v1/invoices", get(handlers::invoices::list))
        .route("/v1/invoices/{id}/pay", post(handlers::invoices::pay))
        .with_state(state)
        .layer(
            tower::ServiceBuilder::new()
                .layer(TraceLayer::new_for_http())
                .layer(CompressionLayer::new())
                .layer(TimeoutLayer::new(std::time::Duration::from_secs(30))),
        )
}

// crates/api/src/error.rs
use axum::{http::StatusCode, response::{IntoResponse, Response}, Json};
use serde_json::json;

#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
pub enum ApiError {
    #[error("unauthorized")]
    Unauthorized,
    #[error("not found")]
    NotFound,
    #[error("{0}")]
    Validation(String),
    #[error(transparent)]
    Domain(#[from] pulse_domain::DomainError),
    #[error("database error")]
    Db(#[from] sqlx::Error),
}

impl IntoResponse for ApiError {
    fn into_response(self) -> Response {
        let (status, code) = match &self {
            ApiError::Unauthorized => (StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED, "unauthorized"),
            ApiError::NotFound => (StatusCode::NOT_FOUND, "not_found"),
            ApiError::Validation(_) | ApiError::Domain(_) => {
                (StatusCode::UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY, "validation")
            }
            ApiError::Db(_) => {
                tracing::error!(error = %self, "database failure");
                (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "internal")
            }
        };

        let message = match status {
            StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR => "internal error".to_string(),
            _ => self.to_string(),
        };

        (status, Json(json!({ "error": { "code": code, "message": message } }))).into_response()
    }
}

pub type ApiResult<T> = Result<T, ApiError>;

// crates/api/src/auth.rs
use axum::{extract::FromRequestParts, http::{request::Parts, StatusCode}};
use sha2::{Digest, Sha256};

pub struct TenantId(pub i64);

pub fn hash_key(raw: &str) -> String {
    let mut h = Sha256::new();
    h.update(raw.as_bytes());
    hex::encode(h.finalize())
}

impl FromRequestParts<std::sync::Arc<crate::AppState>> for TenantId {
    type Rejection = StatusCode;

    async fn from_request_parts(
        parts: &mut Parts,
        state: &std::sync::Arc<crate::AppState>,
    ) -> Result<Self, Self::Rejection> {
        let raw = parts
            .headers
            .get(axum::http::header::AUTHORIZATION)
            .and_then(|v| v.to_str().ok())
            .and_then(|v| v.strip_prefix("Bearer "))
            .ok_or(StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED)?;

        let hash = hash_key(raw.trim());
        let row: Option<(i64,)> = sqlx::query_as(
            "SELECT tenant_id FROM api_keys WHERE key_hash = $1 AND revoked_at IS NULL",
        )
        .bind(hash)
        .fetch_optional(&state.pool)
        .await
        .map_err(|_| StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)?;

        row.map(|(id,)| TenantId(id)).ok_or(StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED)
    }
}

// crates/api/src/handlers/events.rs
use axum::{extract::State, http::StatusCode, Json};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::sync::Arc;
use pulse_domain::IngestEvent;

use crate::{auth::TenantId, error::ApiResult, AppState};

#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
pub struct IngestBody {
    pub events: Vec<IngestEvent>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Serialize)]
pub struct IngestResponse {
    pub accepted: usize,
}

pub async fn ingest(
    State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>,
    TenantId(tenant): TenantId,
    Json(body): Json<IngestBody>,
) -> ApiResult<(StatusCode, Json<IngestResponse>)> {
    if body.events.is_empty() {
        return Err(crate::error::ApiError::Validation("no events".into()));
    }
    if body.events.len() > 1000 {
        return Err(crate::error::ApiError::Validation("max 1000 events per request".into()));
    }

    // validate everything before writing anything
    let mut rows = Vec::with_capacity(body.events.len());
    for e in &body.events {
        let (kind, qty) = e.validate()?;
        rows.push((kind.as_str(), qty, e.meta.clone()));
    }

    let mut tx = state.pool.begin().await?;
    for (kind, qty, meta) in &rows {
        sqlx::query(
            "INSERT INTO events (tenant_id, kind, quantity, meta) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)",
        )
        .bind(tenant)
        .bind(*kind)
        .bind(*qty)
        .bind(meta)
        .execute(&mut *tx)
        .await?;
    }
    tx.commit().await?;

    Ok((StatusCode::ACCEPTED, Json(IngestResponse { accepted: rows.len() })))
}

// crates/api/src/handlers/dashboard.rs
use axum::{extract::State, Json};
use std::sync::Arc;
use pulse_domain::{Dashboard, InvoiceRow, Paise, PlanRow, Quota, UsageDay};

use crate::{auth::TenantId, error::ApiResult, AppState};

pub async fn get(
    State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>,
    TenantId(tenant): TenantId,
) -> ApiResult<Json<Dashboard>> {
    let plans: Vec<(String, i64, i64)> = sqlx::query_as(
        "SELECT plan, COUNT(*)::bigint, (COUNT(*) * 499000)::bigint
         FROM tenants GROUP BY plan ORDER BY 3 DESC",
    )
    .fetch_all(&state.pool)
    .await?;

    let mrr: i64 = plans.iter().map(|(_, _, m)| *m).sum();

    let usage_rows: Vec<(chrono::NaiveDate, String, i64)> = sqlx::query_as(
        "SELECT day, kind, total FROM usage_daily
         WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND day >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '13 days'
         ORDER BY day",
    )
    .bind(tenant)
    .fetch_all(&state.pool)
    .await?;

    let mut usage: Vec<UsageDay> = Vec::new();
    for (day, kind, total) in usage_rows {
        let key = day.format("%Y-%m-%d").to_string();
        let entry = match usage.iter_mut().find(|u| u.day == key) {
            Some(e) => e,
            None => {
                usage.push(UsageDay {
                    day: key,
                    api_calls: 0,
                    storage_writes: 0,
                    job_runs: 0,
                });
                usage.last_mut().expect("just pushed")
            }
        };
        match kind.as_str() {
            "api_call" => entry.api_calls = total,
            "storage_write" => entry.storage_writes = total,
            "job_run" => entry.job_runs = total,
            _ => {}
        }
    }

    let invoice_rows: Vec<(i64, String, i64, String, String)> = sqlx::query_as(
        "SELECT id, number, amount_paise, status, to_char(period_start, 'YYYY-MM')
         FROM invoices WHERE tenant_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 12",
    )
    .bind(tenant)
    .fetch_all(&state.pool)
    .await?;

    let used: i64 = usage.iter().map(|u| u.api_calls).sum();

    Ok(Json(Dashboard {
        mrr: Paise(mrr),
        mrr_change_pct: 12.4,
        active_users: 1842,
        active_users_change_pct: 3.1,
        churn_pct: 1.8,
        plans: plans
            .into_iter()
            .map(|(name, count, m)| PlanRow { name, count, mrr: Paise(m) })
            .collect(),
        usage,
        invoices: invoice_rows
            .into_iter()
            .map(|(id, number, amount, status, period)| InvoiceRow {
                id,
                number,
                amount: Paise(amount),
                status,
                period,
            })
            .collect(),
        quota: Quota { used, limit: 500_000 },
    }))
}

Note on the demo numbers: mrr_change_pct, active_users and churn_pct are hard-coded in this skeleton so the dashboard has something to render before you have historical data. The exercises ask you to compute them properly from a metrics_daily table.

crates/worker — rollups and jobs

// crates/worker/src/main.rs
use std::time::Duration;
use sqlx::PgPool;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    pulse_api::telemetry::init();
    let url = std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")?;
    let pool = pulse_api::db::connect(&url).await?;
    let worker = format!("worker-{}", std::process::id());

    let pool2 = pool.clone();
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        let mut tick = tokio::time::interval(Duration::from_secs(60));
        loop {
            tick.tick().await;
            if let Err(e) = rollup_yesterday(&pool2).await {
                tracing::error!(error = %e, "rollup failed");
            }
        }
    });

    loop {
        if let Err(e) = tick(&pool, &worker).await {
            tracing::error!(error = %e, "worker tick failed");
            tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_secs(5)).await;
        }
    }
}

async fn tick(pool: &PgPool, worker: &str) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let jobs: Vec<(i64, String, serde_json::Value, i32)> = sqlx::query_as(
        r#"UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running', attempts = attempts + 1,
                locked_at = now(), locked_by = $1
           WHERE id IN (
             SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status = 'pending' AND run_at <= now()
             ORDER BY run_at FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10
           )
           RETURNING id, kind, payload, attempts"#,
    )
    .bind(worker)
    .fetch_all(pool)
    .await?;

    for (id, kind, payload, attempts) in jobs {
        let result = match kind.as_str() {
            "rollup_day" => rollup_day(pool, &payload).await,
            other => Err(anyhow::anyhow!("unknown job kind {other}")),
        };
        match result {
            Ok(()) => {
                sqlx::query("UPDATE jobs SET status='done', locked_at=NULL WHERE id=$1")
                    .bind(id).execute(pool).await?;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                let delay = (1i64 << attempts.min(10)).min(3600);
                sqlx::query(
                    "UPDATE jobs SET status='pending', last_error=$2, locked_at=NULL,
                     run_at = now() + make_interval(secs => $3) WHERE id=$1",
                )
                .bind(id).bind(e.to_string()).bind(delay as f64)
                .execute(pool).await?;
                tracing::warn!(id, error = %e, "job failed, will retry");
            }
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

async fn rollup_day(pool: &PgPool, payload: &serde_json::Value) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let day = payload["day"].as_str().ok_or_else(|| anyhow::anyhow!("missing day"))?;
    sqlx::query(
        r#"INSERT INTO usage_daily (tenant_id, day, kind, total)
           SELECT tenant_id, $1::date, kind, SUM(quantity)
           FROM events
           WHERE occurred_at >= $1::date AND occurred_at < $1::date + 1
           GROUP BY tenant_id, kind
           ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, day, kind)
           DO UPDATE SET total = EXCLUDED.total"#,
    )
    .bind(day)
    .execute(pool)
    .await?;
    tracing::info!(day, "rollup complete");
    Ok(())
}

async fn rollup_yesterday(pool: &PgPool) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let yesterday = (chrono::Utc::now().date_naive() - chrono::Duration::days(1))
        .format("%Y-%m-%d")
        .to_string();
    let payload = serde_json::json!({ "day": yesterday });
    sqlx::query(
        "INSERT INTO jobs (kind, payload) VALUES ('rollup_day', $1)
         ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING",
    )
    .bind(payload)
    .execute(pool)
    .await?;
    Ok(())
}

Verifying it

$ docker run -d --name pulse-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres -p 5432:5432 postgres:16
$ export DATABASE_URL="postgres://postgres:postgres@localhost/pulse"
$ sqlx database create && sqlx migrate run

$ cargo run -p api &
$ curl localhost:8080/healthz
$ curl localhost:8080/readyz

# seed a tenant + key
$ psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "INSERT INTO tenants (name, plan) VALUES ('Acme', 'pro');"
$ KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
$ psql "$DATABASE_URL" -c "INSERT INTO api_keys (tenant_id, key_hash, prefix)
    VALUES (1, encode(sha256('$KEY'::bytea), 'hex'), '${KEY:0:8}');"

$ curl -X POST localhost:8080/v1/events \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"events":[{"kind":"api_call","quantity":3},{"kind":"job_run"}]}'

$ curl localhost:8080/v1/dashboard -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" | jq

Gotcha: the sha256 above must match hash_key() — the same bytes, the same encoding. encode(sha256($1::bytea), 'hex') produces lowercase hex, which is what hex::encode produces. A mismatch gives you a 401 you will spend an hour on.

Exercises

  1. Implement metrics_daily and compute mrr_change_pct, active_users and churn_pct from real data instead of the hard-coded values.
  2. Add POST /v1/invoices/{id}/pay and make it idempotent.
  3. Add pagination to /v1/invoices with keyset pagination.
  4. Add a usage_daily backfill command that rolls up the last 90 days.
  5. Write an integration test with sqlx::test covering ingest → dashboard.
  6. Add a request-id middleware that puts x-request-id into every log line.
