03 · The Dashboard Frontend

The Pulse dashboard is a Next.js App Router app with Tailwind CSS v4 and HeroUI v3 (@heroui/react + @heroui/styles). This module covers the scaffold, the component composition, and the two things that are easy to get wrong: the stylesheet import order and accessibility.

The full working project ships alongside this course as heroui-saas-dashboard/ (see the README of that repo for exact versions).

Scaffold

$ npx create-next-app@latest web --typescript --app --tailwind --eslint --src-dir=false
$ cd web
$ npm install @heroui/react @heroui/styles

Add a typecheck script, because next build is not a typecheck you can iterate on:

{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "next dev",
    "build": "next build",
    "start": "next start",
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit",
    "lint": "next lint"
  }
}

$ npm run typecheck
$ npm run build

Both must pass before you call the UI done. A dev server that renders is not the same thing — build catches type errors, invalid exports and server/client boundary mistakes that dev tolerates.

Tailwind v4: no config file

Tailwind v4 is CSS-first. There is no tailwind.config.js; configuration lives in the stylesheet via @theme.

// postcss.config.mjs
const config = {
  plugins: { "@tailwindcss/postcss": {} },
};
export default config;

The global stylesheet — order matters

/* app/globals.css */
@import "tailwindcss";
@import "@heroui/styles";     /* AFTER Tailwind — this is the rule */

/* optional: tune the design tokens HeroUI exposes */
:root {
  --radius-lg: 0.875rem;
}

Gotcha: importing @heroui/styles before tailwindcss compiles but silently loses component styles, because Tailwind's preflight resets them afterwards. The order is not cosmetic.

Styling with the library's variables, not overrides

HeroUI exposes spacing and radius as CSS custom properties. Use them instead of patching component internals:

<div className="p-[var(--spacing-md)] rounded-[var(--radius-lg)] gap-[var(--spacing-sm)] flex flex-col">
  <Card className="shadow-none">
    <Card.Header className="pb-[var(--spacing-sm)]">…</Card.Header>
  </Card>
</div>

Why this matters: overriding .card__body { padding: 12px } breaks the moment the library changes its internal class names, and it fights the design system's density scale. Consuming the variables keeps your layout consistent with the components and survives upgrades.

No provider in v3

HeroUI v3 does not need a provider wrapper. There is no <HeroUIProvider> to add to app/layout.tsx. If you copy a v2 tutorial that wraps the tree in a provider, delete it — at best it is dead code, at worst it duplicates context.

// app/layout.tsx
import type { Metadata } from "next";
import "./globals.css";

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: "Pulse — Usage Analytics",
  description: "SaaS usage analytics dashboard",
};

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en" suppressHydrationWarning>
      <body className="min-h-dvh bg-[var(--background)] text-[var(--foreground)]">
        {children}
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

The compound component API

v3 components compose with dot notation. Card.Header and Card.Content are the ones that replace v2's monolithic props:

import { Card, Badge, ProgressBar } from "@heroui/react";

<Card>
  <Card.Header className="flex items-center justify-between">
    <div>
      <p className="text-sm opacity-70">Monthly recurring revenue</p>
      <p className="text-2xl font-semibold tabular-nums">₹48,200</p>
    </div>
    <Badge color="success">+12.4%</Badge>
  </Card.Header>
  <Card.Content>
    <ProgressBar value={82} aria-label="Quota used" />
  </Card.Content>
</Card>

That pattern repeats for every KPI tile. Card.Header carries the label and trend; Card.Content carries the visual.

Layout: sticky header + responsive left nav

// app/(dashboard)/layout.tsx  — client component
"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { Drawer, Button } from "@heroui/react";
import { SideNav } from "@/components/side-nav";
import { SearchField } from "@/components/search-field";

export default function DashboardLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const [navOpen, setNavOpen] = useState(false);

  return (
    <div className="min-h-dvh">
      {/* sticky header */}
      <header className="sticky top-0 z-40 border-b border-[var(--border)] bg-[var(--background)]/80 backdrop-blur">
        <div className="flex items-center gap-3 px-[var(--spacing-md)] py-[var(--spacing-sm)]">
          <Button
            className="lg:hidden"
            aria-label="Open navigation"
            onPress={() => setNavOpen(true)}
          >
            ☰
          </Button>
          <span className="font-semibold">Pulse</span>
          <div className="ml-auto w-full max-w-sm">
            <SearchField />
          </div>
        </div>
      </header>

      <div className="flex">
        {/* desktop nav: hidden below 1024px */}
        <aside className="hidden lg:block w-64 shrink-0 border-r border-[var(--border)] min-h-[calc(100dvh-57px)]">
          <SideNav />
        </aside>

        {/* mobile nav: a Drawer below 1024px */}
        <Drawer isOpen={navOpen} onOpenChange={setNavOpen} placement="left">
          <Drawer.Content>
            <Drawer.Header>Navigation</Drawer.Header>
            <Drawer.Body>
              <SideNav onNavigate={() => setNavOpen(false)} />
            </Drawer.Body>
          </Drawer.Content>
        </Drawer>

        <main className="flex-1 p-[var(--spacing-md)]">{children}</main>
      </div>
    </div>
  );
}

Two details that make this work:

  • lg: is Tailwind's min-width: 1024px. hidden lg:block on the aside plus lg:hidden on the trigger gives exactly the "collapses below 1024px" behaviour.
  • The sticky header needs a stacking context above the content (z-40) or cards scroll over it.

The dashboard page

// app/page.tsx
import { Card, Badge, ProgressBar, Table, Avatar, Tabs, Tabs.List, Tabs.Panel } from "@heroui/react";
import { KpiCard } from "@/components/kpi-card";
import { UsageChart } from "@/components/usage-chart";
import { InvoiceTable } from "@/components/invoice-table";
import { PlanBreakdown } from "@/components/plan-breakdown";

export default async function Page() {
  const data = await getDashboard();          // server-side fetch, module 05.02 API

  return (
    <div className="flex flex-col gap-[var(--spacing-lg)]">
      <div className="grid gap-[var(--spacing-md)] sm:grid-cols-2 xl:grid-cols-4">
        <KpiCard label="MRR" value={formatInr(data.mrr)} change={data.mrr_change_pct} />
        <KpiCard label="Active users" value={data.active_users} change={data.active_users_change_pct} />
        <KpiCard label="Churn" value={`${data.churn_pct}%`} change={-0.4} />
        <KpiCard label="Quota used" value={`${data.quota.used}/${data.quota.limit}`}>
          <ProgressBar
            value={Math.round((data.quota.used / data.quota.limit) * 100)}
            aria-label={`Quota used: ${data.quota.used} of ${data.quota.limit} API calls`}
          />
        </KpiCard>
      </div>

      <Tabs aria-label="Dashboard sections">
        <Tabs.List>
          <Tabs.Tab id="usage">Usage</Tabs.Tab>
          <Tabs.Tab id="plans">Plans</Tabs.Tab>
          <Tabs.Tab id="invoices">Invoices</Tabs.Tab>
        </Tabs.List>
        <Tabs.Panel id="usage"><UsageChart data={data.usage} /></Tabs.Panel>
        <Tabs.Panel id="plans"><PlanBreakdown plans={data.plans} /></Tabs.Panel>
        <Tabs.Panel id="invoices"><InvoiceTable invoices={data.invoices} /></Tabs.Panel>
      </Tabs>
    </div>
  );
}

The table, with accessible labelling

// components/invoice-table.tsx
"use client";

import { Table, Badge, Dropdown, Button } from "@heroui/react";

export function InvoiceTable({ invoices }: { invoices: InvoiceRow[] }) {
  return (
    <Table aria-label="Recent invoices">
      <Table.Header>
        <Table.Column isRowHeader>Invoice</Table.Column>
        <Table.Column>Period</Table.Column>
        <Table.Column>Amount</Table.Column>
        <Table.Column>Status</Table.Column>
        <Table.Column>Actions</Table.Column>
      </Table.Header>
      <Table.Body>
        {invoices.map((inv) => (
          <Table.Row key={inv.id}>
            <Table.Cell>{inv.number}</Table.Cell>
            <Table.Cell>{inv.period}</Table.Cell>
            <Table.Cell className="tabular-nums">{formatInr(inv.amount)}</Table.Cell>
            <Table.Cell>
              <Badge color={inv.status === "paid" ? "success" : "warning"}>
                {inv.status}
              </Badge>
            </Table.Cell>
            <Table.Cell>
              <Dropdown>
                <Dropdown.Trigger>
                  <Button size="sm" variant="flat" aria-label={`Actions for ${inv.number}`}>
                    ⋯
                  </Button>
                </Dropdown.Trigger>
                <Dropdown.Menu aria-label={`Actions for ${inv.number}`}>
                  <Dropdown.Item id="view">View</Dropdown.Item>
                  <Dropdown.Item id="download">Download PDF</Dropdown.Item>
                  <Dropdown.Item id="void">Void</Dropdown.Item>
                </Dropdown.Menu>
              </Dropdown>
            </Table.Cell>
          </Table.Row>
        ))}
      </Table.Body>
    </Table>
  );
}

aria-label on <Table> gives the grid a name for screen readers, and isRowHeader on the first column makes each row announce "INV-2026-091, row 1" instead of just reading cell values. Without both, a screen-reader user hears an unnamed grid of numbers.

Select and ListBox

// components/plan-filter.tsx
"use client";

import { Select, ListBox } from "@heroui/react";

export function PlanFilter({ value, onChange }: { value: string; onChange: (v: string) => void }) {
  return (
    <Select
      aria-label="Filter by plan"
      placeholder="All plans"
      selectedKey={value}
      onSelectionChange={(k) => onChange(String(k))}
    >
      <ListBox>
        <ListBox.Item id="all">All plans</ListBox.Item>
        <ListBox.Item id="free">Free</ListBox.Item>
        <ListBox.Item id="pro">Pro</ListBox.Item>
        <ListBox.Item id="scale">Scale</ListBox.Item>
      </ListBox>
    </Select>
  );
}

aria-label is required: a Select with only a placeholder has no accessible name, and a screen reader announces an unnamed combobox.

Modal and Drawer

"use client";
import { Modal, Button } from "@heroui/react";

const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);

<Button onPress={() => setOpen(true)}>Invite member</Button>

<Modal isOpen={open} onOpenChange={setOpen}>
  <Modal.Content>
    <Modal.Header>Invite a member</Modal.Header>
    <Modal.Body>
      <InviteForm onDone={() => setOpen(false)} />
    </Modal.Body>
    <Modal.Footer>
      <Button variant="light" onPress={() => setOpen(false)}>Cancel</Button>
      <Button type="submit" form="invite-form">Send invite</Button>
    </Modal.Footer>
  </Modal.Content>
</Modal>

Both Modal and Drawer handle focus trapping, Escape, and restoring focus to the trigger on close. That is a large accessibility win you get for free — do not reimplement it with a div.

Avatar and Badge

<Avatar src={user.avatarUrl} name={user.name} aria-label={user.name} size="sm" />
<Badge color="danger">{unread}</Badge>

Search field

// components/search-field.tsx
"use client";
import { SearchField as HeroSearchField } from "@heroui/react";

export function SearchField() {
  return (
    <HeroSearchField
      aria-label="Search invoices, customers and plans"
      placeholder="Search…"
      className="w-full"
    />
  );
}

Accessibility checklist

  • [ ] Every Select, Table, Modal, Drawer and icon-only Button has an aria-label or an associated visible label.
  • [ ] Table has aria-label and isRowHeader on the first column.
  • [ ] Icon-only buttons say what they do (aria-label="Open navigation"), not what they look like.
  • [ ] Focus is visible: never outline-none without a focus-visible ring.
  • [ ] Colour is not the only signal — the invoice status has text, not just a green dot.
  • [ ] ProgressBar has an aria-label including the actual numbers.
  • [ ] Tab order follows visual order; the nav Drawer comes before main in the DOM.
  • [ ] Contrast ≥ 4.5:1 for body text.

Verifying keyboard navigation

Do this by hand, in this order — it takes two minutes and catches almost everything:

Component Keys to test Expected
Select Tab to focus, Enter/Space to open menu opens, focus moves into it
Select ↓ ↑ highlight moves, announced by the screen reader
Select Enter selects, closes, focus returns to the trigger
Select Esc closes without changing the value
Table Tab focus enters the grid, arrow keys move between cells
Table Home / End first / last cell in the row
Modal Esc closes; focus returns to the button that opened it
Drawer Tab focus is trapped inside while open
Nav Tab from the header reaches the nav links in visual order

Screen-reader spot checks (VoiceOver Cmd+F5 on macOS, NVDA on Windows):

  1. The table announces its name and "row 1 of 12".
  2. The select announces "Filter by plan, combo box, All plans".
  3. The progress bar announces "Quota used: 412000 of 500000".

Wiring the API

// lib/api.ts
const API = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL ?? "http://localhost:8080";

export async function getDashboard(): Promise<Dashboard> {
  const res = await fetch(`${API}/v1/dashboard`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.API_TOKEN}` },
    next: { revalidate: 30 },        // cache for 30s
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`dashboard: ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

Fetch on the server where possible: the token stays out of the browser bundle, and the first paint has data instead of a spinner.

Loading and error states

// app/loading.tsx
export default function Loading() {
  return <div className="p-[var(--spacing-lg)] opacity-60">Loading dashboard…</div>;
}

// app/error.tsx
"use client";
export default function Error({ reset }: { error: Error; reset: () => void }) {
  return (
    <div className="p-[var(--spacing-lg)]">
      <h2 className="font-semibold">Could not load the dashboard</h2>
      <button className="underline" onClick={reset}>Try again</button>
    </div>
  );
}

loading.tsx and error.tsx are App Router conventions — no library needed.

Exercises

  1. Confirm the stylesheet import order by swapping the two @import lines and observing the visual breakage.
  2. Add a fourth KPI tile using Card + Card.Header + Card.Content.
  3. Move every hard-coded padding to var(--spacing-*) and every radius to var(--radius-*).
  4. Add a Select + ListBox filter that actually filters the invoice table.
  5. Run the keyboard table above against your build and fix anything that fails.
  6. Add a Modal to create an invoice and a Drawer for invoice detail, both with correct focus behaviour.
  7. Confirm npm run typecheck and npm run build both pass with zero warnings.

04 · Deployment

A Rust service is one of the easiest things to deploy: a single static binary, no interpreter, no node_modules. This module covers containerising it properly and running it in production.

The multi-stage Dockerfile

# ---- build ----
FROM rust:1.85-bookworm AS builder
WORKDIR /app

# cache dependencies separately from source
COPY Cargo.toml Cargo.lock ./
COPY crates ./crates
RUN cargo build --release --locked -p api -p worker

# ---- runtime ----
FROM debian:bookworm-slim
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN useradd -m -u 10001 app
WORKDIR /app

COPY --from=builder /app/target/release/api /usr/local/bin/api
COPY --from=builder /app/target/release/worker /usr/local/bin/worker

USER app
EXPOSE 8080
ENV RUST_LOG=info
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/api"]
Choice Why
--locked fails the build if Cargo.lock would change
non-root user container escape is much less useful as uid 10001
ca-certificates TLS to Postgres/APIs needs a trust store
no cargo build of tests halves build time
debian:bookworm-slim runtime glibc present, ~75 MB

Distroless / scratch, and static builds

FROM rust:1.85-bookworm AS builder
RUN rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl -p api

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12
COPY --from=builder /app/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/api /api
USER 10001
ENTRYPOINT ["/api"]

Result: a ~10 MB image with no shell, no package manager, and almost no attack surface. Note that sqlx::migrate! embeds your migrations, so there is no file to copy.

Gotcha: with scratch there is no /etc/passwd, no ca-certificates, and no timezone database. Use distroless/static (it includes certs) rather than bare scratch unless you have checked every dependency.

Build cache that actually works

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
FROM rust:1.85-bookworm AS builder
WORKDIR /app

# 1. copy manifests only, build a dummy to warm the dependency cache
COPY Cargo.toml Cargo.lock ./
COPY crates/domain/Cargo.toml crates/domain/
COPY crates/api/Cargo.toml crates/api/
COPY crates/worker/Cargo.toml crates/worker/
RUN mkdir -p crates/domain/src crates/api/src crates/worker/src \
 && echo "fn main(){}" > crates/api/src/main.rs \
 && echo "" > crates/api/src/lib.rs \
 && echo "fn main(){}" > crates/worker/src/main.rs \
 && echo "" > crates/domain/src/lib.rs \
 && cargo build --release || true

# 2. now copy real source — only this layer invalidates on a code change
COPY crates ./crates
RUN touch crates/*/src/main.rs crates/*/src/lib.rs \
 && cargo build --release --locked

Without this dance, every source change re-downloads and re-compiles all ~300 dependencies. It turns a 6-minute CI build into 40 seconds.

Docker Compose for local development

services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
      POSTGRES_DB: pulse
    ports: ["5432:5432"]
    volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

  api:
    build: .
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:postgres@postgres/pulse
      RUST_LOG: info,pulse_api=debug
      BIND_ADDR: 0.0.0.0:8080
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    depends_on:
      postgres: { condition: service_healthy }

  worker:
    build: .
    entrypoint: ["/usr/local/bin/worker"]
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:postgres@postgres/pulse
    depends_on:
      postgres: { condition: service_healthy }

  web:
    build: ./web
    environment:
      NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: http://localhost:8080
    ports: ["3000:3000"]
    depends_on: [api]

volumes:
  pgdata:

Configuration

Twelve-factor: everything from the environment, nothing baked into the image.

// crates/api/src/config.rs
use anyhow::{Context, Result};

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct Config {
    pub database_url: String,
    pub bind_addr: String,
    pub log_format: String,
    pub pool_size: u32,
}

impl Config {
    pub fn from_env() -> Result<Self> {
        Ok(Self {
            database_url: std::env::var("DATABASE_URL")
                .context("DATABASE_URL is required")?,
            bind_addr: std::env::var("BIND_ADDR")
                .unwrap_or_else(|_| "0.0.0.0:8080".into()),
            log_format: std::env::var("LOG_FORMAT").unwrap_or_else(|_| "json".into()),
            pool_size: std::env::var("POOL_SIZE").ok()
                .and_then(|v| v.parse().ok())
                .unwrap_or(10),
        })
    }
}

Fail fast and loudly on a missing required variable — a container that starts and then 500s on every request is worse than one that refuses to start.

Migrations in production

Three approaches, in order of preference:

  1. A separate migration job that runs before the deployment and must succeed. Cleanest: the API never blocks on DDL, and a failed migration stops the deploy.
  2. At API startup (sqlx::migrate!().run()) — simple, but with N replicas they all race. sqlx takes an advisory lock so it is safe, just serialised.
  3. Manually — only acceptable for a single-instance service.
$ sqlx migrate run --database-url "$DATABASE_URL"

Gotcha: a migration that takes 4 minutes on a large table will hold the advisory lock and block every starting replica. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (outside a transaction) and add columns as nullable first.

Zero-downtime deploys

The requirements:

  1. Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM — drain in-flight requests. (Already wired in module 05.02.)
  2. Readiness probe returns 503 while shutting down, so the load balancer stops sending traffic before the process exits.
  3. Long enough terminationGracePeriodSeconds for the drain (30–60 s).
// flip readiness false on shutdown
static SHUTTING_DOWN: std::sync::atomic::AtomicBool =
    std::sync::atomic::AtomicBool::new(false);

pub async fn ready(State(state): State<Arc<AppState>>) -> (StatusCode, Json<Value>) {
    if SHUTTING_DOWN.load(std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed) {
        return (StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, Json(json!({ "status": "draining" })));
    }
    match sqlx::query("SELECT 1").execute(&state.pool).await {
        Ok(_) => (StatusCode::OK, Json(json!({ "status": "ok" }))),
        Err(_) => (StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, Json(json!({ "status": "db down" }))),
    }
}

Kubernetes essentials

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: pulse-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 }
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/pulse-api:1.4.2   # never :latest
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          envFrom:
            - secretRef: { name: pulse-secrets }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }
            limits:   { memory: 512Mi }
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 10001
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false

maxUnavailable: 0 with maxSurge: 1 means capacity never drops during a rollout. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true is possible because the binary writes nothing to disk — a Rust service has no temp files by default.

Memory limits deserve a note: Rust has no GC, so RSS is stable and predictable. Set the limit ~2× steady-state RSS and you will not see OOM kills. That predictability is one of the better operational arguments for Rust.

Observability in production

RUST_LOG=info,pulse_api=debug,sqlx=warn
LOG_FORMAT=json
OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4317

Ship /metrics to Prometheus. Alert on:

Alert Condition
Error rate 5xx > 1% for 5 min
Latency p99 > 1 s for 5 min
Saturation DB pool in-use > 90% for 5 min
Queue stuck jobs_pending rising for 10 min
Crash loop restart count > 3 in 10 min

The frontend

# web/Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:20-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=builder /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=builder /app/.next/static ./.next/static
COPY --from=builder /app/public ./public
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

Enable output: "standalone" in next.config.ts for a ~120 MB image instead of ~1 GB. Deploy it to Vercel if you can — it is less work and the Next.js build pipeline is tuned for it.

Release checklist

  • [ ] cargo clippy -- -D warnings clean
  • [ ] cargo test --workspace and cargo test --doc green
  • [ ] cargo audit and cargo deny check clean
  • [ ] npm run typecheck and npm run build green
  • [ ] Migrations reviewed, and reversible or additive-only
  • [ ] Image tagged with a version, never latest
  • [ ] /healthz and /readyz respond correctly
  • [ ] Graceful shutdown verified (docker stop takes ~2 s, not 10)
  • [ ] Rollback plan: previous image tag is one command away
  • [ ] Dashboards and alerts exist before the deploy, not after

Exercises

  1. Build the multi-stage image and compare its size against a naive single-stage build.
  2. Add the dependency-caching layer and measure the rebuild time after touching one .rs file.
  3. Switch to distroless/static and confirm TLS to Postgres still works.
  4. Verify graceful shutdown: start a 5-second request, docker stop, and confirm it completes.
  5. Make /readyz return 503 during shutdown and observe the load balancer behaviour.
  6. Write the Compose file and get the full stack (Postgres + API + worker + web) running with one command.

01 · Cheat Sheet

Everything you need while writing code, on one page.

Cargo

cargo new myapp            # binary
cargo new --lib mylib      # library
cargo check                # fast type check
cargo run -- --flag        # args after --
cargo test -- --nocapture
cargo build --release
cargo add serde --features derive
cargo tree -d              # duplicate deps
cargo fmt && cargo clippy -- -D warnings
cargo doc --no-deps --open
cargo expand               # macro output (needs cargo-expand)
cargo bench

Types

i8 i16 i32 i64 i128 isize     // signed
u8 u16 u32 u64 u128 usize     // unsigned
f32 f64 bool char
String  &str   // owned / borrowed
[T; N]  Vec<T> // array / vector
(T, U)         // tuple
Option<T>      // Some / None
Result<T, E>   // Ok / Err
Box<T> Rc<T> Arc<T> RefCell<T> Cell<T> Mutex<T> RwLock<T>
HashMap<K,V> BTreeMap<K,V> HashSet<T> BTreeSet<T> VecDeque<T>

Conversions

let s = String::from("x");
let s: String = "x".to_string();
let s: String = "x".into();
let b: &str = &s;                 // deref coercion
let n: i64 = i32_val as i64;      // widening cast
let n: u8 = u8::try_from(300)?;   // fallible narrowing
let v: Vec<char> = s.chars().collect();
let s: String = v.iter().collect();
let n: i32 = "42".parse()?;

02 · Common Errors, Decoded

The compiler messages you will actually see, what they mean, and the fix. Rust's error codes are stable — search rust E0382 and you get the official explanation.

E0382 — borrow of moved value

error[E0382]: borrow of moved value: `s`
  |
3 |     let s = String::from("hi");
  |         - move occurs because `s` has type `String`
4 |     let t = s;
  |             - value moved here
5 |     println!("{s}");
  |               ^^^ value borrowed here after move
help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable

Cause: ownership moved to t, then you used s. Fixes, best first: pass &s instead of s; return the value from the function; if it is genuinely needed twice, s.clone() — but think first.

E0502 — cannot borrow as mutable because also borrowed as immutable

error[E0502]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable
5 | let a = &v;
6 | v.push(1);
  | ^^^^^^^^^ mutable borrow occurs here
7 | println!("{a:?}");

Cause: a shared borrow is still live when you try to mutate. Fix: end the borrow first (use a before v.push, or scope it in { }), or collect the data you need out of a before mutating.

E0499 — two mutable borrows

error[E0499]: cannot borrow `v` as mutable more than once at a time

Cause: usually a loop mutating a collection it is iterating. Fix: iter_mut(), index-based access, or collect-then-modify.

E0596 — cannot borrow as mutable, not declared as mutable

error[E0596]: cannot borrow `x` as mutable, as it is not declared as mutable
help: consider changing this to be mutable: `mut x`

Fix: let mut x. If x is a field accessed through &self, the method needs &mut self — or interior mutability.

E0106 — missing lifetime specifier

error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier
1 | fn longest(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str {
  |               ----     ----     ^ expected named lifetime parameter

Cause: two input references, so the compiler cannot tell which one the output comes from. Fix: fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str.

E0597 — does not live long enough

error[E0597]: `s` does not live long enough
  |
5 |     let r = &s;
  |              ^ borrowed value does not live long enough
6 | }
  | - `s` dropped here while still borrowed

Cause: a reference outlives its owner — often a struct holding a borrow of a local. Fix: make the owner live longer, or make the struct own the data (String/Arc<str> instead of &str).

E0515 — returning a reference to local data

error[E0515]: cannot return value referencing local variable `s`

Fix: return an owned value, or take the destination as a parameter (fn fill(&self, out: &mut String)).

E0308 — mismatched types

The most common error in Rust, and the most generic. Read the expected / found pair, not the code frame.

error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:3:18
  |
3 |     let x: i32 = "hello";
  |            ---   ^^^^^^^ expected `i32`, found `&str`

Common variants:

Message Meaning
expected i32, found () a trailing ; turned your value into a statement
expected String, found &str add .to_string() or .into()
expected Option<T>, found T wrap in Some(...)
expected u32, found i32 explicit cast: as u32 or try_from

E0277 — trait bound not satisfied

error[E0277]: the trait bound `MyStruct: Debug` is not satisfied
   = help: the trait `Debug` is not implemented for `MyStruct`
   = note: add `#[derive(Debug)]` to `MyStruct`

The help: and note: lines are usually the complete answer. The three most common causes:

  1. Missing #[derive(Debug)] / Clone / PartialEq.
  2. A type that is not Send used across threads (see E0277 + Send).
  3. ? on an error type with no From impl.

E0277 + Send — the async killer

error: future cannot be sent between threads safely
   = help: within `impl Future`, the trait `Send` is not implemented for `Rc<u32>`
note: required by a bound in `tokio::spawn`

Cause: a non-Send value (usually Rc, RefCell, or a guard) is held across an .await inside a spawned task. Fix: scope the value so it drops before the .await, or replace Rc with Arc and RefCell with Mutex.

E0433 / E0432 — unresolved import or path

error[E0432]: unresolved import `crate::db::Pool`
error[E0433]: failed to resolve: use of undeclared crate or module `serde`

Fixes: add the dependency to Cargo.toml; declare mod db;; check the underscore-vs-hyphen crate name; check pub visibility on every step of the path.

E0061 — wrong number of arguments

error[E0061]: this function takes 2 arguments but 1 argument was supplied

Often caused by a library version bump. Check cargo doc --open for the signature you actually have.

E0507 — cannot move out of borrowed content

error[E0507]: cannot move out of `self.field` which is behind a shared reference

Fix: .clone() it, take &self.field instead, or use std::mem::take / Option::take when you legitimately want to move out.

E0282 / E0283 — type annotations needed

error[E0282]: type annotations needed for `Vec<T>`

Fix: let v: Vec<i32> = Vec::new(); or Vec::<i32>::new(). Usually happens with collect() — annotate the target type: let v: Vec<_> = it.collect();.

cannot find macro / derive not found

error: cannot find derive macro `Serialize` in this scope

Fix: use serde::Serialize; — the derive macro is a separate import from the trait in many crates. Also check the crate's feature flags (serde needs derive).

Borrow-checker fights, and their real fixes

Symptom Real fix
Mutating in a loop over the collection iter_mut, index loop, or collect-then-modify
Returning &local return owned, or pass &mut out-param
Two &mut into one Vec split_at_mut, chunks_mut, iter_mut
Self-referential struct store an index or offset, not a slice
Storing a borrow in a long-lived struct own the data (String, Arc)
"I just need to cache this here" Arc<Mutex<…>>, or restructure
Closure captures conflict move the closure, or narrow the capture

Rule of thumb: every borrow error is a question about ownership. Answer the question; do not silence it with clone().

Runtime panics

Panic Cause
index out of bounds v[i] with i >= v.len() — use get
called Option::unwrap() on a None value no value — handle None
called Result::unwrap() on an Err value: … read the inner error
attempt to add with overflow debug-only — use checked_add
already borrowed: BorrowMutError RefCell double borrow
already mutably borrowed: BorrowError RefCell borrow while mutably borrowed
byte index N is not a char boundary slicing a String mid-character
cannot block the current thread from within a runtime block_on inside async
there is no reactor running async call outside a runtime

Clippy lints worth fixing immediately

Lint Meaning
needless_borrow &x where x works
redundant_clone a clone whose result is never used distinctly
clone_on_copy .clone() on a Copy type
ptr_arg &Vec<T> in a signature — use &[T]
manual_map / manual_flatten an iterator method exists
single_char_pattern split(", ") vs split(',')
unwrap_used a panic in library code
large_enum_variant one variant much bigger — box it
needless_collect collecting into a Vec only to iterate
derivable_impls a hand-written Default that derive covers

Reading a long error

  1. Read the error code and the first line — that is the category.
  2. Read the help: block — it is usually the fix.
  3. Read the note: block — it explains the rule you broke.
  4. Only then look at the code frame, and look at both locations it points to.
  5. If it is a macro error, run cargo expand to see the real code.

Nine times out of ten, the compiler has already told you the answer in help:.

03 · Interview Questions with Answers

Grouped by depth. The answers are the short version you would actually say out loud; each points at the module with the detail.

Fundamentals

What are the three ownership rules?

Every value has exactly one owner; there is only one owner at a time; when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped. Together they give memory safety without a garbage collector.

What is the difference between &T and &mut T?

&T is a shared, read-only borrow — many may exist at once. &mut T is an exclusive borrow — exactly one, and no shared borrows may coexist. The exclusivity is what makes data races impossible to express.

Why can't you have &mut and & at the same time?

Because the compiler's guarantee to a &mut holder is "nobody else can observe this value". Without it, &mut could not be optimised or safely sent across threads.

What does the borrow checker actually check?

That every reference is valid for its whole use (no dangling), and that aliasing-plus-mutation never happens simultaneously. It does this with lifetimes, which are regions of code, not runtime values.

When do you need explicit lifetimes?

When the compiler cannot infer which input a returned reference derives from — typically a function with two or more reference inputs returning a reference, or a struct storing a reference.

String vs &str?

String owns a heap buffer and is growable. &str is a borrowed view (pointer + length) into UTF-8 owned by someone else. Take &str in parameters; return String when you must allocate.

Why can't you index a String with s[0]?

Because a String is UTF-8 and there is no single obvious meaning for "element 0" — byte 0, code point 0, or grapheme 0 all differ. Use chars(), bytes(), or s.get(0..n) which returns Option.

Option<T> vs null?

Option is an enum in the type system: the compiler forces you to handle None. There is no implicit null, no NullPointerException, and Option<&T> costs nothing extra thanks to niche optimisation.

Type system

impl Trait vs dyn Trait?

impl Trait is static dispatch — monomorphised per type, inlined, zero cost, but cannot hold heterogeneous values. dyn Trait is a fat pointer with a vtable — one indirect call, one copy of the code, works in a Vec<Box<dyn Trait>>.

What is monomorphisation, and its downside?

Generics are compiled once per concrete type, which is why they are fast. The costs are binary size and compile time.

What makes a trait object-safe?

No generic methods, no methods returning Self, no associated constants. Anything that would require knowing the concrete type at the call site breaks the vtable.

Associated type vs generic parameter?

An associated type allows exactly one implementation per type (Iterator::Item). A generic parameter allows several (Add<i32> and Add<f64>).

What does Sized mean, and why ?Sized?

Sized means the size is known at compile time. str, [T] and dyn Trait are unsized, so a generic taking them by value needs ?Sized and a reference.

Why can't you implement a foreign trait for a foreign type?

The orphan rule: at least one of the trait or the type must be local to your crate. It prevents two crates from providing conflicting impls.

Memory and pointers

Box vs Rc vs Arc?

Box is unique ownership with one heap allocation. Rc is reference-counted sharing on one thread (non-atomic counter). Arc is the atomic version, safe across threads, ~10–20× more expensive to clone.

When do you need RefCell?

When you must mutate through a shared reference and cannot express it with the compile-time borrow checker — e.g. a graph or an observer list. Borrows are checked at runtime and panic on violation.

What is interior mutability, and its cost?

Mutating through &T using Cell/RefCell/Mutex/atomics. Cell is free; RefCell costs a runtime flag check; Mutex costs a lock.

How do you leak memory in safe Rust?

Create an Rc cycle. Two Rcs pointing at each other never reach zero. Break it with Weak.

What is Drop, and when does it run?

A destructor trait, run when the owner goes out of scope, in reverse declaration order, including during unwinding from a panic. It is why RAII works for locks, files and transactions.

Concurrency

Send vs Sync?

Send: the value can be moved to another thread. Sync: &T can be shared between threads. Rc is neither; Arc<T> is both when T: Send + Sync.

How does Rust prevent data races?

A data race needs two threads, one writing, no synchronisation. That requires &mut accessible from two threads, or a shared borrow alongside a mutation — both forbidden. Send/Sync extend the argument across thread boundaries.

Mutex<T> vs RwLock<T>?

Mutex allows one accessor of any kind; RwLock allows many readers or one writer. RwLock only wins when reads dominate and critical sections are long enough for contention to matter.

What is mutex poisoning?

If a thread panics while holding the lock, the mutex is marked poisoned and later lock() calls return Err. into_inner() on the error recovers the data.

Threads vs async — when each?

Threads for CPU-bound work and a small number of long-running tasks; async for many concurrent I/O waits. Async multiplexes waiting; it does not speed up computation.

What does async fn return, and when does it run?

A Future — a state machine. Nothing runs until something polls it (.await or a runtime).

Why must futures be Pinned?

A future's states may contain references into itself. Moving it after polling would invalidate those references, so Pin guarantees a stable address.

What happens when you select! and one branch loses?

The losing future is dropped, which is cancellation. If it was mid-operation, you can get a partial write — which is why non-cancellable work should be spawned.

Errors and API design

panic! vs Result?

panic! is for programmer errors and violated invariants. Result is for expected failures the caller can act on. "File not found" is a Result; "index out of bounds in code that checked the length" is a panic.

thiserror vs anyhow?

thiserror derives a typed error enum for libraries — callers can match on variants. anyhow is a boxed dynamic error with context for applications. Never expose anyhow in a public library API.

Why #[non_exhaustive] on a public error enum?

So you can add variants without a breaking change, since downstream matches are not exhaustive.

Why should a handler return a generic message on 5xx?

To avoid leaking internals (SQL text, file paths, stack frames) to a client. Log the real error server-side.

What is a smart constructor?

A fn parse(...) -> Result<Email, Error> that validates and returns a newtype. It makes invalid states unrepresentable: any Email in the type system is valid.

Performance

Why are iterators as fast as loops?

After inlining, the iterator chain becomes the same machine code, minus the bounds checks that the compiler can now prove unnecessary.

What are zero-cost abstractions here, and which are not?

Free: iterators, generics, newtypes, Option<&T>. Not free: dyn dispatch, Box/Rc/Arc, format!, RefCell, clone().

How would you find a performance problem?

Profile first: perf or cargo flamegraph, or samply for async. Find the widest leaf frame. Only then change code, and re-measure with criterion.

When is clone() the wrong answer?

When it hides a design problem — usually a function that should borrow instead of own, or a struct that should hold an Arc.

What is the biggest single performance win available?

Choosing the right algorithm and data structure. HashSet instead of a linear scan is 1000×; no compiler flag competes.

Ecosystem and practice

How do you structure a large Rust project?

A workspace with a domain crate that has no I/O (fast tests, stable API), plus api and worker binaries. Logic in lib.rs, main.rs thin.

What does cargo clippy -D warnings in CI buy you?

A consistent floor of idiom and a class of bugs caught before review — redundant_clone, ptr_arg, large_enum_variant, unwrap_used.

How do you test an HTTP handler without a network?

app.oneshot(request) with tower::ServiceExt. It runs routing, extractors, middleware and error mapping in-process.

How do you handle schema changes safely?

Migrations that are additive and reversible: add nullable columns, backfill, then constrain. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY for large tables. Never edit an applied migration — checksums will reject it.

Why commit Cargo.lock for a binary?

Reproducible builds. cargo build --locked in CI then fails if a dependency would change, which is exactly the alert you want.

Questions to ask them

A good signal in an interview is asking about the hard parts:

  • What is your compile time, and what have you done about it?
  • Where does async hurt you most?
  • How do you handle the Send + 'static boundary in spawned tasks?
  • Do you use unsafe anywhere, and how is it reviewed?
  • What is your policy on adding dependencies?

04 · A 30-Day Study Plan

Two hours a day for 30 days gets you from zero to shipping a Rust service. The plan assumes you code every day — reading alone does not work for this language.

How to use it

  • 60% typing, 40% reading. Type the examples; do not paste them.
  • Every day ends with something that compiles. No day is purely conceptual.
  • Keep a notes.md of every compiler error you hit and how you fixed it. By day 30 it is the most useful document you own.
  • Do not skip day 9. Ownership is the hinge the whole language turns on.

Week 1 — Language basics

Day Topic Read Build
1 Toolchain, cargo 01.01, 01.02 Install, cargo new, run hello world
2 Variables, types 02.01 A temperature converter; hit an overflow in debug and release
3 Functions, control flow 02.02 FizzBuzz, then an expression evaluator
4 Structs, enums 02.04 A Shape enum with area() and Display
5 Pattern matching 02.04 A config parser with typed values
6 Collections 02.06 Word-frequency counter over a real text file
7 Review + exercises — Redo every exercise from days 2–6

Week 2 — The hard core

Day Topic Read Build
8 Ownership 02.03 Deliberately trigger E0382, E0502, E0499; write down each fix
9 Borrowing + lifetimes 02.03 longest_word, split_kv, a Line<'a> view type
10 Traits 02.05 A Repository trait with two implementations
11 Generics 02.05 Generic largest, then make it work for &str
12 Error handling 02.07 A CLI with thiserror in a lib and anyhow in the bin
13 Modules 02.08 Split a single-file program into lib.rs + modules + a second binary
14 Review — Refactor your day-12 CLI: no unwrap(), &[T] not &Vec<T>

Week 3 — Ecosystem and real code

Day Topic Read Build
15 Testing 03.03 Unit + integration + doc tests for the day-12 CLI
16 Smart pointers 02.09 Rc<RefCell<T>> tree; break a cycle with Weak
17 Threads 02.10 Bounded worker pool with thread::scope
18 rayon 02.10 Parallel word count; measure the speedup
19 Cargo in depth 03.01 Add profiles, a workspace, sccache; measure build time
20 Clippy + fmt + CI 03.04 Get clippy -D warnings green; add a GitHub Actions workflow
21 CLI tool 04.01 clap tool with subcommands, exit codes, assert_cmd tests

Week 4 — Async and a real service

Day Topic Read Build
22 Async basics 02.11 join! vs sequential; measure the difference
23 Async pitfalls 02.11 Reproduce a blocked executor, then fix it
24 Axum 04.02 Two routes, a JSON handler, an error type with IntoResponse
25 SQLx 04.03 A migration, query_as!, and a sqlx::test integration test
26 Auth + validation 04.02 A FromRequestParts extractor and a validated newtype
27 Background jobs 04.04 The Postgres queue: claim, complete, fail, retry
28 Observability 03.06 tracing with JSON, /healthz, /readyz, /metrics
29 Capstone 05.01–05.02 Wire the API together end to end
30 Ship it 05.04 Multi-stage Docker image, Compose stack, graceful shutdown

The daily loop

$ cargo new day_07 --bin
$ cd day_07
$ cargo add ...
# write code
$ cargo check          # constantly
$ cargo clippy -- -D warnings
$ cargo fmt
$ cargo test

Ten minutes at the end of each day: write down what surprised you. That is where the learning consolidates.

Milestones to check yourself against

After You should be able to
Day 7 Write a 100-line program with structs, enums and a HashMap
Day 14 Explain every borrow error you hit, and fix it without clone()
Day 21 Ship a CLI tool with tests, CI and a release binary
Day 30 Deploy a small async service with a database, a queue and metrics

If you have less time

A compressed 10-day version, keeping only the load-bearing parts:

  1. 01.02 + 02.01 + 02.02 — get productive
  2. 02.03 — ownership (do not compress this one)
  3. 02.04 + 02.06 — data and collections

  5. 02.07 — errors
  6. 03.03 — testing

Common ways people stall

Stall Fix
Fighting the borrow checker for days Re-read 02.03, then write the smallest reproducing example and ask "who owns this?"
Copying code without typing it Type it. The muscle memory is the point
Avoiding async because it is confusing Do day 22. It clicks after you break it once
Trying to build a huge project on day 3 Build small things that finish
Reading three books and writing no code One book, and code every day
Giving up at the first Pin error Nobody understands Pin on day one. Skip it, come back

Finding crates

Site Use
crates.io the registry
docs.rs rendered docs for every crate and version — your default reference
lib.rs curated, categorised, better discovery than crates.io
blessed.rs opinionated "use this one" recommendations per domain
Are we web yet? web ecosystem status
Are we game yet? gamedev ecosystem status
Are we embedded yet? embedded status

blessed.rs is the fastest way to stop wondering which of five HTTP clients to pick.

Tools to install

cargo install cargo-watch        # rebuild on save
cargo install cargo-expand       # see macro output
cargo install cargo-nextest      # faster tests
cargo install cargo-llvm-cov     # coverage
cargo install cargo-audit        # vulnerabilities
cargo install cargo-deny         # licenses, duplicates, advisories
cargo install cargo-mutants      # does your test suite test anything?
cargo install cargo-flamegraph   # profiling
cargo install cargo-semver-checks
cargo install cargo-zigbuild     # painless cross-compilation
cargo install sccache            # shared compile cache
cargo install trunk              # wasm app bundler
cargo install wasm-pack          # wasm npm packaging
cargo install sqlx-cli           # migrations
cargo install tokio-console      # async task inspector
cargo install samply             # profiler with a UI
cargo install --locked bacon      # background cargo check with a TUI

bacon deserves a mention: it watches your project and shows errors in a pane while you type. It changes how the edit-compile loop feels.

Communities

Where Culture
Rust Discord fast help, #beginners is welcoming
users.rust-lang.org slower, higher-quality answers
r/rust news and discussion
Rust Zulip language development, for contributors
Local meetups search "Rust" + your city; most are beginner-friendly

How to ask a good question: post the code, the full error, and what you tried. Better: post a minimal reproducible example — building it usually solves the problem before you post.

Conferences and talks

  • RustConf (US, annual) — talks on YouTube
  • Rust Nation UK (London)
  • EuroRust (rotating European city)
  • Rust India and regional meetups
  • Rust Belt Rust, RustFest (historically)

The production-experience talks are the most useful: what broke, what they measured, what they would do differently.

Learning by reading code

The fastest way to write idiomatic Rust is to read good Rust. In rough order of accessibility:

Project Why read it
ripgrep clean CLI + high-performance internals
fd small, readable, excellent clap usage
bat terminal output done well
serde the derive-macro architecture
axum extractors and tower integration
tokio the executor and runtime internals (hard)
polars large-scale data engineering in Rust
hyperfine small, well-tested CLI
alacritty a real application, not a library
rust-analyzer a huge codebase doing real compiler work

Start with fd — it is small enough to read in an afternoon and idiomatic throughout.

Anti-resources

Honest list of things that waste time:

  • Tutorials that predate 2021. Editions changed use paths, closures and IntoIterator; pre-2018 tutorials will actively mislead you.
  • Copy-pasting from Stack Overflow answers older than the crate version you use. Check the date and the crate version in the answer.
  • Trying to learn unsafe, Pin and macros in week one. They are advanced for a reason.
  • Rewriting a C library "to learn Rust". Pick something you actually want to exist.
  • Benchmarking without --release. You will conclude Rust is slow.

The one-paragraph summary

Read The Book once, type everything. Then read Rust for Rustaceans. Then build something real, and read docs.rs for every crate you touch. Ask in users.rust-lang.org when you are stuck for more than 30 minutes. Read fd's source. That path, in that order, is the fastest one that actually works.
